Your job is to read a daily conversation log\nand extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.\n\n## Schema (AGENTS.md)\n\n# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema\n\n> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.\n> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.\n\n## The Compiler Analogy\n\n```\ndaily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)\nLLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)\nknowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)\nlint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)\nqueries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)\n```\n\nYou don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.\n\n---\n\n## Architecture\n\n### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)\n\nDaily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the \"raw sources\" - append-only, never edited after the fact.\n\n```\ndaily/\n├── 2026-04-01.md\n├── 2026-04-02.md\n├── ...\n```\n\nEach file follows this format:\n\n```markdown\n# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD\n\n## Sessions\n\n### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title\n\n**Context:** What the user was working on.\n\n**Key Exchanges:**\n- User asked about X, assistant explained Y\n- Decided to use Z approach because...\n- Discovered that W doesn't work when...\n\n**Decisions Made:**\n- Chose library X over Y because...\n- Architecture: went with pattern Z\n\n**Lessons Learned:**\n- Always do X before Y to avoid...\n- The gotcha with Z is that...\n\n**Action Items:**\n- [ ] Follow up on X\n- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits\n```\n\n### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)\n\nThe LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.\n\n```\nknowledge/\n├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary\n├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log\n├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles\n├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts\n└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)\n```\n\n### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)\n\nThe schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the \"compiler specification.\"\n\n---\n\n## Structural Files\n\n### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog\n\nA table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.\n\nFormat:\n\n```markdown\n# Knowledge Base Index\n\n| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |\n|---------|---------|---------------|---------|\n| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |\n| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |\n```\n\n### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log\n\nAppend-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.\n\nFormat:\n\n```markdown\n# Build Log\n\n## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01\n- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md\n- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]\n- Articles updated: (none)\n\n## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | \"How do I handle auth redirects?\"\n- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]\n- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]\n```\n\n---\n\n## Article Formats\n\n### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)\n\nOne article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.\n\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Concept Name\"\naliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]\ntags: [domain, topic]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-01.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-04-03.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-01\nupdated: 2026-04-03\n---\n\n# Concept Name\n\n[2-4 sentence core explanation]\n\n## Key Points\n\n- [Bullet points, each self-contained]\n\n## Details\n\n[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup\n- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session\n```\n\n### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)\n\nCross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.\n\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Connection: X and Y\"\nconnects:\n  - \"concepts/concept-x\"\n  - \"concepts/concept-y\"\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-04.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-04\nupdated: 2026-04-04\n---\n\n# Connection: X and Y\n\n## The Connection\n\n[What links these concepts]\n\n## Key Insight\n\n[The non-obvious relationship discovered]\n\n## Evidence\n\n[Specific examples from conversations]\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/concept-x]]\n- [[concepts/concept-y]]\n```\n\n### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)\n\nFiled answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.\n\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Q: Original Question\"\nquestion: \"The exact question asked\"\nconsulted:\n  - \"concepts/article-1\"\n  - \"concepts/article-2\"\nfiled: 2026-04-05\n---\n\n# Q: Original Question\n\n## Answer\n\n[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]\n\n## Sources Consulted\n\n- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...\n- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...\n\n## Follow-Up Questions\n\n- What about edge case X?\n- How does this change if Y?\n```\n\n---\n\n## Core Operations\n\n### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)\n\nWhen processing a daily log:\n\n1. Read the daily log file\n2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state\n3. Read existing articles that may need updating\n4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:\n   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source\n   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article\n5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article\n6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries\n7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`\n\n**Important guidelines:**\n- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles\n- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates\n- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/\n- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained\n- Every article must have YAML frontmatter\n- Every article must link back to its source daily logs\n\n### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)\n\n1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)\n2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index\n3. Read those articles in full\n4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations\n5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md\n\n**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.\n\n### 3. Lint (Health Checks)\n\nSeven checks, run periodically:\n\n1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles\n2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles\n3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet\n4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled\n5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)\n6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A\n7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete\n\nOutput: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).\n\n---\n\n## Conventions\n\n- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension\n- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate\n- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)\n- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)\n- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated\n- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article\n\n---\n\n## Full Project Structure\n\n```\nllm-personal-kb/\n|-- .claude/\n|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)\n|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches\n|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference\n|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start\n|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)\n|-- daily/                           # \"Source code\" - conversation logs (immutable)\n|-- knowledge/                       # \"Executable\" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)\n|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism\n|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log\n|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles\n|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts\n|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)\n|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools\n|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles\n|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)\n|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks\n|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)\n|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants\n|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers\n|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks\n|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session\n|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log\n|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction\n|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)\n```\n\n---\n\n## Hook System (Automatic Capture)\n\nHooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.\n\n### `.claude/settings.json` Format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"hooks\": {\n    \"SessionStart\": [{ \"matcher\": \"\", \"hooks\": [{ \"type\": \"command\", \"command\": \"uv run python hooks/session-start.py\", \"timeout\": 15 }] }],\n    \"PreCompact\": [{ \"matcher\": \"\", \"hooks\": [{ \"type\": \"command\", \"command\": \"uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py\", \"timeout\": 10 }] }],\n    \"SessionEnd\": [{ \"matcher\": \"\", \"hooks\": [{ \"type\": \"command\", \"command\": \"uv run python hooks/session-end.py\", \"timeout\": 10 }] }]\n  }\n}\n```\n\nCommands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.\n\n### Hook Details\n\n**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)\n- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second\n- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log\n- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{\"hookSpecificOutput\": {\"hookEventName\": \"SessionStart\", \"additionalContext\": \"...\"}}`\n- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session\n- Max context: 20,000 characters\n\n**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)\n- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)\n- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)\n- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process\n- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set\n\n**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)\n- Same architecture as session-end.py\n- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window\n- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)\n- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it\n\n**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.\n\n### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)\n\nSpawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:\n- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags\n- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`\n\nThis ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.\n\n**What flush.py does:**\n1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)\n2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file\n3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)\n4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)\n5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`\n6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`\n7. Cleans up temp context file\n8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.\n\n### JSONL Transcript Format\n\nClaude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:\n\n```python\nentry = json.loads(line)\nmsg = entry.get(\"message\", {})\nrole = msg.get(\"role\", \"\")     # \"user\" or \"assistant\"\ncontent = msg.get(\"content\", \"\")  # string or list of content blocks\n```\n\nContent can be a string or a list of blocks (`{\"type\": \"text\", \"text\": \"...\"}` dicts).\n\n---\n\n## Script Details\n\n### compile.py - The Compiler\n\nUses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:\n\n```python\nasync for message in query(\n    prompt=compile_prompt,\n    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(\n        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),\n        system_prompt={\"type\": \"preset\", \"preset\": \"claude_code\"},\n        allowed_tools=[\"Read\", \"Write\", \"Edit\", \"Glob\", \"Grep\"],\n        permission_mode=\"acceptEdits\",\n        max_turns=30,\n    ),\n):\n```\n\n- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log\n- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly\n- `permission_mode=\"acceptEdits\"` auto-approves all file operations\n- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files\n- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)\n\n**CLI:**\n```bash\nuv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only\nuv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything\nuv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md\nuv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run\n```\n\n### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval\n\nLoads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.\n\nAt personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.\n\n**CLI:**\n```bash\nuv run python scripts/query.py \"What auth patterns do I use?\"\nuv run python scripts/query.py \"What's my error handling strategy?\" --file-back\n```\n\nWith `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.\n\n### lint.py - Health Checks\n\nSeven checks:\n\n| Check | Type | Catches |\n|-------|------|---------|\n| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |\n| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |\n| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |\n| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |\n| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |\n| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |\n| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |\n\n**CLI:**\n```bash\nuv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks\nuv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)\n```\n\nReports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.\n\n---\n\n## State Tracking\n\n`scripts/state.json` tracks:\n- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs\n- `query_count` - total queries run\n- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint\n- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost\n\n`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).\n\nBoth are gitignored and regenerated automatically.\n\n---\n\n## Dependencies\n\n`pyproject.toml` (at project root):\n- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use\n- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management\n- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data\n- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)\n\nNo API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.\n\n---\n\n## Costs\n\n| Operation | Cost |\n|-----------|------|\n| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |\n| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |\n| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |\n| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |\n| Structural lint only | $0.00 |\n| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |\n\n---\n\n## Customization\n\n### Additional Article Types\n\nAdd directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.\n\n### Obsidian Integration\n\nThe knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.\n\n### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval\n\nAt ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.\n\n\n## Current Wiki Index\n\n# Knowledge Base Index\n\n| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |\n|---------|---------|---------------|---------|\n| [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] | /doctor diagnostics, plugin cache versioning migration, MCP re-auth, compound-engineering plugin, GitHub MCP vs gh CLI, and Fable 5 + advisor incompatibility (opus-4-8 disabled) | 2026-06-10.md, 2026-04-14.md, 2026-06-03.md, 2026-06-09.md | 2026-06-16 |\n| [[concepts/custom-claude-code-skills]] | Three new skills (web-scraping, ingest-resource, improve-system) built for the SecondBrain vault; plus git update-index --refresh as non-destructive resolution for CRLF phantom diffs | 2026-05-22.md, 2026-06-17.md | 2026-06-17 |\n\n\n## Existing Wiki Articles\n\n### concepts\\accidental-git-init-home-directory.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Accidental Git Init at Home Directory Root\"\naliases: [phantom VS Code changes, home directory git init, accidental git init, empty .git folder, 10k phantom changes]\ntags: [git, vscode, windows, gotcha, configuration, source-control]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-20.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-20\nupdated: 2026-05-20\n---\n\n# Accidental Git Init at Home Directory Root\n\nOn 2026-05-20, a VS Code instance showed 10,000+ pending changes in its source control panel. The root cause was an accidental `git init` run at `C:\\Users\\eric_rash\\` (the home directory root), causing git to treat the entire user profile as an untracked repository. Because the resulting `.git` folder was completely empty — no commits, no stashes, no refs, no remote — deleting it was safe and immediately resolved the phantom change count.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- An accidental `git init` at the home directory root causes every file in the user profile to appear as untracked/uncommitted changes in VS Code and any git-aware tool that walks upward looking for a `.git` folder.\n- Tools such as VS Code's source control panel and `git status` traverse parent directories to find the nearest `.git`; a folder at `~/.git` will be found by any git invocation from anywhere under the user profile, overriding project-level repositories.\n- An empty `.git` (bare skeleton only — no commits, no `COMMIT_EDITMSG`, no `packed-refs`, no remote) is safe to delete outright without losing any work.\n- Diagnostic check: inspect the `.git` directory for refs, a `COMMIT_EDITMSG`, or a `packed-refs` file; absence of all three confirms a no-op init.\n- Always verify the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) when seeing unexpectedly large or nonsensical change counts in source control panels before taking any remediation action.\n\n## Details\n\nThe 10,000+ phantom change count appeared immediately when VS Code opened, before any project edits were made — the signature pattern of a home-directory `git init`. VS Code's built-in Git extension walks upward from the workspace root to find the nearest `.git` folder; a `.git` at the home directory root satisfies that search for every workspace opened anywhere under the user profile, masking the project-level `.git` folders that should govern each individual repository.\n\nThe safe deletion procedure is: (1) confirm `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` returns the home directory, not a project subdirectory; (2) inspect the `.git` folder contents to verify the init produced nothing (no commits, no stash, no remotes); (3) delete `C:\\Users\\<username>\\.git` (or `~/.git` on Mac/Linux). After deletion, VS Code's source control panel returns to normal, correctly treating each project's own `.git` as an independent repository. The root cause is most often a terminal session that was run from `~` by accident before `cd`-ing into a project, followed by a `git init` typed from memory.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — Broader pattern of diagnosing and resolving configuration-drift issues in development environments; the accidental git init is another class of environment misconfiguration that produces misleading tool output at scale.\n- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — Confirming the `.git` folder was genuinely empty before deleting exemplifies the same direct-verification discipline: inspect the actual state rather than acting on what a large change count implies.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-20.md]] — Diagnosis and deletion session (12:25): phantom change root cause, empty `.git` folder confirmation, and safe deletion.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\applied-performance-okr-system.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Applied Performance Unit OKR System\"\naliases: [Applied Performance OKRs, performance unit OKRs, OKR operating cadence, Applied Performance KRs, AJ Blake OKR co-ownership, Applied-Performance-Hub, Thursday check-in, OKR staff meeting, first Thursday rollout]\ntags: [productivity, okr, baylor-athletics, applied-performance, project-management, leadership]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-01.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-04.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-01\nupdated: 2026-06-04\n---\n\n# Applied Performance Unit OKR System\n\nOn 2026-06-01, a complete OKR system for the Applied Performance unit was materialized into the SecondBrain Obsidian vault as a hub note (`Projects/Applied-Performance-Hub.md`) plus four project notes. The design process resolved four key architectural decisions — framing, statistical thresholds, content constraints, and audience philosophy — and produced a locked 11-slide running order built around a single-athlete RTP narrative with minimal text and strong visual anchors. A subsequent validation pass confirmed all slides were layout-clean and fixed a dark-mode visibility bug on the final slide.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Single-athlete framing throughout:** roster-comparison views were explicitly rejected as \"off-topic for the individual RTP framing.\" The presentation's decision-support narrative only holds together when the audience follows one athlete's trajectory from injury through return-to-competition decisions. Adding a roster view introduces a different clinical use case that fragments narrative coherence.\n- **Visual-first audience philosophy:** the intended audience \"eats with their eyes\" — conversational delivery carries the explanatory load while slides provide visual anchors, not text. Minimal text per slide; strong imagery and color-coded indicators are the design primitives.\n- **Z-score traffic-light thresholds: −1.5 SD / −2 SD.** Applied in the Excel demo to translate raw metrics into actionable status flags. −1.5 SD = caution/yellow; −2 SD = concern/red. The leave-behind template implements the same logic, ensuring the presentation and the artifact practitioners actually use share the same statistical foundation.\n- **Screenshots-only (no live build):** consistent with the leave-behind template format. All data visualization examples appear as screenshots rather than live-built charts, eliminating technical failure risk in a conference setting.\n- **11-slide running order:** bridge → decision-first framing (×2) → generalizing → metric selection → blank template → populated/flagged → charted → stakeholder report → take-home materials → close.\n- **Slide 9 — Sample Stakeholder Report:** single-athlete trend chart + color-coded status flag + one plain-language interpretive line. Models the exact artifact the audience would produce and deliver to coaching/medical staff, completing the \"here is the workflow\" → \"here is the output\" arc.\n- **Josse referenced verbally only (not on-screen):** a named methodological reference was kept off slides for sensitivity reasons; verbal attribution suffices for academic credentialing without creating a circulating visual artifact.\n- **Slide validation (Session 23:56):** All 11 slides confirmed layout-clean at 1440×900 and 375×667. Synthetic keyboard event dispatch (`keydown`) is unreliable for slide navigation in browser automation — smooth-scroll does not complete on synthetic key events in browser extension automation contexts. Use direct navigation-dot element clicks for reliable automated HTML slide deck validation.\n- **Dark-background slides require adaptive nav chrome:** Slide 11 uses a dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`); the default nav-dot and slide-counter colors (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`) are invisible against it. Fix: an `on-dark` CSS class toggled on `<body>` by the `setActive()` JavaScript function enables CSS overrides for nav elements on dark slides. This pattern generalizes to any HTML slide deck with alternating light/dark slide backgrounds.\n\n## Details\n\nThe presentation's core design challenge is bridging the gap between analytical rigor and practitioner legibility for a mixed audience of sports scientists, athletic trainers, and coaches. A talk that leads with methodology (sensor setup, reliability coefficients, statistical assumptions) loses practitioners in the first two minutes; a talk that shows only colored flags without any basis loses the sports scientists. The \"decision-first framing (×2)\" in the running order addresses this: the talk opens with the end product — the practitioner's decision — and only then traces backward to the analytical workflow that supports it. The repetition reinforces the framing before technical detail begins.\n\nThe z-score threshold design (−1.5 / −2 SD) was chosen for the Excel demo because it is transferable: any clinician working with any monitoring dataset can understand and apply standard deviation cutoffs without statistical training beyond \"how far from the average.\" The traffic-light metaphor (green/yellow/red) maps intuitively to go/caution/stop decisions without requiring the audience to interpret numbers directly. The leave-behind template implements the same −1.5 / −2 SD thresholds automatically, so practitioners who use it after the session are working with the same statistical logic demonstrated in the talk — reducing drift toward arbitrary threshold modification post-session.\n\nSlide 9's stakeholder report design was added specifically to address the \"so what do I hand to the coach/AT?\" question that sports scientists routinely face after building a monitoring pipeline. The three-element structure (trend chart + status flag + one interpretive sentence) is the minimum viable stakeholder report: more complex outputs tend to go unread or generate confusion when shared with coaching staff who do not routinely interpret data visualizations. The time budget for the talk was kept deliberately soft — enriching content depth was prioritized over strict adherence to 20 minutes, on the premise that a substantive overrun is less damaging than a rushed, thin presentation for an engaged sports science audience. The frontend-slides skill was loaded after all content decisions were locked to execute the build phase.\n\nFollowing the content design session (20:28), a validation pass (Session 23:56) confirmed all 11 slides rendered correctly at both standard and mobile viewport sizes. The initial browser automation approach used synthetic keydown events to navigate between slides — this proved unreliable because the presentation's smooth-scroll transition does not complete when triggered by a synthetic key event in browser extension automation contexts. Switching to direct navigation-dot element clicks resolved this. A dark-mode visibility bug was discovered on Slide 11, whose dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`) made both the slide counter text and the inactive navigation dots invisible in their default dark-gray color (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`). The fix uses a `setActive()` JavaScript function that toggles an `on-dark` class on the `<body>` element each time a new slide becomes active, enabling CSS rules to override counter and dot colors when on a dark-background slide. This pattern — a JS class toggle driving CSS overrides for the nav chrome — is the correct approach for HTML slide decks that mix light and dark slide backgrounds: fixed CSS color values for UI elements will fail on at least one background type, while a theme-aware JS class toggle adapts correctly to each slide's context. The same failure class was independently encountered in the Swiss Modern coaching staff deck built the same day; see [[concepts/sports-coaching-slide-design-system]] for the `box-sizing` and `file://` URL gotchas encountered during that deck's construction.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/skylar-zinnecker-cmj-rtc-reports]] — Individual RTC reports built from VALD ForceDecks data for a single athlete; shares the single-athlete framing, Baylor institutional branding, and color-coded status indicators (Exceeds Baseline / Progressing) with the stakeholder report slide design.\n- [[concepts/tezino-camp-prep-spc-monitoring]] — SPC-based monitoring dashboard with first-class explainability requirements for coaching and medical staff; shares the \"every metric needs a plain-language justification\" communication principle and threshold-based flag logic.\n- [[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]] — The dual-model (actual vs. compliant counterfactual) ACWR overlay is another athlete monitoring communication artifact designed to make statistical content interpretable for practitioners — the same decision-support framing used in the presentation.\n- [[connections/athlete-monitoring-communication-grammar]] — The cross-cutting visual vocabulary (color coding, threshold flags, trend + flag + sentence) that independently recurs across the presentation, Zinnecker reports, Tezino SPC monitoring, and the Swiss Modern coaching deck.\n- [[concepts/sports-coaching-slide-design-system]] — A parallel S&C coaching staff slide deck built the same day (Session 23:43) using the Swiss Modern preset; shares the traffic-light color constraint and HTML slide build context. The session moved from secondary-modifier composite work into full camp ramp architecture and multi-model deliverable framing, establishing an in-season GPS reference, polarized day-type targets, a work-block macro unit, and a framework for delivering 2–3 candidate models for head coach Dave Aranda to choose from. On 2026-06-08, all six candidate models were machine-validated and completed. On 2026-06-13, the missing coach-facing PDF was generated via headless Chrome and both commits were pushed to GitHub, completing the Monday-meeting deliverable package.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Anchor metric = active minutes**, not player load (which is an outcome of training rather than a planning input) and not reps (which are the practice micro-unit). All macro camp ramp targets are expressed in active minutes per day.\n- **In-season game-week GPS reference (100%):** calibrated from Baylor's own 2024/2025 GPS data. Full game week = ~370 active minutes Mon–Thu. Game day = 92 min. Day-level rhythm: Mon 69 / Tue 105 / Wed 88 / Thu 98 active minutes.\n- **Polarized day-type targets:** green 85 / yellow 112 / red 132 active minutes (non-overlapping, ~25+ min gaps between levels). Historical Baylor camps had green/yellow/red day types separated by only ~10 min — \"training monotony\" — which these targets correct by creating genuinely distinct loading stimuli per day type.\n- **Macro unit = work-blocks, not calendar weeks.** Block 1: 3 days, Block 2: 3 days, Block 3: 4 days, Block 4: 4 days, Taper, Game week. Fatigue accumulates across consecutive practice days between off/film days; block lengths (3/3/4/4) do part of the macro ramping work naturally.\n- **Six candidate models completed (2026-06-08):** 14-day vs 15-day camp length × Conservative/Moderate/Aggressive intensity — six combinations machine-validated against the GPS-calibrated targets. **Moderate 15-day is the recommended model.** Source of truth: `docs/fall-camp/2026-06-08-candidate-camp-models-v2.md`.\n- **Deliverable artifacts (as of 2026-06-13):** two HTML decks (coach toggle view + internal staff view with color coding) and two PDFs — internal/color PDF and coach-facing PDF (no traffic-light color coding, matches v1 format, generated via headless Chrome from the coach-facing HTML). Committed as `3a87fe8` (coach PDF) and `d05d83b` (doc refresh); pushed to GitHub.\n- **Peak in Block 4 (Aug 18–21):** 120% overload before taper into Mock Game (Aug 29) and Auburn opener (Sep 5). The 70/100/120 textbook ramp applies at the day level, with color following dress/tempo designations.\n- **Secondary-modifier composite closed:** reps gate the GREEN↔YELLOW boundary. Calibrated values from B1: 74%→80% overall / 75%→88% FC25.\n\n## Details\n\nThe work-block reframing is architecturally significant for how the macro ramp is calculated and communicated. Calendar weeks (Sunday-to-Saturday) cut across the actual training-stimulus structure: Fall Camp practices occur in clusters separated by off days or film-only days, and fatigue accumulates within those clusters rather than resetting at a weekly boundary. Blocks 1–4 have lengths of 3/3/4/4 practice days respectively, and this variation does part of the macro ramping work naturally — a 3-day block at the same average daily intensity as a 4-day block represents a genuinely lower total cumulative stimulus. The block-length difference is as much a design lever as the per-day targets themselves. Historical Baylor camps ran too hot too early, with cumulative load reaching approximately 180% of game-week norms in Weeks 2–3, then having to back off before players were fresh for the opener. The work-block model delays peak overload until Block 4 to structurally prevent that pattern.\n\nThe in-season game-week GPS reference provides the calibration anchor for \"100%\" — the full competitive-season baseline. All camp targets are expressed as percentages of this reference. The 100% reference (370 active minutes Mon–Thu) was derived from Baylor's own GPS data rather than from Kansas State's model: K-State is used as a structural template (periodization philosophy, block logic, color-day definitions), but all quantitative targets are calibrated to Baylor's observed game-week load from 2024 and 2025 camps. The six-model framework (14-day vs 15-day × Conservative/Moderate/Aggressive) accommodates the gap between the GPS-calibrated polarized targets (85/112/132) and the lighter bands shared at the May staff meeting (80–90/90–105/105–120): the conservative models honor the staff's prior framing while the moderate and aggressive models progressively implement the full polarized vision. The Moderate 15-day model was identified as the recommendation after machine validation confirmed it satisfies both the training-stimulus requirements and the calendar constraints of Fall Camp 2026. The coach-facing PDF generated on 2026-06-13 presents the models without traffic-light color coding, matching the v1 deck format and appropriate for direct distribution to coaching staff ahead of the Monday Aranda meeting. See [[concepts/baylor-fall-camp-practice-planning-model]] for the full domain model context (Color Triad, K-State Rosetta Stone, rep ramp, accountable periods) that this macro architecture builds on top of.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/baylor-fall-camp-practice-planning-model]] — The foundational domain model (Color Triad, K-State Rosetta Stone, rep ramp, two-currency model, B1 calibration) that this macro load architecture implements and quantifies; The session locked three critical structural decisions — the color model, the rep ramp structure, and the two-currency planning/validation split — and produced a 3-phase roadmap for delivering the model as a coach-facing tool. On 2026-06-02, the first calibration artifact was built: `scripts/extract_fc25_reps.py` extracted 74 accountable periods from FC25 historical data, initiating the B1 calibration branch, with a 14-item ordered roadmap defining the critical path to the late-June coach deliverable. On 2026-06-04, a macro load architecture session added a third planning level — active minutes as the macro anchor metric — and reframed the periodization unit from calendar weeks to work-blocks, extending the two-currency model to a three-level planning hierarchy.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **The Color Triad (Intended / Scripted / Realized):** the central architectural insight. Every practice day has three color manifestations — what the coach *intends* (the day-type plan), what gets *scripted* (the actual practice script), and what was *realized* (post-practice GPS actuals). The tool's primary job is catching drift between them.\n- **Color = single coarse composite day-type:** a practice is classified as one color (green, yellow, red, or equivalent); no shades or gradations. Yancy explicitly warned against granularity creep: \"if I give you a green-day template and you go into coach mode and over-script it, it's not a green day anymore.\"\n- **Rep ramp lives at block level:** the macro ramp across Fall Camp blocks is 88→124→152→180→taper reps. Days within a block undulate by color. This resolves the tension between MorphoCycle (weekly in-season shape) and Fall Camp (multi-week macro build).\n- **Two-currency model (session level):** plan in *reps* (counted only on accountable periods: TEAM / 7on7 / 9on7), validate in *PL/player* (existing GPS metric from Catapult). These are cleanly separated — a new rep field on accountable periods is required in the data model.\n- **Third level — active minutes (macro level, 2026-06-04):** active minutes function as the macro-ramp anchor metric, sitting above reps and PL/player. The in-season game-week GPS reference (100% = ~370 active minutes Mon–Thu) provides calibration. Polarized day-type targets: green 85 / yellow 112 / red 132 active minutes. This corrects historical Baylor camp \"training monotony\" (green/yellow/red previously only ~10 min apart).\n- **Work-blocks as macro periodization unit (2026-06-04):** fatigue accumulates across consecutive practice days between off/film days, not across calendar weeks. Block 1: 3 days / Block 2: 3 days / Block 3: 4 days / Block 4: 4 days / Taper / Game week. Block lengths (3/3/4/4) do part of the macro ramping work naturally.\n- **K-State model (the \"Rosetta Stone\"):** color is a coarse composite checklist, not a formula; ramp lives at the block level; reps counted only on accountable periods; philosophy is template + guardrails, not rigid prescription.\n- **B1 calibration initiated (2026-06-02):** `scripts/extract_fc25_reps.py` ran successfully, yielding 74 accountable periods with 8 rows flagged for human QA. Secondary-modifier composite closed (2026-06-04): reps gate GREEN↔YELLOW boundary at 74%→80% overall / 75%→88% FC25.\n\n## Details\n\nThe session on 2026-05-29 resolved a long-standing conceptual tension: Aranda's MorphoCycle is designed as a weekly in-season periodization shape, but Fall Camp is a multi-week macro build arc. During camp, a \"heavy\" day in week 1 is categorically different from a \"heavy\" day in week 3 because the accumulated load context changes. The resolution was to assign color to the *day-template* level (what pattern of work structures this day) while letting the *rep ramp* carry the macro intensity arc across blocks. The Color Triad is load-bearing for software design: Intended↔Scripted is where over-coaching failure is caught *before* the practice happens; Intended↔Realized (post-practice GPS vs. plan) maps to the existing `ComparisonChart` in the load simulator. The 3-phase delivery sequence is locked: (1) calibrate the macro camp ramp from Baylor historical data and codify day templates per color; (2) deliver day templates to coaches as a late-June artifact; (3) wire the domain model into the software simulator (B3–B7). Planning artifacts — `CONTEXT.md` and `docs/practice-planning-grill-state.md` — were committed to main as `1ab45c7` (2026-05-29).\n\nThe 2026-06-04 macro load session extended the two-currency model (reps + PL/player) to a three-level planning hierarchy: active minutes govern the macro-level ramp across blocks (how much total volume is appropriate in a 3-day vs. 4-day block, how a green day compares across weeks); reps govern session-level planning on accountable periods (the micro planning unit); PL/player governs validation (GPS actuals vs. plan). The three levels are calibrated from distinct sources: active minutes from Baylor's own GPS game-week data (2024/2025 camps); reps from the FC25 extractor and B1 calibration; PL/player from Catapult's native metric. The macro-level calibration revealed that historical Baylor camps ran too hot too early (~180% cumulative in Weeks 2–3) and that day-type differentiation was inadequate (near-identical duration for green/yellow/red). The work-block unit and polarized active-minute targets directly address both errors. A full macro load model article capturing the specific quantitative targets and multi-model deliverable approach is at [[concepts/baylor-fall-camp-macro-load-model]].\n\nThe B1 calibration work begun on 2026-06-02 represents the transition from domain-model design to empirical calibration. The `extract_fc25_reps.py` script extracts rep counts from FC25 historical practice data, counting only accountable period types (TEAM, 7on7, 9on7) consistent with the two-currency model. The 14-item roadmap written on 2026-06-02 provides an ordered critical path: making the extractor idempotent (Item 3), a user QA pass on 8 flagged rows (Item 4), and then setting color-band guardrails (Items 8–9) before building the macro calendar artifact coaches will use for planning (Item 10). On 2026-06-04, the secondary-modifier composite was closed: reps gate the GREEN↔YELLOW boundary at 74%→80% overall and 75%→88% in FC25 data. See [[concepts/fall-camp-rep-extraction-pipeline]] for the full extractor design and roadmap detail.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/baylor-fall-camp-macro-load-model]] — The 2026-06-04 macro load architecture built on top of this domain model: work-blocks, polarized day-type active-minute targets, GPS calibration, and multi-model deliverable approach.\n- Active feature development continued into May 2026, including a Projected-vs-Actual comparison view and ongoing work to reconcile the app's data model with Catapult's real-world sync behavior.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Neon (serverless Postgres) returns `practice_date` and `synced_at` columns as native JS `Date` objects rather than strings; these had to be serialized to ISO strings in the API routes before being passed to React client components.\n- The Vercel project was not yet linked, so the MCP deploy tool could not deploy directly - `npx vercel link` had to be run interactively in a separate terminal first, as a one-time prerequisite.\n- The `CATAPULT_TOKEN` value could not be pasted directly into chat (likely due to special characters); the workaround was to add it to `.env.local`, then have the assistant read the file and push the value to Vercel via the CLI.\n- A persistent dark navigation bar was added to the authenticated layout, linking to the previously-unlinked `/reference` and `/admin` pages; it is hidden on `/login` and visible on all authenticated pages. A third top-level tab, `/comparison`, was planned on 2026-05-12 to surface the new Projected-vs-Actual comparison view (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]).\n- `.vercel/` remains gitignored per standard practice (the project link itself is not committed), and `CLAUDE.md` was updated with the simulator's architecture, known gotchas, and deploy commands for future sessions.\n\n## Details\n\nThe Neon date-serialization issue is a reusable lesson beyond this one app: any Next.js project querying Neon (or other Postgres providers using the `pg`/`@neondatabase/serverless` drivers) should expect timestamp/date columns to come back as JS `Date` objects, which are not directly serializable across the server-to-client component boundary. The fix - explicitly converting these fields to ISO strings inside API routes before they reach client components - resolved the deployment-blocking error.\n\nTwo pages, the Reference Card (`/reference`) and GPS Sync (`/admin`), existed in the codebase but had no way to reach them from the UI; adding the nav bar made them discoverable. The GPS Sync panel is functionally complete but not yet useful in practice - it will only become \"live\" once Catapult has actual GPS data for the practice dates being tested, which ties this deployment to the broader, ongoing challenge of getting reliable Catapult data into Baylor Athletics' various tools. Outstanding work includes connecting GitHub auto-deploy (Vercel dashboard, Settings > Git, with root directory set to `simulator`) so future pushes to `main` deploy automatically without a manual CLI step.\n\nA month later, on 2026-05-12, development resumed with a `ComparisonChart` feature overlaying projected vs. actual practice load on `/practices/[id]/compare`, plus a confirmed plan to promote it to a top-level `/comparison` nav tab (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]). Building that chart surfaced a Catapult sync-aggregation issue - the same period type (\"1 ON 1\") appearing twice, non-adjacently, in a single practice's data - which the team chose to leave aggregated for now rather than redesign the sync model mid-season (see [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]]). This is the same recurring theme as the GPS Sync panel's dependency on Catapult data: the app's data model and Catapult's actual data don't always line up cleanly, and reconciling them is an ongoing, incremental process rather than a one-time fix.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/keystone-os-tezino-project]] - a reproducible Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) analysis pipeline for Baylor Women's Tennis was refined and finalized, producing a branded HTML report, Excel workbook, and Python script (`build_acwr.py`). The session applied two key methodological refinements — weekly-sampled ACWR smoothing and an NCAA-compliant counterfactual ramp overlay — and fixed a critical bug in how the counterfactual prescription inherited real load data.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Weekly-sampled ACWR lines** replaced noisy daily plots: the ACWR ratio is sampled at weekly cadence rather than plotted at each daily interval, producing a far more readable trend line while preserving the acute-to-chronic calculation's statistical validity.\n- **NCAA-compliant counterfactual ramp overlay (Model B):** a prescription showing what load trajectory would keep ACWR ≤1.3 through January re-entry. Parameters: ~4,200 yd/wk maintenance through break (~55% of fall norm), then ~12%/wk rebuild starting at ~4,900 yd. True compliant peak: 1.28 ACWR at Jan 16, versus the non-compliant actual trajectory's 4.00 spike.\n- **Counterfactual overlay bug:** the initial compliant ramp inherited the fall load tail (Dec 8 actual peak of 1.69) because the overlay started within the acute window. Correct approach: start the counterfactual prescription only *after* actual load clears the acute window, so the overlay represents only the hypothetical re-entry trajectory, not real historical data. This is the most reusable lesson from this build.\n- **File organization pattern:** do not assume file disappearance equals a sync issue — the user had moved files intentionally to `CRS_Project/WTN/ACWR_Analysis/`. Verify file locations before regenerating output. `build_acwr.py`'s output path was updated to the new location; the stale duplicate `CRS_Project/ACWR_Analysis/` folder was removed.\n- **Playwright screenshot placement:** screenshots from automation tools should not be saved inside OneDrive-synced project folders, which can cause sync conflicts or unwanted uploads; use scratch directories outside sync scope.\n\n## Details\n\nACWR compares the most recent week's training load (acute) against the trailing four-week average (chronic), producing a ratio that identifies elevated injury risk when it spikes above approximately 1.3 — the NCAA-recognized threshold for managing re-injury risk during return-to-play windows. The core challenge in designing a compliant return-from-break ramp is a constrained optimization: the athlete must rebuild to full training load (lower bound), cannot exceed 1.3 ACWR without elevated risk (upper bound), and the chronic window entering re-entry reflects the lower maintenance load from the break period. The ~12%/week rebuild rate represents a practical path that lifts the chronic baseline while keeping weekly acute spikes within the ceiling.\n\nThe counterfactual ramp overlay is a narrative tool for coaching staff and athletic trainers: it shows not just what happened (the actual, potentially non-compliant load trajectory), but what a compliant path would have looked like. This dual-model framing makes the policy case for deliberate load management concrete: \"a compliant ramp would have peaked at 1.28; the actual trajectory peaked at 4.00.\" The critical implementation constraint is that the counterfactual must begin only after the actual load data has cleared the acute window. Violating this constraint causes the overlay to absorb real training data into what should be a purely hypothetical projection — in this session's bug, starting the overlay too early made the compliant peak appear as 1.69 (inheriting a real Dec 8 peak) rather than the true modeled value of 1.28. This inflated baseline distorts the policy comparison and can mislead coaching staff about how achievable the compliant path is. The fix requires identifying the exact date when the most recent chunk of real load rolls off the 7-day acute window, then anchoring the counterfactual's first point there.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-deployment]] — Another Baylor Athletics data pipeline with a similar architecture: a reproducible Python script, branded HTML output, and a sports-science domain model that must handle real-world data quirks.\n- [[concepts/keystone-os-tezino-project]] — A related project that also builds sport-science readiness narratives from athlete monitoring data; the two-model (actual vs. compliant counterfactual) framing here parallels the Tezino project's intended vs. actual readiness arc across a training cycle.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-29.md]] — ACWR analysis refinement session (11:18): weekly sampling, compliant ramp design and parameters, counterfactual overlay bug discovery and fix, file organization correction.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\book-advisor-system.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Book Advisor System (Library + Persona Architecture)\"\naliases: [book advisor, library advisor, CREATING-ADVISORS.md, BookInbox, advisor acceptance test, miss-log, on-library question, off-library question, advisor persona note, cross-book convergence, Knowledge/library]\ntags: [knowledge-management, second-brain, obsidian, memsearch, llm, workflow, sports-science]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-12.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-12\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Book Advisor System (Library + Persona Architecture)\n\nThe Book Advisor System is a SecondBrain-integrated architecture for creating AI advisors grounded in specific ingested books. Each advisor is defined by two components: a persona note (scoping the advisor's domain and voice) and a set of memsearch-indexed, atomized book entries (the knowledge base). The 2026-06-12 session completed a pilot using Periodization Ch1–2 and produced a comprehensive end-to-end guide (`Knowledge/library/CREATING-ADVISORS.md`) covering the full advisor creation and operating loop.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Two-component architecture, no code changes per advisor:** a new advisor requires exactly one persona note + ingested book entries. The system is parameterized at the content layer, not the tooling layer — adding a new domain (e.g., biomechanics, nutrition) means writing a persona note and ingesting a book, not modifying any code.\n- **Acceptance test has two required checks:** (1) an on-library question must be answered with cited entries — the Periodization pilot answered a step-loading question with 5 entries (step-loading, supercompensation, fatigue-fitness 3:1); (2) an off-library question must disclose a grounding gap and refuse to answer, even when memsearch returns high scores — the pilot correctly refused a protein supplementation question despite 0.98 similarity scores.\n- **Judge grounding by entry *content*, not retrieval score:** high memsearch scores indicate topical adjacency, not prescriptive match. A 0.98 score for a protein question against a periodization library is plausible (periodization content touches energy systems and nutrient timing) but non-prescriptive. Score thresholds cannot substitute for content inspection as a grounding gate.\n- **Miss-log tracks grounding gaps for curriculum planning:** off-library disclosures are logged even when retrieval scores were high, creating an audit trail that both validates epistemic honesty and identifies topics most worth ingesting next. Recurring misses signal high-value ingestion candidates.\n- **Cross-book convergence check activates on second domain book:** when a second book in the same domain lands in `BookInbox`, a synthesis pass identifies where multiple sources agree or diverge on key points — enabling the advisor to surface convergent authority rather than single-source opinions.\n- **`CREATING-ADVISORS.md` is the canonical 8-section guide:** covers mental model, anatomy, creation workflow, curation, cost/model split, operating loop, hard-won lessons, and a checklist. Written to `Knowledge/library/CREATING-ADVISORS.md`, linked from `library/README.md`, committed, pushed, and indexed in the SecondBrain vault through commit `bf66cec`.\n\n## Details\n\nThe advisor system is designed for grounded, domain-specific knowledge retrieval rather than general-purpose question answering. The persona note establishes the advisor's identity and scope — constraining what topics it is expected to address — while the memsearch-indexed entries provide the actual knowledge substrate. Because memsearch performs semantic similarity search over atomized entries, responses can cite specific source material rather than synthesizing from parametric model knowledge. This grounding is the key architectural distinction between a book advisor and an ungrounded LLM query: the advisor's responses can be traced to specific ingested content, and the system is explicitly designed to refuse questions that fall outside the ingested corpus.\n\nThe off-library behavior is the subtler and more important design requirement. An advisor that answers off-library questions confidently — even when its retrieval scores are high — is functionally indistinguishable from a hallucinating general-purpose LLM from the user's perspective. The 2026-06-12 pilot confirmed this failure mode is real: a protein question received 0.98 memsearch scores from a periodization library because periodization content discusses energy systems and nutrient timing peripherally. Without an explicit content-inspection step after retrieval, the advisor would have answered with high-scoring but non-prescriptive entries — giving the appearance of grounded knowledge while actually extrapolating from tangential content. The miss-log records these disclosures systematically, creating a dual-purpose artifact: it validates the advisor's epistemic honesty session-by-session and accumulates a curriculum of content gaps over time. Topics that consistently miss are the topics most worth ingesting next, turning the miss-log into a demand signal for `BookInbox`.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/ingest-book-skill]] — The pipeline that populates the book advisor's knowledge base: deterministic extraction, orchestration, and Sonnet-quality atomization into memsearch-indexed entries.\n- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The underlying semantic search infrastructure the book advisor uses for retrieval; the pilot revealed that retrieval scores are not sufficient to determine advisor grounding quality and must be supplemented by content inspection.\n- [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]] — The SecondBrain vault where `Knowledge/library/CREATING-ADVISORS.md` and advisor entries live; the vault's plain-markdown, no-plugin constraint shapes the advisor system's output format.\n- [[connections/retrieval-score-vs-advisor-grounding]] — The non-obvious finding from the pilot: high retrieval scores can indicate topical adjacency without prescriptive content, making score-based grounding decisions unreliable and requiring content-level evaluation.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-12.md]] — Pilot completion session (18:08): acceptance test results (on-library 5-entry answer, off-library grounding-gap disclosure with 0.98 score), miss-log design, CREATING-ADVISORS.md 8-section guide written and pushed, vault synced through bf66cec.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\bu-cheer-summer-2026-training.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"BU Cheer Summer 2026 Training Program Deliverables\"\naliases: [BU Cheer SUM2026, Cheer/SUM2026, Box 2-Day Workout Card Template, OfficialCard.xlsm, Card_FILLED.xlsx, cheer summer training, WT formula engine, barbell codes, external link xlsm, TrainingCard, openpyxl merge regions]\ntags: [baylor-athletics, cheerleading, excel, training-program, sports-science, deliverables, python]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-05.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-05\nupdated: 2026-06-05\n---\n\n# BU Cheer Summer 2026 Training Program Deliverables\n\nOn 2026-06-05, a three-file summer training packet was built for Baylor University Cheer's Summer 2026 program in `Cheer/SUM2026/`: `TrainingCard.xlsx`, `BU_Cheer_Summer_2026_OfficialCard.xlsm`, and `Calendar.docx`. \"daily/2026-05-12.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-12\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Catapult Period Aggregation: Duplicate Non-Adjacent Periods and Sync Wording\n\nWhile debugging the [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]] on 2026-05-12, the Baylor Load Simulator's sync logic was found to mishandle a real-world Catapult quirk: the same period type can be logged twice, non-adjacently, within a single practice. The team decided to keep the existing aggregation-only sync behavior for now, and fixed a separate piece of misleading sync-status wording.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- On practice P15, Catapult recorded the period type \"1 ON 1\" twice at non-adjacent positions (the 3rd and 8th periods of the practice), but the load simulator's sync logic aggregates same-named period types into a single row, merging the two occurrences and losing chronological fidelity.\n- The same practice also produced a phantom \"9 ON 7\" period with no corresponding GPS data.\n- A \"time-adjacency heuristic\" was discussed - distinguishing \"continuation periods\" (back-to-back occurrences of the same type, which should aggregate) from \"distinct periods\" (the same type recurring later in the practice, which should be kept separate) - but the team decided to **keep the current aggregation-only behavior** for now; the practice face remains the canonical organizing structure, and this will be revisited during fall camp once more data is available.\n- UI wording was corrected: \"X periods not yet synced\" becomes \"X periods have no GPS data\" - these are meaningfully different states (sync pending vs. genuinely missing data), and the distinction matters for coaching-staff UX.\n- An optional \"lock order\" flag for hand-ordered periods was discussed as a low-urgency future feature, allowing staff to manually fix period ordering when aggregation produces confusing results.\n\n## Details\n\nThis is another instance of Catapult's actual data not matching the clean, one-period-type-per-slot model that an integration naturally assumes - but at the level of period sequencing rather than authentication or tokens (compare [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] and [[connections/catapult-token-friction-across-baylor-projects]], which document Catapult friction at the credential layer). Here, Catapult's own period log for practice P15 contained \"1 ON 1\" twice, separated by several other periods, plus an apparently spurious \"9 ON 7\" period with no GPS counterpart. The sync logic's current behavior - aggregate by period-type name regardless of position - merges the two \"1 ON 1\" occurrences into a single row, which is lossy but was judged acceptable given the practice face (the planned structure of the practice) remains the canonical organizing reference.\n\nThe time-adjacency heuristic considered as an alternative would have distributed non-adjacent same-named periods into separate rows while still aggregating adjacent (\"continuation\") occurrences - a more chronologically faithful model, but one requiring more practice data to validate before committing to it. Deferring this until fall camp (when significantly more practice data will be available) reflects a \"ship the simple version now, revisit with more data later\" approach consistent with other incremental decisions on this project, such as the single-metric scope chosen for [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]. Separately, the \"not yet synced\" -> \"no GPS data\" wording fix addresses a distinct UX issue: a period showing \"not yet synced\" implies a sync will eventually happen, whereas a period with genuinely no GPS match (like the phantom \"9 ON 7\") never will - conflating the two states was misleading to coaching staff reading the UI.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]] - The comparison chart feature whose development surfaced this Catapult sync-aggregation issue.\n- [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] - A broader local reference for Catapult's API, documenting other Catapult data/credential quirks at a different layer (auth/tokens vs. period sequencing here).\n- [[connections/catapult-friction-spans-auth-and-data-layers]] - Places this period-ordering issue alongside Catapult's token-layer friction as part of a broader pattern of Catapult data diverging from naive integration assumptions.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-12.md]] - Sync debugging and aggregation-policy discussion (16:40).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-ai-skill-porting.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Porting Skills from claude.ai Web UI to Local ~/.claude/skills/\"\naliases: [claude.ai skill scraping, /customize/skills, skill porting, web UI skill extraction, Playwright skill scrape, five-slides-generator Marp, pbir-report-builder, everything-search skill, articulation-skill, skill-evaluator]\ntags: [claude-code, skills, automation, tooling, playwright, workflow]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-28.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-28\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Porting Skills from claude.ai Web UI to Local ~/.claude/skills/\n\nOn 2026-05-28, eight personal skills authored in the claude.ai web UI were ported to the local `~/.claude/skills/` directory for use inside Claude Code. Because the web UI does not provide a bulk export mechanism, skills were extracted individually via Playwright browser automation. Only the `SKILL.md` content is recoverable from the web UI — supporting files (scripts, reference templates, JSON schemas) are not downloadable and must be recreated separately.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Extraction method:** navigate to `claude.ai/customize/skills`, click each skill, toggle the \"Code view\" control, then extract the raw markdown from the line containers — Playwright automates this sequence reliably.\n- **Eight skills ported (2026-05-28):** `starter-design-tokens`, `starter-icp-positioning`, `starter-voice-profile`, `five-slides-generator`, `articulation-skill`, `skill-evaluator`, `pbir-report-builder`, `everything-search`. Two web-UI skills were skipped — `skill-creator` and `mcp-builder` — because local plugin versions already covered their functionality.\n- **Supporting files are not recoverable from the web UI:** `pbir-report-builder/references/json-templates/*`, `skill-evaluator/scripts/*.py`, and `everything-search/scripts/search.py` are referenced in the corresponding `SKILL.md` files but are not accessible through the web UI scrape. These files must be recreated from scratch if running the skills locally.\n- **Naming collision strategy:** use a `-web` suffix on skills whose name conflicts with an existing local skill (e.g., `five-slides-generator-web`). No conflicts occurred in the 2026-05-28 batch.\n- **Keep references lean:** skill reference directories should contain only files that `SKILL.md` actually cites. Binary formats (`.pptx`, `.docx`) were explicitly excluded — `5_Sides_Content_Templates.docx` was converted to a lean `talking-points.md` extracting only the timing budget and speaker-note structure, discarding social-post and video-script templates as out-of-scope for the slide skill.\n- **Research-intent skills must not include finished examples:** skills designed to conduct fresh research (\"every statistic from web search\") should not reference completed example outputs as supporting files — doing so undermines the design intent by biasing the model toward lifting from the example rather than researching anew.\n- **Marp as optional parallel format:** the `five-slides-generator` skill was enhanced to offer Marp markdown output as an optional Step 8 format alongside the existing pptxgenjs path. The VS Code Marp extension (not the Marp CLI) is sufficient for preview and export (HTML/PDF/PPTX) via the command palette — the CLI is unnecessary when the extension is installed.\n\n## Details\n\nThe web UI extraction process works because claude.ai's `/customize/skills` page renders each skill's raw SKILL.md content in a \"Code view\" that can be read by Playwright's DOM traversal. The workflow is: authenticate to claude.ai in a Playwright-controlled browser, navigate to `/customize/skills`, click each skill tile to expand it, toggle \"Code view\" on, and collect the text from the code block. This approach is fragile against UI redesigns but reliable against the current claude.ai layout. The main practical limitation is that the extraction surfaces only the SKILL.md file — any companion files in a skill's `scripts/` or `references/` subdirectory exist only on the claude.ai server and are not served to the client during the Code view render.\n\nFor skills whose supporting files are missing after a port, the correct recovery strategy is to recreate them from the SKILL.md's instructions and examples rather than attempting any other extraction path. In practice, SKILL.md files written for the web UI are often self-contained enough that the skill functions adequately without the supporting files, but skills with heavy template or script dependencies (e.g., `pbir-report-builder` needing JSON schema templates, or `skill-evaluator` needing its Python scoring scripts) will produce degraded output or fail outright until the files are recreated. Recording which skills have missing dependencies — as action items in the daily log — is the recommended approach so the gap is not silently forgotten.\n\nThe decision to convert `.docx` to `.md` for the five-slides-generator's talking-points reference illustrates a broader principle for skill reference management: binary formats introduce format friction (requiring additional tools to read), risk content-lifting over fresh research, and are harder to diff and review in version control. Extracting only the semantically durable structure (timing budget + speaker-note conventions) from the `.docx` into a lean markdown file produced a reference that is both smaller and more useful for the skill's actual purpose.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-meta-skills-bundle]] — An earlier (2026-05-20) selective installation of skills from a zip bundle, sharing the same \"evaluate each skill for relevance and omit redundancies\" discipline applied to the web UI porting batch here.\n- [[concepts/custom-claude-code-skills]] — Three skills built from scratch on 2026-06-10 for the SecondBrain vault; the porting workflow here is complementary — bringing in existing skills from the web UI rather than authoring new ones.\n- [[concepts/printing-press-cli-slash-commands]] — The printing-press ecosystem provides another path to skill registration; the porting workflow here is a direct alternative that does not require the interactive printing-press flow.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-28.md]] — Skill porting session (16:04): Playwright extraction method, 8 skills ported, supporting-file gap identified, lean-reference and research-intent design decisions, Marp optional format addition to five-slides-generator.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-code-cli-marketplace-setup.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Claude Code CLI Marketplace Setup (cli-printing-press + GSD)\"\naliases: [cli-printing-press, get-shit-done-cc, GSD, printing-press plugin, CLI marketplace, npx skills add, thedotmack/claude-mem]\ntags: [claude-code, tooling, cli, automation, infrastructure, windows]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-13.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-13\nupdated: 2026-05-13\n---\n\n# Claude Code CLI Marketplace Setup (cli-printing-press + GSD)\n\nOn 2026-05-13, a full CLI development environment was assembled inside Claude Code on Windows: the `cli-printing-press` marketplace plugin was registered in `settings.json`, GSD (`get-shit-done-cc`) was installed globally adding 66 skills, and companion skills were installed via `npx skills add` after the default bundled sidecar path failed. Three notable maintenance passes have been documented: a 2026-06-10 session that resolved plugin cache migration, stale MCP authentications, and temp-directory accumulation; a 2026-06-03 session that diagnosed and resolved a missing `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` for the GitHub MCP plugin; and a 2026-06-09 session that switched the default model to Fable 5 and discovered that the advisor model (opus-4-8) is incompatible with Fable 5 requests. Plugins installed under the old layout fail version checks even though their skills may still work via a fallback path; the fix is to reinstall via `/plugins`.\n- Four stale `temp_github_*` directories were found in the plugins cache, left over from interrupted installs in late May/early June — safe to delete once confirmed unused. Interrupted plugin downloads can both lose a plugin's cache entry and leave orphan `temp_github_*` folders; `/plugin` reinstall + `/reload-plugins` restores the cache, and the orphan folders require manual deletion.\n- For MCP servers not actively used from Claude Code (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar), disconnecting them in claude.ai's connector settings permanently silences `/doctor` re-auth warnings and eliminates the tool-schema token overhead of loading unused MCP tool definitions each session.\n- The `compound-engineering` plugin was installed via `/plugin` and activated with `/reload-plugins`, adding `ce-*` skills/agents for planning, code review, commits, and PR workflows. `/effort` was set to \"high\" as the new session default.\n- **GitHub MCP plugin vs. `gh` CLI (2026-06-03):** the `github@claude-plugins-official` MCP plugin requires a `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable to pass `/doctor`. The advisor model (opus-4-8) is incompatible with the Fable 5 request model — requests return 400 errors — and was disabled. When switching request models, the advisor model must also be verified for compatibility or disabled; mismatched advisor+request combinations produce API errors that are not immediately obvious as a configuration conflict.\n\n## Details\n\nThe `/doctor` command acts as a quick health check across MCP connections, plugin installs, and cache state. On 2026-06-10 it caught a cache-format mismatch that was not the user's fault: a Claude Code update changed how plugins are cached on disk (from a flat directory per plugin to a versioned subdirectory), and `cli-printing-press` had been installed before that change. The plugin's files were technically present, but the version-check logic looked in the new versioned path and didn't find them — the recommended fix was simply to reinstall the plugin via `/plugins` so it lands in the new layout. The MCP re-auth findings (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar) were treated as low priority: rather than re-authenticating connectors that may not be exercised from Claude Code at all, the suggested path was to disconnect them at the source (claude.ai connector settings), which both stops the recurring `/doctor` warning and reduces the standing tool-schema footprint in every session.\n\nOn 2026-06-03, a separate `/doctor` run flagged the `github@claude-plugins-official` MCP server as invalid — specifically, no `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable was set. The two resolution options are: (1) disable the plugin entirely in `.claude/settings.json` — the simplest fix when the plugin genuinely adds no value; or (2) set `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` using an existing PAT with compatible scopes, avoiding a new token generation. In this case, `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` already existed with sufficient scopes, so `setx GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN <value>` was used. Note: `setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately but requires fully restarting VS Code for the change to propagate to the Claude Code process — see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] for the stale-environment gotcha this can trigger.\n\nOn 2026-06-09, a maintenance session switched the default model from Sonnet-tier to Fable 5 and changed effort to medium. The advisor feature, which provides secondary-model review of responses, uses a separately-specified model (opus-4-8 in this configuration). When the request model is Fable 5, the opus-4-8 advisor returns 400 API errors because the two models are incompatible in the advisor/request pairing. The advisor was disabled as a result. The lesson: model switches require verifying the full model configuration stack — not just the primary request model but also any secondary models (advisor, sub-agent defaults, tool-use overrides) that may have incompatible pairings. `/doctor` does not currently flag advisor+request model incompatibilities; the failure manifests as 400 errors at runtime rather than as a startup diagnostic. The 2026-06-09 session also confirmed the orphan `temp_github_*` cleanup pattern: these folders appear whenever a plugin download is interrupted and can safely be deleted after confirming they are not associated with any active plugin install.\n\nBoth maintenance passes confirm the same operational pattern: the `/doctor` command's value is proportional to how regularly it is run and how promptly its findings are triaged. Issues like the plugin cache migration, the unused GitHub MCP plugin, the advisor incompatibility, and the orphan temp folders can accumulate silently for weeks without causing visible failures, but each unresolved `/doctor` warning represents either a real reliability risk or unnecessary token overhead that degrades session quality.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n-
