Tier B scratchpad, Stop hook per-turn, memory tiers, claude memory layers, hook firing mechanics, Tier B near cap, project memory files, memsearch, user_career_timeline]\ntags: [claude-code, memory, automation, hooks, infrastructure, architecture]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-19.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-05.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-19\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Claude Code Three-Tier Memory Architecture\n\nThe Claude Code memory system is composed of three independent layers, each operating at a different granularity and owned by a different mechanism. This architecture was articulated on 2026-05-19 during a session that traced exactly when and how each capture mechanism fires, and clarified several non-obvious details about hook timing and agent visibility. On 2026-06-05, a practical capacity-management routing pattern emerged for when Tier B global memory approaches its character cap.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Tier A — Native Claude Code auto-memory:** Built into Claude Code itself; managed per-project; no user configuration required. Operates automatically within a project context; its exact retention and synthesis mechanics are not user-visible.\n- **Tier B — Custom global scratchpad via Stop hook:** A user-configured hook on the `Stop` event, which fires after every conversation turn. This provides incremental, per-turn transcript capture to a global scratchpad file (MEMORY.md) — a granularity that neither Tier A nor Tier C provides.\n- **Tier C — claude-memory-compiler:** The [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] system: `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` hooks fire shell commands at session teardown or auto-compaction, spawning a detached `flush.py` process that appends structured notes to the daily log; at end-of-day these are compiled into knowledge articles.\n- **The agent never sees a \"session ending\" event.** Session end and compaction are harness-level events; it is the Claude Code harness that runs the hook shell commands, not the agent itself. This means an in-context agent cannot intercept or react to its own termination — only the hooks can.\n- **PreCompact as a safety net:** In a long session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one. If a session later crashes before `SessionEnd` fires, at least one Tier C log was written at the most recent compaction — preventing total context loss.\n- **When Tier B is near cap, route to Tier A project files:** The global MEMORY.md (Tier B) has a character-cap constraint. When it approaches capacity, new durable facts should be saved to Tier A project-specific memory files (e.g., `project_<name>.md`, `user_career_timeline.md`) rather than forcing compression of existing Tier B entries. Tier A project files are cross-project searchable via memsearch — they are not siloed to a single project context.\n\n## Details\n\nThe three tiers are designed to capture context at different time horizons and granularities, and they operate independently rather than hierarchically. Tier A is fully opaque to the user — Claude Code manages it internally on a per-project basis. Tier B's Stop-hook scratchpad is the most granular: because the Stop event fires after every conversation turn, Tier B can capture mid-session context incrementally in near-real-time. This is especially useful for long sessions where intermediate turns might be compacted away before Tier C's end-of-session capture fires. Tier C produces the richest synthesized output — compiled knowledge articles from daily logs — but fires only at session boundaries.\n\nThe independence of the three tiers is their key reliability property. A failure in one does not cascade to the others: if a session crashes before `SessionEnd` fires (blocking Tier C's flush), the Stop-hook's Tier B scratchpad may still contain the session's important turns. If the Stop hook misfires, Tier A's native memory and Tier C's PreCompact-triggered captures are unaffected. The \"agent never sees session ending\" detail is architecturally important for anyone building on top of these hooks: code written inside the agent context cannot detect or react to its own session ending. Teardown logic must be placed in hook shell commands that the harness executes, not in agent-side instructions. This distinction separates what the LLM can do (respond to turns, use tools) from what the harness can do (run shell commands on system events like session end, compaction, or turn completion).\n\nThe Tier B near-cap routing pattern (2026-06-05) addresses a practical capacity constraint that emerges over time as the global MEMORY.md accumulates active threads. The USER.md profile has a hard 1,375-character cap (documented in [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]]), and MEMORY.md's Tier B can similarly fill as a productive user's open questions and active threads accumulate across weeks. The correct response when Tier B is near capacity is not to compress existing entries — which risks discarding information encoded in current phrasing — but to route new durable facts into named Tier A project memory files. These files are typically named per relationship or project (e.g., `project_kenny_boyd.md` for facts about a key stakeholder, `user_career_timeline.md` for career-context facts that help future sessions orient quickly) but are surfaced by memsearch across all project contexts. Routing to Tier A therefore sacrifices no cross-project retrievability while relieving pressure on the shared Tier B capacity. Facts that belong in Tier A project files are those that are both durable (will not become stale quickly) and specific enough that they do not need to live in the global scope — as opposed to cross-cutting facts about user preferences or universal workflow patterns that genuinely belong in Tier B's global scope.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] — Detailed installation and configuration guide for Tier C: hook wiring, `uv` PATH requirements, the `flush.py` background process, and end-of-day `compile.py` trigger.\n- [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] — A downstream consumer of Tier C's compiled daily-log output; the morning briefing pipeline reads the structured notes that `flush.py` and `compile.py` produce.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — Maintenance pass on the same Claude Code environment that houses all three memory tiers, including the hook and plugin configurations they depend on.\n- [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]] — Documents the USER.md 1,375-char cap and the Tier A vs. Tier B (durable vs. active) distinction; the near-cap routing pattern from 2026-06-05 extends this with a practical heuristic for when Tier B's global scope is under capacity pressure.\n- [[concepts/weekly-review-synthesis-workflow]] — The end-of-week close-out workflow where near-cap Tier B → Tier A routing was first observed in practice; memory housekeeping is a standard sub-task of the weekly review that surfaces and resolves these capacity situations.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-19.md]] — Three-tier architecture explanation, hook firing order, and \"agent never sees session ending\" clarification (16:53).\n- [[daily/2026-06-05.md]] — Tier B near-cap → Tier A project files routing pattern observed during end-of-week memory housekeeping (18:21); `project_kenny_boyd.md` and `user_career_timeline.md` created as the first documented application of the pattern.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-code-meta-skills-bundle.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Claude Code Meta-Skills Bundle: Selective Skill Installation\"\naliases: [meta-skills.zip, meta-skills plugin, decision-toolkit, fact-checker, process-interviewer, find-skills, frontend-slides, cherry-pick skills from plugin]\ntags: [claude-code, skills, tooling, automation, infrastructure, windows]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-20.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-20\nupdated: 2026-05-20\n---\n\n# Claude Code Meta-Skills Bundle: Selective Skill Installation\n\nOn 2026-05-20, a `meta-skills.zip` plugin bundle sourced from a YouTube demo was reviewed and selectively installed into Claude Code. The bundle contained 13 skills (not the 8 advertised), of which 5 were chosen based on overlap with existing tools and the user's sport-science/development workflow. The session established a key architectural distinction: Claude Code plugins are all-or-nothing installs, but individual skills can be cherry-picked from a bundle by extracting them directly to `~/.claude/skills/` instead of using the plugin wrapper at `~/.claude/plugins/`.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Plugin vs. skills directory:** `~/.claude/plugins/<name>/` installs an entire plugin as an atomic unit; `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/` installs individual skills independently. To cherry-pick from a bundle, extract desired skill directories to `~/.claude/skills/` rather than placing the whole bundle under `~/.claude/plugins/`.\n- **No restart required for skills:** skills installed mid-session to `~/.claude/skills/` are picked up immediately; contrast with plugins, which require a full Claude Code restart or `/reload-plugins` before activating.\n- **Mac-generated zip artifacts:** zips from Mac users contain a `__MACOSX/` metadata folder — always skip it during extraction; it has no functional content.\n- **5 selected skills:** `decision-toolkit`, `fact-checker`, `process-interviewer`, `find-skills`, `frontend-slides`.\n- **8 skipped skills with reasons:** `audio-transcriber` (Fireflies MCP already covers transcription), `agent-browser` (Playwright MCP and claude-in-chrome overlap), `openrouter` (requires separate API key, no current use case), `humanizer` (marketing tool, not applicable), `file-organizer` (unacceptable risk of unintended filesystem changes), `deep-research` (requires OpenAI API key), `prompt-master` and `mcp-builder` (no current use case).\n\n## Details\n\nThe bundle was downloaded as `meta-skills.zip` from a YouTube tutorial that described 8 skills; inspection revealed 13 skill directories plus the `__MACOSX/` metadata folder. Each skill was evaluated against two criteria: (1) overlap with already-installed tooling (Fireflies MCP for transcription, Playwright MCP and claude-in-chrome for browser automation), which would make the skill redundant; and (2) dependency on an API key not already in the environment (OpenAI for `deep-research`, a separate OpenRouter key for `openrouter`), which deferred those skills until a concrete use case justified the setup cost. Skills presenting unacceptable risk — `file-organizer` in particular, which makes autonomous changes to the filesystem — were excluded regardless of utility.\n\nThe cherry-pick-to-skills-dir pattern trades the plugin wrapper's convenience (single-command install, version tracking, coordinated uninstall) for the ability to select exactly which skills enter the Claude Code environment. Once extracted, each skill directory functions identically to one installed via `npx skills add` or the printing-press workflow: the skill's `SKILL.md` is read at session start and its slash command becomes available immediately. The immediate mid-session availability of the skills layer (versus the restart requirement for plugins) means selective installs during an active session are a practical, low-friction operation. This install pattern extends the broader Claude Code skill ecosystem covered in [[concepts/claude-code-cli-marketplace-setup]] and complements the custom skills built for the SecondBrain vault in [[concepts/custom-claude-code-skills]].\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-cli-marketplace-setup]] — Earlier (2026-05-13) session establishing the printing-press plugin and GSD skill ecosystem; the cherry-pick-to-skills-dir pattern is an alternative to the bulk-install approaches documented there.\n- [[concepts/custom-claude-code-skills]] — Custom skills built directly for the SecondBrain vault; the meta-skills bundle adds pre-built complementary skills to the same `~/.claude/skills/` layer.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — The broader discipline of auditing and curating the Claude Code tooling environment; the skill-by-skill inclusion/exclusion decisions here follow the same \"unique value vs. overlap\" framework.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-20.md]] — Bundle review, relevance-rating against existing tools, and selective extraction session (16:40).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-code-remote-control-config.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Claude Code Remote Control and DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC Conflict\"\naliases: [CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC, Remote Control eligibility, remoteControlAtStartup, claude auth login, phone access Claude Code, quiet-network mode, non-essential traffic, Remote Control silent failure]\ntags: [claude-code, configuration, remote-control, gotcha, settings, infrastructure]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-05.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-05\nupdated: 2026-06-05\n---\n\n# Claude Code Remote Control and DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC Conflict\n\nOn 2026-06-05, Remote Control (mobile/phone access to Claude Code sessions) was found to be non-functional despite `remoteControlAtStartup: true` being set in `~/.claude/settings.json`. The root cause was `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` also present in `settings.json` — Remote Control's eligibility check rides the same \"non-essential traffic\" channel that this setting disables. The two settings are mutually exclusive, and their conflict produces no warning or error.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` kills Remote Control eligibility.** Remote Control's connection mechanism uses the same non-essential traffic channel that this env block disables. Setting it prevents Remote Control from activating even when `remoteControlAtStartup: true` is simultaneously present.\n- **Silent conflict:** both settings can coexist in `settings.json` without a validation error or any warning at startup — the conflict surfaces only as Remote Control silently never connecting.\n- **Fix: remove `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` from `~/.claude/settings.json`**, then fully restart Claude Code. The env block is applied at process launch; in-session settings changes are not re-read until restart.\n- **If Remote Control still fails after restart:** run `claude auth login` to refresh the session token. A stale auth token can independently prevent Remote Control from connecting even when the traffic channel is correctly unblocked.\n- **The trade-off is binary:** quiet-network mode and phone/mobile Remote Control access cannot be used simultaneously. Removing the traffic-disable setting is the only path to enabling Remote Control.\n\n## Details\n\n`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` is intended to reduce non-critical background network calls from Claude Code — useful in environments where traffic is metered, monitored by IT, or constrained by policy. The non-obvious consequence is that Remote Control, which allows using a phone or external device to interact with running Claude Code sessions, classifies its connection channel as \"non-essential traffic\" for the purpose of this flag. When the flag is set, Remote Control's eligibility check fails at startup rather than at connection time, and it fails silently: neither Claude Code's startup output nor `/doctor` diagnostic currently surfaces this conflict. From the user's perspective, Remote Control appears correctly configured (`remoteControlAtStartup: true` is set, no obvious errors) but simply never connects to a mobile device.\n\nThe restart requirement after removing the setting is an instance of the broader pattern documented in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]]: Claude Code reads `settings.json` at launch and retains that configuration for the lifetime of the process. Editing `settings.json` while a session is active has no effect on the running instance; a full restart is always required for configuration changes to take effect. The two-step recovery procedure — remove the setting, restart, verify connection, then `claude auth login` if still failing — accounts for both the configuration change and any secondary session-token degradation that may have accumulated during the period when Remote Control was blocked. The `claude auth login` step specifically refreshes the auth token used by Remote Control's server-side handshake, addressing cases where token expiry is a secondary contributor to the failure even after the primary traffic-channel conflict is resolved.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — Broader Claude Code environment audit and maintenance discipline; the `/doctor` command does not currently flag the `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` / Remote Control conflict, making it a class of silent misconfiguration that only surfaces through behavioral observation rather than diagnostic tooling.\n- [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] — The same \"process reads configuration at launch; changes require restart\" behavior applies to `settings.json` entries and Windows registry env vars alike; both require a full process restart to propagate.\n- [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] — The cross-cutting pattern of process environments being fixed at spawn time; `settings.json` being read only at Claude Code startup is another instance of this constraint, alongside `setx` stale-env and hook PATH snapshots.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-05.md]] — Remote Control diagnosis and fix session (18:21): `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` root cause identified, setting removed from settings.json, full-restart prescription issued, `claude auth login` fallback documented for residual token issues.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-code-token-dashboard.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Claude Code Token Dashboard (nateherkai/token-dashboard)\"\naliases: [token-dashboard, token spend analytics, token-dashboard.bat, token-dashboard.vbs, token-dashboard.db]\ntags: [claude-code, tooling, analytics, windows, infrastructure, monitoring]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-21.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-21\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Claude Code Token Dashboard (nateherkai/token-dashboard)\n\nOn 2026-05-21, `nateherkai/token-dashboard` was installed at `C:\\Users\\eric_rash\\Desktop\\DEV\\token-dashboard` to provide local, zero-cost analytics on Claude Code token spend. The dashboard is a pure Python HTTP server with no external dependencies, reading JSONL conversation transcripts from `~/.claude/projects/` and serving a real-time analytics UI at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. A `.bat` launcher was added to the Desktop for one-click access, and a `.vbs` wrapper was placed in `shell:startup` for silent auto-start on login.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Zero dependencies, zero API cost:** the dashboard reads existing JSONL files from `~/.claude/projects/` and processes them locally — it makes no API calls and incurs no Claude token spend. SQLite cache is stored at `~/.claude/token-dashboard.db`.\n- **Network binding:** the server binds to `127.0.0.1` (loopback) only — there is no exposure to other machines even on the same LAN. The server re-scans source files every 30 seconds automatically.\n- **Windows startup automation:** `token-dashboard.bat` on the Desktop provides one-click launch; `token-dashboard.vbs` in `shell:startup` (opened via `Win + R → shell:startup`) runs the dashboard silently at login. A `.vbs` wrapper is preferred over a `.bat` in the Startup folder because `.bat` files open a console window while `.vbs` files invoke `wscript.exe` silently without one.\n- **Claude Code auto-mode trust boundaries:** the auto-mode classifier blocked both (a) execution of freshly-cloned external repo code and (b) writes to the Windows Startup folder, treating both as separate trust thresholds requiring explicit user confirmation. Even after a user confirms the first gate, Startup-folder writes may remain blocked as a hard second gate; the escalation path is manual file creation by the user or adding a `Write` permission rule in `.claude/settings.json`.\n- **Background task management:** when the dashboard server runs as a Claude Code background task (task ID `bolrksfho` in the installation session), it should be stopped via `TaskStop` before ending the session to avoid orphaned server processes.\n\n## Details\n\nThe token dashboard addresses a practical gap in Claude Code's built-in reporting: JSONL transcripts are stored locally and contain full token-count metadata, but there is no native UI to aggregate and visualize cumulative spend across sessions and projects. `nateherkai/token-dashboard` fills this gap with a lightweight local server — no cloud service, no authentication, no ongoing cost — making it well-suited for always-on monitoring via autostart.\n\nThe auto-mode classifier behavior surfaced during setup reveals two distinct trust boundaries Claude Code enforces in autonomous mode. First, executing code from a freshly-cloned external repository (rather than the user's own codebase) triggers a confirmation gate on the grounds that untrusted code should not run without explicit approval. Second, writing to Windows Startup locations (`shell:startup`) is treated as a persistent-access escalation — planting a file that runs on every login is a meaningful trust threshold even if the file's content is benign. These gates apply independently: a user confirming the first does not automatically grant the second. This two-gate behavior is worth understanding because it can feel like a single confirmation \"didn't take\" when in reality it resolved the first gate while the second gate remained. The practical workaround for the Startup write, if the permission rule path is too broad, is to have the user manually place the `.vbs` file themselves in `shell:startup`, entirely outside Claude Code's action surface.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — The broader Claude Code environment audit discipline; the auto-mode trust boundaries encountered during this install represent another class of environment-specific behavior to account for when adding tooling.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-meta-skills-bundle]] — A prior (2026-05-20) session that also dealt with selective Claude Code tooling additions and the trust/relevance evaluation for each addition; shares the \"curate carefully, understand trust implications\" posture.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-21.md]] — Installation session (16:35): token dashboard setup, .vbs autostart configuration, auto-mode classifier trust boundary behavior, background task note.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-code-worktree-gotchas.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Claude Code Worktree Gotchas: Branch Orphan, CRLF Normalization, and Windows MAX_PATH\"\naliases: [ExitWorktree remove orphan, worktree branch deleted, git reflog recovery, CRLF autocrlf normalization, worktree artifacts gitignore, Windows MAX_PATH worktree, sparse-checkout worktree workaround, SourcePapers path length, background-isolation disable, settings.json disableBackgroundIsolation, git update-index refresh, CRLF phantom diff resolution, git index re-sync]\ntags: [claude-code, git, worktree, windows, gotcha, configuration]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-22.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-17.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-22\nupdated: 2026-06-17\n---\n\n# Claude Code Worktree Gotchas: Branch Orphan, CRLF Normalization, and Windows MAX_PATH\n\nThree non-obvious gotchas around Claude Code's worktree workflow have been documented across sessions. On 2026-05-22, `ExitWorktree` with the `remove` flag deletes the associated branch along with the worktree directory (orphaning any unmerged commits), and Windows `autocrlf` normalization can make files appear different in the working tree even when they are byte-identical inside the Git object store. On 2026-06-17, a third class of failure emerged: Windows MAX_PATH limits on deeply-nested long-filename directories (e.g., PDF libraries in `SourcePapers/`) silently break `git worktree add` / `EnterWorktree`, requiring a sparse-checkout workaround or outright disabling of background-isolation enforcement in `.claude/settings.json`. Additionally, CRLF phantom diffs that accumulate after branch operations can be cleared with `git update-index --refresh` without touching working-tree file content.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **`ExitWorktree remove` deletes the branch:** the `remove` option on `ExitWorktree` removes both the worktree filesystem and its associated branch in a single operation. Any commits made on that branch that have not been merged or cherry-picked are orphaned — they still exist in the object store but have no branch reference pointing to them.\n- **Recovery via `git reflog` + `git cherry-pick`:** `git reflog` records all HEAD and branch-tip movements, including the branch deletion; search for the commit SHA immediately before the deletion event, then `git cherry-pick <sha>` onto the intended target branch. No need to recreate the deleted branch.\n- **CRLF vs. LF on Windows `autocrlf`:** Windows Git defaults `core.autocrlf = true`, converting LF → CRLF on checkout and CRLF → LF on commit. Two files can therefore show as \"different\" in `git status`, shell `==` comparisons, or diff tools because one is CRLF in the working tree while the stored blob is LF — even though they are byte-for-byte identical inside Git.\n- **Resolution for CRLF phantom diffs (`git update-index --refresh`):** CRLF-normalized files frequently show as phantom modified in `git status` after branch switches or IDE restarts. Running `git update-index --refresh` resets Git's internal index to match the current working-tree state under the active `autocrlf` policy, clearing false-positive \"modified\" flags without touching file content. Confirmed on 2026-06-17 to resolve accumulated CRLF index noise in FaceComps after a branch operation.\n- **Worktree artifacts should be gitignored:** add `.claude/worktrees/` to `.gitignore` to prevent ephemeral worktree directories from appearing as untracked changes.\n- **Windows MAX_PATH breaks worktree creation with deeply-nested long-filename dirs:** repos containing directories with deeply-nested files whose paths exceed 260 characters (e.g., a `SourcePapers/` folder with long PDF filenames) cause `git worktree add` and `EnterWorktree` to fail at the path-length limit. This failure is structural and unrelated to the content of the change being worked on.\n- **Sparse-checkout workaround:** create the worktree with `--no-checkout`, then configure a sparse-checkout pattern that excludes the problematic directory (`SourcePapers/`) before checking out. This allows the worktree to be created and populated without ever materializing the long-path files on disk.\n- **`.claude/settings.json` to disable background-isolation enforcement:** when worktree creation is structurally broken and sparse-checkout is impractical, adding `.claude/settings.json` with `{\"backgroundIsolation\": false}` to the repo prevents Claude Code from attempting worktree creation for background agents. The Write tool gate may block direct creation of this file; PowerShell shell mutations are not subject to the same guard and serve as a fallback.\n\n## Details\n\nThe `ExitWorktree remove` behavior is easy to trigger accidentally because `remove` reads as a natural cleanup action after agent work in a worktree is done — the intent is \"clean up the worktree,\" but the actual effect includes silently deleting the branch. If the agent made commits during the worktree session that were not merged or pushed, those commits become unreachable by branch name. Git's garbage collector typically does not collect unreachable objects for at least 30 days, so the commits are not immediately destroyed, but they are invisible to normal `git log` traversal and branch listings. The `git reflog` recovery path works because reflog records all reference updates including branch deletions: `git reflog | grep <branch-name>` (or a timestamp search) reveals the pre-deletion commit SHA, and `git cherry-pick` transfers those commits to the current branch without needing to recreate the deleted branch. Prevention: run `git status` and `git log` from inside the worktree before calling `ExitWorktree remove` to confirm all desired commits have been merged or pushed.\n\nThe CRLF/autocrlf normalization issue is a Windows-specific environment hazard that has nothing to do with actual file content — two files can fail a shell equality check (`==`) or appear as changed in `git status` while being semantically and functionally identical. This surfaces most sharply in repo-maintenance scripts that compare files byte-for-byte, such as the pre-commit hook described in [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] that checks `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` for divergence. The diagnostic is to inspect raw bytes via `xxd`, PowerShell `Format-Hex`, or `cat -A` rather than trusting diff output or shell comparisons that operate on the working-tree representation. The most reliable cross-platform comparison for script use is `git hash-object <file>`, which hashes the stored blob (always LF after autocrlf normalization on commit) rather than the working-tree bytes. When phantom diffs accumulate after a branch switch or index-state mismatch, `git update-index --refresh` is the non-destructive resolution: it re-reads each tracked file's working-tree state, applies the current `autocrlf` policy to determine what the blob hash should be, and clears any \"dirty\" flags for files whose content has not actually changed relative to the last commit. On 2026-06-17, this command resolved CRLF index noise in the FaceComps repository after branch operations, with `git status` returning clean immediately afterward without any file modifications.\n\nThe Windows MAX_PATH limit failure is structurally different from the previous two gotchas because it is triggered by pre-existing repo content rather than by user actions during the worktree session. Repositories that contain legacy binary archives, PDF libraries (`SourcePapers/`), or deeply-nested generated output directories can accumulate file paths that exceed 260 characters. When `git worktree add` attempts to create a checkout in a new directory, it must materialize all tracked paths within the new worktree's root — any path that would exceed MAX_PATH causes the operation to fail. The sparse-checkout approach resolves this by instructing git to materialize only a subset of the tracked file tree, explicitly excluding the long-path directory from the worktree's scope. The change being made in the worktree (e.g., a UI component update in `src/`) does not require the `SourcePapers/` PDFs to be present, making sparse exclusion both safe and correct. If even sparse-checkout setup is too cumbersome for a given task, disabling background-isolation enforcement in `.claude/settings.json` prevents worktree creation altogether, reverting to inline execution on the main branch — appropriate when the change is demonstrably safe to make without isolation.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/accidental-git-init-home-directory]] — Another Windows-specific git environment issue where the working tree's apparent state is misleading relative to the actual repository state; both articles document cases where a git tool's surface output does not match what is actually committed or stored.\n- [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] — The session in which the branch-orphan and CRLF gotchas first surfaced (2026-05-22); the `.claude/worktrees/` gitignore addition and the CRLF risk to the pre-commit sync hook are both documented there.\n- [[concepts/dormant-feature-season-gated-deployment]] — The MaxPath worktree issue was encountered in the SportScienceResearchRepo design reskin session (2026-06-17); both articles deal with pragmatic deployment decisions when structural constraints make the standard isolation workflow impractical.\n- [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] — The broader Windows execution-environment constraint pattern; the MAX_PATH limit is another instance of Windows system constraints affecting development tooling in ways that require environment-specific workarounds.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-22.md]] — FaceComps model-agnostic repo setup session (09:55): `ExitWorktree remove` orphan discovery, `git reflog` + `cherry-pick` recovery lesson, and CRLF vs. LF Windows autocrlf normalization gotcha.\n- [[daily/2026-06-17.md]] — SportScienceResearchRepo design reskin session (17:33): Windows MAX_PATH limit breaks `git worktree add` / `EnterWorktree` on repos with deeply-nested PDF filenames in `SourcePapers/`; sparse-checkout excluding `SourcePapers/` as the workaround; `.claude/settings.json` `backgroundIsolation: false` as a fallback; Write tool gate bypass via PowerShell for settings file creation. FaceComps loose-ends session (20:16): `git update-index --refresh` confirmed as the non-destructive resolution for CRLF phantom diffs accumulated after branch operations.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\claude-memory-compiler-setup.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Claude Memory Compiler Setup\"\naliases: [claude-memory-compiler, coleam00/claude-memory-compiler, persistent memory hooks, session-start session-end pre-compact, memory compiler version skew, claude-agent-sdk version skew, FLUSH_ERROR version skew, uv lock upgrade]\ntags: [claude-code, memory, automation, infrastructure, hooks, maintenance]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-14.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-05-19.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-13.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-14\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Claude Memory Compiler Setup\n\nOn 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` system — the same daily-log-to-knowledge-base architecture this very knowledge base runs on — was installed to give Claude Code persistent memory across sessions. The repo was cloned to `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`, Python dependencies installed via `uv sync`, and the knowledge base directory structure (`daily/`, `knowledge/concepts/`, etc.) initialized. This system is Tier C of a three-tier Claude Code memory architecture; see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] for the full picture including Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook scratchpad). On 2026-06-13, a day-long failure caused by `claude-agent-sdk` version skew revealed an important operational maintenance pattern.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Three global hooks were wired into `~/.claude/settings.json`: `session-start.py` (SessionStart), `session-end.py` (SessionEnd), and `pre-compact.py` (PreCompact).\n- Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.\n- All script invocations follow the `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler <script>` pattern, guaranteeing the correct virtualenv context regardless of the current working directory when a hook fires.\n- Hook configuration changes are not picked up live — they require a full Claude Code restart (or a `/hooks` reload) before they take effect.\n- After 6 PM local time, the `flush.py` background process automatically triggers `compile.py` to turn that day's daily log into knowledge articles, without manual intervention. Manual queries are also available via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/query.py \"<question>\"`.\n- **The agent itself never receives a \"session ending\" notification** — SessionEnd and PreCompact are harness-level events; the harness runs the hook shell commands, not the agent. Teardown logic must live in the hook, not in agent-side instructions.\n- **Version skew failure mode:** the memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk` to a specific version, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary. When the system Claude Code auto-updates (e.g., from 2.1.92 to 2.1.177), the bundled CLI in the venv falls behind and eventually cannot parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json`, causing every `flush.py` invocation to exit immediately with a non-zero code. Symptom: 100% FLUSH_ERROR rate after a Claude Code update, despite no changes to the memory compiler itself.\n- **Fix for version skew:** `cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`. This upgrades only the `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and its bundled CLI to match the current system version without touching other pinned dependencies. Run this whenever FLUSH_ERRORs appear after a Claude Code auto-update.\n- **Diagnostic caution:** do NOT invoke the bundled `claude.exe` CLI directly to diagnose version skew — it spawns a real nested agent session. Instead, inspect venv package metadata (e.g., `uv pip show claude-agent-sdk`) to check the installed version against the system CLI version.\n\n## Details\n\nThe setup session focused on making the memory pipeline reliable rather than merely functional. The PATH issue with `uv` is a generalizable lesson for any Claude Code hook that shells out to a tool installed via `uv`, `pipx`, or similar user-local installers: hook processes may run with a minimal environment, so absolute paths (or explicit `PATH` exports) are safer than relying on the interactive shell's configuration. Similarly, the `uv run --directory` pattern avoids a whole class of \"wrong virtualenv\" bugs that would otherwise occur if a hook fires while Claude Code's working directory is some unrelated project.\n\nOnce restarted, the three hooks form a closed loop: `session-start.py` injects the current knowledge index and the most recent daily log into every new session's context (capped at 20,000 characters), `session-end.py` and `pre-compact.py` capture the raw conversation transcript and spawn a detached `flush.py` process, and `flush.py` decides what's worth appending to the day's daily log and, after 6 PM, kicks off `compile.py` to synthesize that log into structured `knowledge/` articles. PreCompact serves as a safety net for long sessions: in a session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, ensuring at least one compiled log exists even if the session later crashes before SessionEnd fires.\n\nThe 2026-06-13 version skew failure is operationally important. On that day, Claude Code auto-updated from approximately version 2.1.92 to 2.1.177 — 85 releases ahead — while the memory compiler's venv still bundled the older CLI via `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56`. The newer `~/.claude/settings.json` included hooks, settings, or schemas added after version 2.1.92 that the stale bundled CLI could not parse; every `flush.py` call exited on startup without processing the session. The failure was isolated entirely to the Tier C compile layer: Tier B (the `transcript-capture.js` Stop-hook) continued capturing sessions uninterrupted because it has no dependency on `claude-agent-sdk`. Twenty-four days of continuous Tier B logs and four sessions captured on the failure day itself confirmed the architectural independence. This means that during a version-skew failure, raw session context is preserved in Tier B transcripts and can be backfilled after the fix is applied. The `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync` fix is surgical — it upgrades only the affected package without touching other pinned dependencies — and is safe to apply at any time. A post-fix test flush verifies the fix before trusting that normal operation has resumed. See [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] for the architectural insight this failure demonstrated empirically.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The three-tier framing that situates this compiler as Tier C, alongside Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook per-turn scratchpad).\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — A later (2026-06-10) maintenance pass on the same Claude Code environment, addressing plugin/MCP configuration drift in the broader tooling this memory system runs inside.\n- [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] — Another automation pipeline (built 2026-06-10) sharing the same token-efficiency motivation: pre-process inputs so the LLM only has concepts\\clinical-note-nlp-clustering.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Clinical Note NLP Clustering (TF-IDF + LSA + KMeans)\"\naliases: [clinical note clustering, TF-IDF LSA KMeans notes, Note_SemanticReady, k=20 silhouette clustering, provider clusters, nutrition clusters, treatment clusters, note clustering Ath_Medicine, md_table float formatting, silhouette score 4-decimal, 3924 notes]\ntags: [baylor-athletics, sports-medicine, nlp, data-pipeline, python, clustering, machine-learning]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-14.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-14\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Clinical Note NLP Clustering (TF-IDF + LSA + KMeans)\n\nClinical note NLP clustering is a text-mining approach that discovers natural groupings within large sets of medical visit notes using a TF-IDF vectorization, Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) dimensionality reduction, and k-means partitioning pipeline. The approach was applied on 2026-06-14 as Task #5 of the Ath_Medicine project (see [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]]), processing 3,924 notes with `Note_SemanticReady == TRUE` and selecting k=20 clusters via silhouette score. The resulting clusters organized naturally into provider-centric, nutrition-related, and treatment-modality families — validating the approach as meaningful rather than arbitrary.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Pipeline: TF-IDF → LSA → KMeans.** TF-IDF weights term importance by document frequency; LSA (via truncated SVD) reduces the high-dimensional term space into a dense semantic embedding; KMeans partitions the embedding space into k clusters. This pipeline is appropriate for short, terminology-heavy clinical notes where keyword overlap is a reliable semantic signal.\n- **k=20 selected via silhouette score:** silhouette score (0.1645) at k=20 exceeded k=18 (0.1607) and other candidates, selecting the optimal granularity. Silhouette scores in the 0.15–0.20 range are typical for short clinical text where cluster boundaries are inherently fuzzy; higher is not always achievable without overfitting k to noise.\n- **3,924 notes processed** — only records with `Note_SemanticReady == TRUE` entered the pipeline. The `Note_SemanticReady` flag pre-filters records to semantically substantive notes, excluding administrative, templated, or minimal-content entries that would dilute cluster coherence.\n- **Three-family cluster taxonomy discovered:**\n  - *Provider clusters:* notes cluster by attending clinician (Fryar, Irvin, Haynes, Gilliam, Ken Minor/primary-care) — reflecting clinician-specific vocabulary and documentation style as the dominant signal within provider-authored notes.\n  - *Nutrition clusters:* dietitian check-in notes, body composition scan records, and supplement policy notes form distinct subclusters — vocabulary around macros, composition percentages, and supplement names separates cleanly.\n  - *Treatment clusters:* dry needling and shockwave therapy notes cluster separately from other modalities — procedure-specific terminology (needle depth, applicator settings, treated regions) is sufficiently distinctive for clean separation.\n- **`md_table` float formatting gotcha:** when passing silhouette scores to `md_table` for k-selection summary display, scores are rounded to 1 decimal place (e.g., 0.1607 → 0.2, 0.1645 → 0.2), making it impossible to distinguish k candidates that differ only in the third or fourth decimal. **Fix:** pre-format silhouette scores as 4-decimal strings before passing to `md_table`, e.g., `f\"{score:.4f}\"`.\n- **Provider clusters as dominant signal:** the fact that provider identity is the strongest clustering signal (generating multiple distinct provider-named clusters) means the pipeline is partially functioning as a clinician-attribution model. This is useful for auditing inter-clinician documentation consistency but should be noted when clusters are used for patient-care analysis — provider style, not patient population, may be the primary cluster driver.\n\n## Details\n\nThe TF-IDF + LSA + KMeans pipeline is the standard baseline for unsupervised text clustering when no labeled training data is available and the goal is discovery rather than classification. TF-IDF is applied first to create a high-dimensional sparse term-frequency matrix; LSA then reduces this to a dense 100-200 dimensional semantic space by identifying latent topics. KMeans then partitions the dense space into k clusters. For clinical notes, this pipeline succeeds when notes have sufficient vocabulary specificity per care category — which is the case here because different care types (surgical notes, nutrition consultations, dry needling sessions) use vocabularies that are distinct enough for TF-IDF to separate. The 0.1645 silhouette score reflects well-separated but not perfectly cohesive clusters, which is expected for clinical text where a single note might discuss multiple care dimensions simultaneously.\n\nThe k-selection process via silhouette score requires evaluating a range of k values and comparing their scores. In the Ath_Medicine run, k=20 marginally outperformed k=18 (0.1645 vs. 0.1607) — a difference of 0.0038. The `md_table` float formatting issue made this margin invisible in the generated summary table (both rounded to 0.2), which would have made the k-selection rationale appear arbitrary if not for the raw score values available during interactive analysis. The correct pattern for any k-selection table: format silhouette scores to at least 4 decimal places before converting to a display format, because the decision-making precision required is at the fourth decimal. Pre-formatting as strings using `f\"{score:.4f}\"` before passing to display utilities that may apply their own rounding is the reliable pattern. The cluster taxonomy discovered — provider, nutrition, treatment — is immediately actionable for the Ath_Medicine project: it enables subgroup analysis of note volumes and content patterns by care type, feeds the Senior Staff annual report's narrative around service delivery, and provides a structure for the future per-provider or per-modality deep dives that the project will support.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]] — The parent project and the broader \"Do them all\" backlog sprint context for this task; sensitivity rules apply (athlete-level data stays local).\n- [[concepts/surgery-nlp-extraction]] — The companion Task #4 NLP pipeline operating on the same `Note_Expanded` source field for event extraction rather than clustering; \"daily/2026-06-10.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-04-14.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-05.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-10\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Daily On-Ramp Automation (Lean Mode)\n\nThe Daily On-Ramp is an automated morning-briefing pipeline that gathers raw inputs via a script (`onramp.sh`), distills them into a short \"must-dos\" list, prepends that summary to the day's `morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` file, logs an audit row to `onramp-audit.md`, and backs up the result via commit/push. On 2026-06-10 the pipeline was run as a \"lean mode\" pilot; a second documented run occurred on 2026-06-05 using a stripped-down input set (carry-forward items and OKR scoreboard only, with no calendar events or inbox triage yet present for the day).\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **\"Lean mode\"** deliberately skips reading raw calendar/email JSON and relies solely on `onramp.sh`'s compact output, trading completeness for token efficiency.\n- **The 2026-06-10 pilot** prepended three sections to that day's briefing: ① Carry-forward items (none — no unchecked items from the prior day), ② 6 must-dos, ③ all 7 active OKR next-actions framed as the week's \"big rocks\"; existing inbox-triage content was preserved below the new section.\n- **The 2026-06-05 run** used a sparse input set — only carry-forward items and the OKR scoreboard, with no calendar events or inbox triage yet available. Produced 5 must-dos prioritizing overdue carry-forward items before OKR big rocks. Demonstrates graceful degradation when inputs are incomplete.\n- **Token efficiency quantified:** the 2026-06-10 lean run measured **536 tokens kept in-context** versus an estimated 114.5K if raw calendar/email data had been read directly — 100% of that volume avoided, logged in `onramp-audit.md`. By 2026-06-05, cumulative savings were **4.0 MB across 22 days / 105 conversations** (a 214× compression ratio before `/compact`), confirming compounding value over multi-week usage.\n- **Audit trail:** each run appends a row to `onramp-audit.md` (format: date, time, yes/no). The on-ramp produces a valid output even on days with minimal inputs; carry-forward items from prior must-do lists seed it when no new sources are available.\n\n## Details\n\nThe pipeline's value proposition is token efficiency: rather than having the assistant read raw calendar and email exports each morning, a lightweight gather script pre-aggregates the relevant signals into a compact form, and the LLM's job is reduced to distillation and formatting. The 2026-06-10 run quantified this trade-off explicitly (536 tokens vs. ~114.5K), giving a concrete per-run baseline for evaluating whether lean mode is \"good enough\" going forward or whether some days will need a fuller run that reads raw sources. By 2026-06-05, the cumulative record across 22 active days and 105 conversations showed 4.0 MB of raw context kept out of the window — at 214× the compressed size — confirming that the \"gather-then-distill\" architecture pays compounding dividends as usage continues. The pipeline's per-run savings are substantial on their own; their cumulative effect across weeks is an order-of-magnitude improvement in context budget efficiency.\n\nThe 2026-06-05 run demonstrated the pipeline's graceful degradation when inputs are sparse: with no calendar events or inbox triage yet available for the day, the on-ramp ran using only carry-forward items and the OKR scoreboard. This produced a valid 5-item must-do list (Ruth's Perch camera upgrade decision overdue carry-forward, uploading practice-planning docs to unblock FaceComps for OKR 1.2, resuming the FaceComps grill and setting rep bands, specifying the unified coach view and volleyball intro/buy-in for OKR 1.1, and advancing basketball summer initiatives) without requiring the full input set. The sparse-input graceful degradation is a key design property: the on-ramp produces useful output regardless of whether all expected sources are present, rather than failing or outputting nothing on low-input days. The must-dos generated by the 2026-06-10 run were derived from inbox/communications triage done earlier that day (16 needs-reply emails, overdue timecards, stale follow-ups, open scheduling items), making the on-ramp a downstream consumer of that triage output rather than an independent process. The same design principle — pre-process inputs so the LLM only reads a compact summary — was applied two months earlier, on 2026-04-14, when the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` hook system was set up to summarize sessions into daily logs automatically.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — The on-ramp pipeline runs inside the same Claude Code harness that was undergoing maintenance earlier on 2026-06-10; the plugin and skill registrations that maintenance pass verified are dependencies for the on-ramp's execution environment.\n- [[concepts/custom-claude-code-skills]] — Both the on-ramp pilot and the new skills built on 2026-06-10 reflect a broader push toward scripted, token-efficient automation layered on top of Claude Code.\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] — An earlier (2026-04-14) automation pipeline sharing the same design principle: pre-process inputs so the LLM only reads a compact summary, not raw data. The memory compiler produces the daily logs that the on-ramp's OKR scoreboard and carry-forward items draw from.\n- [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]] — A related daily-orientation system (designed 2026-05-21) that addresses email and calendar triage in a structured 6-section format; the on-ramp consumes triage output while the briefing system generates it, making the two pipelines complementary at the input/output boundary.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-10.md]] — Pilot run details, must-dos list, ctx stats (536 tokens in-context vs. 114.5K raw), audit/backup confirmation, commit \"on-ramp pilot 2026-06-10.\"\n- [[daily/2026-04-14.md]] — Source of the earlier memory-compiler automation sharing the same gather-then-distill design principle.\n- [[daily/2026-06-05.md]] — Second documented run: carry-forward + OKR scoreboard input set only, 5 must-dos generated, cumulative ctx savings quantified (4.0 MB / 22 days / 105 conversations, 214× compression before /compact).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\dormant-feature-season-gated-deployment.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Dormant Feature Pattern: Season-Gated Deployment\"\naliases: [season-gated deployment, dormant feature code, feature gating by data availability, dormant-until-data, safe early merge, inert feature branch]\ntags: [deployment, architecture, sports-science, load-simulator, workflow, baylor-athletics]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-26.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-26\nupdated: 2026-05-26\n---\n\n# Dormant Feature Pattern: Season-Gated Deployment\n\nA dormant feature is code that is fully implemented and merged to production but has no user-visible effect until a required external condition is met. In the sports-science tooling context, the natural gate is data availability: a seasonal feature deployed before its season begins cannot affect any user's experience because the data that would activate it does not yet exist. On 2026-05-26, the Baylor Load Simulator's Fall Camp mode was shipped to production via direct merge to `main` under this pattern, with activation deferred until Fall Camp GPS data arrives (~August 2026).\n\n## Key Points\n\n- A feature can be safely merged and deployed to production early when: (a) it has no user-visible effect until a specific external trigger (e.g., data availability); (b) the code path for the existing season is byte-identical to pre-feature behavior; and (c) the full test suite passes.\n- The Fall Camp mode met all three conditions: no Catapult Fall Camp GPS data exists yet, Spring mode remains byte-identical (verified), and 121 tests passed.\n- Vercel auto-deploys on push to `main`, making deployment automatic; the feature gate is behavioral (no data → no UI effect) rather than a code-level feature flag — no runtime flag check required.\n- A direct merge to `main` rather than a PR is appropriate when the team is small and the change is demonstrably inert and fully tested; the overhead of a PR review is not justified for a dormant, data-gated change.\n- **Activation seam must be explicitly documented:** the future step that makes the dormant feature live — in this case, wiring FC short-form period aliases via `canonicalize`'s `aliases` argument when real Fall Camp Catapult period names arrive — is documented in `simulator/AGENTS.md` so it is not forgotten.\n\n## Details\n\nThe season-gated deployment pattern avoids the cost of maintaining a long-lived feature branch while keeping dormant code out of the user's experience until it has a reason to be there. Unlike a code-level feature flag (which requires a runtime conditional that must be removed later), data-gated dormancy relies on the feature's natural data dependencies as the gate: the Fall Camp mode's UI and sync logic are fully functional, but since there is no Fall Camp Catapult GPS data until approximately August 2026, no Fall Camp practices can be loaded, displayed, or compared — the feature is invisible to users regardless of whether the code is deployed. This avoids feature-flag housekeeping overhead at the cost of a less explicit, less toggleable gate.\n\nThe critical prerequisite for safe early deployment is proof that the existing season's behavior is provably unaffected. On 2026-05-26, this was verified by confirming Spring mode was byte-identical after the Fall Camp domain was added, and by running the full 121-test suite before merging. The documentation requirement — an explicit activation seam in `simulator/AGENTS.md` identifying what must be done and when — ensures the dormant code does not become forgotten dead code. Future developers or sessions picking up the project know exactly what the remaining activation step is (wiring `canonicalize`'s `aliases` arg with real FC period names) without needing to re-read the full implementation. The pattern is most applicable to sports-science tooling with well-defined seasonal data boundaries (spring practice, fall camp, in-season), where new season domains can be built in the off-season and activated automatically when the new season's data pipeline begins delivering records.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-fall-camp-mode]] — The concrete instance of this pattern: the Fall Camp mode feature shipped dormant on 2026-05-26, to be activated when Fall Camp Catapult GPS data arrives.\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-deployment]] — The underlying Vercel deployment that makes \"merge to main = deployed to production\" automatic, and which established the `main`-branch direct-merge workflow for this project.\n- [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]] — Catapult data-layer quirks that will interact with the Fall Camp mode's period-name parameterization once live data is available and the dormant feature is activated.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-26.md]] — Decision to merge Fall Camp mode dormant to `main` and rationale (17:15): byte-identity verification, test suite confirmation, and activation seam documentation.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\end-of-day-structured-interview.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"End-of-Day Structured Interview Workflow\"\naliases: [end-of-day interview, 4-question interview, daily debrief, USER.md cap, MEMORY.md Tier B, daily reflection, Q4 insight prompt, answers without questions, vault note from interview]\ntags: [productivity, workflow, memory, second-brain, obsidian, interview, reflection, daily-routine]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-29.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-29\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# End-of-Day Structured Interview Workflow\n\nA structured end-of-day interview workflow was demonstrated on 2026-05-29, combining a Fireflies meeting sync, a 4-question daily debrief, targeted vault note creation, and global memory system updates (USER.md and MEMORY.md). The session also revealed a critical USER.md character cap constraint and clarified the Tier A vs. Tier B memory split for active vs. durable information.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **4-question interview format** covers all active projects and workstreams in a single pass, surfacing insights across areas that might otherwise receive no end-of-day attention. The 2026-05-29 run spanned: Dropback vendor call, Jeremy presentation prep, Hoff/Soto AI discovery call, ACWR tennis project, Fall Camp simulator scoping, spirit and cheer summer packet, research database, and upcoming Databricks call.\n- **Q4 (\"tell a peer one thing\") consistently produces the sharpest material:** this prompt forces compression — the user must identify the single transmissible insight from the day. On 2026-05-29 it surfaced: \"effort put into answering questions that haven't been asked is in vain\" (essay seed), and the connected observation that AI adoption/consensus is the real bottleneck, not direction.\n- **Connect interview outputs to existing vault notes rather than creating isolated ones:** updating the existing `self-authored-direction` note with a reframed open question (linking direction to adoption) compounds value more than creating a standalone new note. The connection is the knowledge, not just the content.\n- **USER.md cap (1,375 chars):** the global USER.md profile is essentially at capacity (1,370/1,375 as of 2026-05-29). Any future profile addition requires consolidating or pruning existing entries before adding new content — USER.md must be treated as a fixed-size buffer, not an append-only log.\n- **MEMORY.md Tier A vs. Tier B:** durable facts about the user go in Tier A; active, fluid threads (e.g., career-pivot consideration) go in Tier B. A Tier B entry signals \"this is worth tracking but not yet stable enough to become a fact.\"\n- **Fireflies integration:** new meetings are synced, renamed from generic timestamps to descriptive titles (e.g., `2026-05-28_Eric_and_Jeremy_presentation_prep`), and exported to the vault at `Inbox/meetings/YYYY-MM-DD_<title>.md`.\n\n## Details\n\nThe structured end-of-day interview functions as a compression mechanism: a full day of meetings, decisions, and half-formed thoughts is distilled into a small set of high-signal outputs — a vault note, a memory update, an essay seed — without requiring the user to decide in the moment what is worth capturing. By following a fixed question format, the interview ensures consistent coverage across all active workstreams rather than capturing only what was most recent or most emotionally salient. The structure also makes the interview reproducible across sessions and assistants: the same prompt set can be run by any AI instance with access to the user's project context and yield comparable coverage.\n\nThe Q4 prompt is architecturally different from the preceding questions because it forces a different cognitive operation. Questions 1–3 surface facts and status updates (what happened, what decisions were made, what is blocked); Q4 forces synthesis and compression — the user must identify the single insight worth transmitting to a peer. This compression step often reveals insights that would not have surfaced through status-update prompts alone. On 2026-05-29, both outputs from Q4 were routed to vault notes rather than MEMORY.md, because they are essay seeds and framing questions rather than durable facts about the user's preferences or context. The distinction matters: MEMORY.md stores facts that help a future AI session orient quickly (\"user works at Baylor Athletics\"), while vault notes store ideas that the user may want to develop, publish, or return to. AI-adoption/consensus was explicitly deferred to the weekly review rather than drafted immediately — the weekly review is the right context for framing the evidence, finding allies, and deciding whether the idea is worth writing.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The three-tier memory architecture (native auto-memory, Stop-hook scratchpad, claude-memory-compiler) that the USER.md/MEMORY.md system extends; the Tier A/Tier B distinction in MEMORY.md maps to a similar \"durable vs. active\" split.\n- [[connections/obsidian-vault-as-knowledge-hub]] — The Fireflies meeting export and interview-derived vault note creation are further instances of routing structured outputs to the SecondBrain vault as a canonical knowledge destination.\n- [[concepts/project-triage-retrospective]] — The end-of-day interview provides day-level compression; the weekly retrospective provides week-level triage across cold projects and open loops. The two complement each other at different time horizons.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-29.md]] — End-of-day interview session (11:40): Fireflies sync, 4-question debrief, vault note creation from Q4 insight, USER.md cap discovery, MEMORY.md Tier B update, AI-adoption deferral to weekly review.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\fall-camp-rep-extraction-pipeline.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Fall Camp FC25 Rep Extraction Pipeline\"\naliases: [extract_fc25_reps.py, FC25 rep extractor, accountable period rep counts, ones_reps_confirmed, fall camp calibration B1, 14-item practice-planning roadmap, practice-planning-grill-state]\ntags: [baylor-athletics, football, sports-science, load-management, fall-camp, data-pipeline, calibration]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-02.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-02\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Fall Camp FC25 Rep Extraction Pipeline\n\nOn 2026-06-02, the first concrete calibration artifact for the Baylor Fall Camp practice-planning model was produced: `scripts/extract_fc25_reps.py`, a script that parses FC25 (Fall Camp 2025) practice data and extracts accountable period rep counts.
