On 2026-06-17, 35 meetings were scanned from a 30-day rolling window; 14 had apparently generic titles, 6 proved to be stale cache entries already renamed in a prior session, and 8 were genuinely renamed. A critical operational lesson emerged: the local Fireflies database cache can be stale and report meetings as \"generic\" even after prior renaming — always re-verify against the live API before acting.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Workflow steps:** (1) scan Fireflies meetings from a rolling time window, (2) identify meetings with generic or timestamp-only titles, (3) propose descriptive names based on content/participants, (4) confirm proposed names with user, (5) apply renames via Fireflies API, (6) re-sync local DB.\n- **Stale local cache gotcha:** the local Fireflies DB cache retains records from prior sessions and may report a meeting as \"generic title\" even after it was renamed in a previous session. On 2026-06-17, 6 of 14 apparently-generic meetings were already renamed — the cache had not been refreshed. Always re-verify current title state against the live Fireflies API before counting a meeting as \"needs rename.\"\n- **Local DB re-sync required after rename:** after API renames complete, the local database must be explicitly re-synced; otherwise future scans will continue to report the old generic names from the stale local store.\n- **Context disambiguation for same-day meetings:** when multiple meetings occur on the same day from different organizational contexts, do not group them thematically. On 2026-06-17, a TCU/Roach Institute Sport Science Symposium cluster (4 sessions) co-occurred with an unrelated Baylor Athletics Website Redesign call and a separate staff talk — the user confirmed these were independent events, not part of the symposium.\n- **Rename count anatomy:** 35 scanned → 14 apparently generic → 6 stale cache (already renamed, skipped) → 8 genuinely renamed via API.\n\n## Details\n\nThe batch rename workflow addresses a common accumulation pattern in Fireflies: AI-generated meeting notes receive auto-generated titles based on timestamps or generic participant names, and these titles are not useful for navigation in a knowledge management system. When meeting notes are exported to SecondBrain (`Inbox/meetings/YYYY-MM-DD_<title>.md`), a title like \"Meeting - Jun 16, 2026 at 2:00 PM\" produces an unnavigable filename that cannot be found by topic. The batch rename converts these to descriptive, topic-oriented titles before or during the export cycle, making the vault's meeting note corpus searchable by subject matter rather than only by date. Descriptively named meeting files also improve downstream knowledge graph quality: graphify extracts entity names and relationships from meeting content, but community labels and node descriptions are clearer when the source file name reinforces the meeting's topic.\n\nThe stale cache failure mode is the most operationally important finding from the 2026-06-17 session. In a multi-session rename workflow — where some meetings were renamed in a previous session and a new session continues — the local cache may retain the old \"generic\" classification for meetings that were actually renamed. This produces two failure modes: (1) re-proposing names for already-renamed meetings, causing redundant user confirmation prompts, and (2) an inflated \"genuinely generic\" count that misrepresents the actual backlog. The correct diagnostic step is to pull fresh state from the live Fireflies API for the targeted time window before classifying any meeting as \"needs rename.\" After the 2026-06-17 session, the re-sync correctly distinguished the 8 newly-renamed meetings from the 6 pre-existing renames, confirming the stale cache had been the source of the false positives.\n\nThe context disambiguation requirement reflects a frequent real-world pattern: major events (conferences, symposia, site visits) tend to dominate a day's meeting schedule and can create a temptation to group all same-day meetings under the dominant theme. The TCU/Roach Institute Sports Science Symposium generated four sessions on June 16 that naturally belong together as a cluster. However, two other meetings on the same day — a Baylor Athletics Website Redesign call and a separate staff talk — were explicitly confirmed by the user as independent of the symposium. A rename workflow that inferred thematic relatedness from date alone would have incorrectly titled these meetings as symposium sessions. Participant list inspection and brief content review are necessary before grouping nominally co-occurring meetings.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]] — The Fireflies integration documented there (new meetings synced, renamed, exported to the vault) is the per-session counterpart to this periodic batch-rename workflow; both serve the goal of maintaining a well-organized `Inbox/meetings/` corpus in SecondBrain.\n- [[concepts/graphify-meetings-corpus-analysis]] — The meetings corpus graphify run (also 2026-06-17) consumed the renamed meeting notes as input; the 8 renames completed before the graphify run improved entity and community quality in the resulting knowledge graph.\n- [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]] — The vault where renamed meeting notes are archived; descriptive filenames are essential for navigability given the no-plugin, no-Dataview constraint that rules out dynamic filename-based queries.\n- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — The stale cache gotcha is a specific instance of the \"verify against the authoritative source, not the intermediate representation\" principle: the local cache is a proxy that can diverge from Fireflies API ground truth after prior rename operations.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-17.md]] — Fireflies batch rename session (16:12 / 17:29): 35 meetings scanned from 30-day window, 14 apparently generic, 6 stale cache false positives filtered and skipped, 8 genuinely renamed via Fireflies API, local DB re-synced; TCU/Roach Institute symposium cluster vs. unrelated same-day calls disambiguated by user confirmation.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\fireflies-meeting-rename-workflow.md\n```markdown\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Fireflies Meeting Batch Rename Workflow\"\naliases: [Fireflies rename, meeting batch rename, Fireflies generic title, Fireflies stale cache, Fireflies API rename, meeting title cleanup, Fireflies local DB re-sync, timestamp-only meeting titles, symposium cluster naming]\ntags: [fireflies, workflow, productivity, knowledge-management, obsidian, second-brain, automation]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-17.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-17\nupdated: 2026-06-17\n---\n\n# Fireflies Meeting Batch Rename Workflow\n\nThe Fireflies meeting batch rename workflow is a process for identifying meetings with generic timestamp-only titles, proposing descriptive replacements, obtaining user confirmation, and executing renames via the Fireflies API. On 2026-06-17, 35 meetings were scanned; 14 had generic timestamp-only titles; 6 turned out already renamed from a prior session (stale local DB cache); and 8 were genuinely untitled — all from the Jun 16 TCU/Roach Institute symposium cluster plus one Jun 17 staff talk. All 8 were renamed via the Fireflies API and the local DB was re-synced afterward. Properly renamed meetings are a prerequisite for downstream knowledge-management operations such as graphify corpus runs and memsearch indexing, since a meeting titled \"TCU Roach Institute Symposium — Biomechanics Keynote\" contributes a semantically meaningful node while \"Meeting — 2026-06-16 14:32:00\" does not.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Batch scan pattern:** scan the meeting library for titles matching generic patterns (bare timestamps, \"Meeting with...\", auto-generated date strings) and group candidates for review before proposing replacements. Reviewing all candidates together before executing any rename prevents divergent naming conventions across related sessions.\n- **Stale local DB cache gotcha:** the local Fireflies DB cache can report meetings as having generic titles even after a prior rename was applied via the API in an earlier session. Always re-verify the candidate list against the live Fireflies API before counting meetings that need renaming — a meeting showing as \"untitled\" in the local cache may already have a good title in Fireflies proper. On 2026-06-17, 6 of 14 candidates were stale cache false positives from a prior session.\n- **Re-sync local DB after renames:** after executing renames via the Fireflies API, explicitly re-sync the local DB. Without re-sync, subsequent operations see stale state and may re-flag already-renamed meetings in the next session.\n- **Cluster vs. unrelated same-day meetings:** meetings from a symposium, conference, or multi-session event on the same date form a natural naming cluster (shared prefix: organization + event name; per-session suffix: topic or speaker). Unrelated calls that occurred on the same calendar day are not part of the cluster and must be named independently based on their own content.\n- **User confirmation is architecturally required for cluster disambiguation:** the workflow cannot correctly assign cluster membership without domain knowledge that only the meeting participant has. On 2026-06-17, the Baylor Athletics Website Redesign meeting occurred on the same date as the TCU Roach Institute symposium and would have incorrectly received a symposium prefix without user review.\n- **Naming conventions:** descriptive titles are preferred over timestamp-only names; symposium sessions include the organization, event name, and session topic; standalone calls include the participant names or the discussion topic.\n- **2026-06-17 metrics:** 35 meetings scanned → 14 generic-title candidates → 6 stale cache (already renamed, skipped) → 8 genuinely untitled → all 8 renamed successfully.\n\n## Details\n\nThe batch rename workflow operates against the Fireflies meeting library to convert auto-generated timestamp-only titles into descriptive, searchable names. Timestamp titles make the library effectively unsearchable and prevent graphify or memsearch tools from producing meaningful results from meeting-note corpora. The rename workflow is therefore a prerequisite for any downstream knowledge-management operation on meeting notes. When graphify runs over a corpus of 78 meeting notes, a meeting titled \"TCU Roach Institute Applied Sport Science Symposium — Biomechanics Keynote\" contributes a semantically rich node with natural connections to adjacent sport-science concepts, while \"Meeting — 2026-06-16 14:32:00\" generates only a date-string node with no cross-community edges. The quality of the downstream knowledge graph is directly proportional to the quality of meeting titles in the source corpus.\n\nThe stale cache gotcha is the operationally most important failure mode in the rename workflow. When a batch rename session is interrupted or only partially completed, the local Fireflies DB retains the pre-rename title for any meeting whose rename API call was not followed by a local DB re-sync. On the next session, the cache-based scan reports those meetings as candidates again — they appear to still have generic titles from the local perspective, even though Fireflies proper already holds the correct title. The consequence of not detecting this is wasted API calls and, more seriously, the risk of overwriting a good title with a newly-proposed one that may differ in wording. The diagnostic check is straightforward: for any candidate that was worked in a recent prior session, verify the current title via a direct Fireflies API read before proposing a new name. If the API returns a non-generic title, mark it as stale in the local cache and skip it rather than re-processing. The explicit post-rename re-sync step closes the loop by updating the local DB immediately after each successful batch rename operation, preventing the next session from encountering the same stale state.\n\nThe cluster naming convention addresses an important disambiguation challenge in calendar-dense periods. A symposium, training camp, or multi-day conference can produce 4–8 back-to-back Fireflies meetings on the same date, all from the same event. These naturally share a naming prefix (the event name and organization) with per-session suffixes (session title, speaker, topic). Any meeting recorded on the same date that is not part of the event — a vendor call, a staff check-in, a separate project meeting — must not receive the event name as its prefix. This requires user confirmation of the full proposed rename list because the workflow's automated detection can only identify calendar date co-occurrence, not event membership. The user's domain knowledge distinguishes \"this call was part of the symposium\" from \"this call happened to occur on the same day as the symposium but is a completely separate conversation about website redesign.\"\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/graphify-incremental-merge]] — Running graphify over meeting notes produces more meaningful knowledge graphs when meetings have descriptive titles; the batch rename workflow is a prerequisite that improves the semantic quality of graphify's extracted node labels and enables meaningful God Node identification.\n- [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]] — Fireflies integration (meeting sync, rename, vault export) is documented there as the canonical per-session meeting-capture workflow; the batch rename workflow complements that per-session step by addressing meetings missed during initial capture or imported from bulk library syncs.\n- [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]] — Renamed and exported Fireflies meeting notes land in `SecondBrain/Inbox/meetings/`; the vault's plain-markdown constraint means all Fireflies exports must be in standard markdown format compatible with the vault's wikilink and frontmatter conventions.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-17.md]] — Batch rename session (16:12–17:29): 35 meetings scanned, 14 generic-title candidates identified, 6 stale cache false positives detected and skipped, 8 genuinely untitled meetings renamed via Fireflies API, local DB re-synced, TCU/Roach Institute symposium cluster pattern documented, Baylor Athletics Website Redesign meeting explicitly disambiguated from symposium cluster based on user confirmation.\n```\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\graphify-incremental-merge.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Graphify Incremental Merge Workflow\"\naliases: [graphify merge, graphify incremental, knowledge graph merge, graphify pipeline, graphify-out memory, graphify update, graphify node extraction, PowerShell graphify quoting, graphify bridge node, graphify chunk truncation, graphify salvage, entity deduplication graphify, first-name ambiguity graph]\ntags: [knowledge-management, obsidian, tooling, keystoneos, workflow, graph]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-11.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-17.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-16\nupdated: 2026-06-17\n---\n\n# Graphify Incremental Merge Workflow\n\nGraphify can be run incrementally — processing a single new document and merging its extracted nodes into an existing knowledge graph rather than rebuilding the graph from scratch. On 2026-06-11, a product roadmap course note (~1,405 words) was processed by graphify for the KeystoneOS project, extracting 29 nodes that were merged into the existing graph, growing it from 61 to 90 nodes, 140 to 173 edges, and maintaining 9 semantic communities. Trace results are stored in `graphify-out\\memory\\` for future `--update` queryability, and a PowerShell quoting gotcha was discovered and resolved. On 2026-06-17, a full meetings corpus run (78 documents) surfaced two additional lessons applicable to all graphify runs: chunk output truncation recovery and entity deduplication failure when bare first names are present in an organizational corpus.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Incremental merge, not full rebuild:** graphify supports adding new source material to an existing graph without reprocessing the entire corpus. The merge integrates newly extracted nodes and edges into the existing graph structure, with community detection re-run on the merged result.\n- **2026-06-11 growth metrics:** 61 → 90 nodes (+29), 140 → 173 edges (+33), 9 communities maintained. Input was a ~1,405 word product roadmap course note.\n- **Bridge nodes reveal cross-community insights:** the `Adoption Is the Bottleneck` node bridges two distinct communities (Roadmap Process & Alignment ↔ Roadmap Strategy & Prioritization) because the underlying note explicitly links the milestone-selection rule (target adoption barriers) to both strategic planning and execution alignment — a non-obvious structural connection made visible in the graph.\n- **Trace results saved to `graphify-out\\memory\\`:** the rationale behind bridge relationships is saved for future `--update` queryability, making the graph's reasoning auditable and extensible across sessions.\n- **PowerShell inline script quoting gotcha:** when constructing graphify merge commands in PowerShell, inline scripts (JSON payloads, multi-line arguments, strings with special characters) are mangled by PowerShell's quoting rules. The fix: write complex content to a temp file first, then reference the file path in the command.\n- **Chunk output truncation recovery (2026-06-17):** graphify processes large corpora in chunks; output can be truncated mid-stream at token limits. Salvage approach: extract nodes and edges arrays from markdown-fenced and partial JSON content produced before the truncation point. On 2026-06-17 this recovered 142/142 nodes and 171/197 edges (87%) from a truncated chunk without re-running the full chunk. Re-running is not always necessary when node completeness is high.\n- **Entity deduplication — first-name ambiguity in orgs (2026-06-17):** bare first-name nodes are unreliable targets for speculative semantic merging in organizational corpora with multiple professionals sharing common first names. In the 2026-06-17 meetings corpus, Tyler, Kevin, and Cody each resolved to 2 distinct people (Tyler Held / Tyler Wright, Kevin Robinson / Kevin Washington, Cody Soto / Cody Hall). False `semantically_similar_to` merges must be removed; always confirm first-name disambiguation with the user before merging.\n\n## Details\n\nThe incremental merge workflow is architecturally distinct from a full-corpus rebuild. Rather than re-ingesting all source documents, graphify processes a single new document, extracts its semantic entities and relationships, and merges them into the existing graph's node and edge set. This makes the workflow practical for large, growing knowledge graphs: each new document takes seconds to process and merge while the accumulated graph structure grows organically. The trace artifact saved to `graphify-out\\memory\\` records the provenance of bridge relationships — which source material linked which previously-disconnected communities — enabling future graph traversal to explain why two concepts are structurally connected. Saving traces is especially valuable for incrementally built graphs where the rationale for any given edge may span multiple source documents added in separate sessions.\n\nThe PowerShell quoting issue is a Windows-specific friction point in the graphify workflow. PowerShell's argument-handling rules for complex string arguments differ from bash's rules: JSON payloads, multi-line strings, and arguments containing double quotes, backslashes, or special characters are subject to nested escape sequences that mangle the intended content when passed inline. The reliable pattern is to write the complex content to a temporary `.json` or `.txt` file and reference that file by path in the graphify command. This sidesteps PowerShell's quoting rules entirely — the file is read raw, without shell interpolation — and matches the same principle documented for hook scripts in [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]: prefer file-based argument passing over inline strings when the shell's quoting semantics would transform the content.\n\nChunk output truncation is a reliability concern for any graphify run over a large corpus or a single long document that generates substantial output. The salvage approach works because graphify's output format is structured: nodes and edges are output as JSON arrays within markdown code fences. Content before the truncation point is often well-formed even if the overall output is incomplete. Extracting the nodes object and edges object from pre-truncation content yields a partial but usable graph segment. The decision to accept partial recovery vs. re-run the full chunk depends on the ratio of recovered to total edges and the sensitivity of the analysis to missing relationships. For most exploratory knowledge graph use cases, 85-90% edge recovery is sufficient. For the full-corpus meetings case, see [[concepts/graphify-meetings-corpus-analysis]] for the specific recovery metrics and the additional entity deduplication challenges that arise at corpus scale.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/graphify-vault-separation]] — The architectural decision to route graphify's output to the Obsidian vault rather than application repositories; this article covers the complementary operational question of how to use graphify incrementally once that destination is established.\n- [[concepts/keystoneos-project-registry]] — The same KeystoneOS Round 2 session (Phase A: Ingest) ran the graphify merge alongside Phase B's DEV sweep; both are components of the same four-phase KeystoneOS infrastructure build-out.\n- [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] — Another case where PowerShell's execution environment produced malformed command content; the file-based workaround pattern (write to temp file, reference file path) is structurally identical in both cases.\n- [[concepts/graphify-meetings-corpus-analysis]] — The full meetings corpus graphify run (78 documents, 2026-06-17) that surfaced the chunk truncation salvage and entity deduplication lessons documented here.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-11.md]] — Graphify incremental merge session (11:38): roadmap course note processed, 29 nodes extracted, KeystoneOS graph grown from 61→90 nodes / 140→173 edges / 9 communities, `Adoption Is the Bottleneck` bridge node traced and saved to `graphify-out\\memory\\`, PowerShell quoting gotcha documented, commit `d7a936b` pushed.\n- [[daily/2026-06-17.md]] — Meetings corpus graphify session (16:12 / 17:29): chunk truncation salvage pattern confirmed (142/142 nodes, 171/197 edges recovered from truncated chunk 2), first-name entity deduplication failure mode discovered and corrected (3 false merges removed across 6 distinct people).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\graphify-meetings-corpus-analysis.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Graphify Meetings Corpus Analysis\"\naliases: [meetings graphify, meeting notes graph, graphify meetings corpus, SecondBrain meetings graph, God Nodes meetings, BAIR Research Initiative graph, graphify-out meetings, 78 meeting notes, meeting entity deduplication, chunk truncation salvage]\ntags: [knowledge-management, obsidian, graphify, meetings, second-brain, workflow, networking]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-17.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-17\nupdated: 2026-06-17\n---\n\n# Graphify Meetings Corpus Analysis\n\nOn 2026-06-17, graphify was run over the full SecondBrain `Inbox/meetings/` corpus (78 meeting notes), producing an interactive knowledge graph at `C:\\Users\\eric_rash\\Desktop\\SecondBrain\\Inbox\\meetings\\graphify-out\\`. After a chunk truncation salvage and a user-guided entity-deduplication correction, the final graph contained 531 nodes, 489 edges, and 99 communities. This full-corpus run is distinct from the incremental single-document merge pattern documented in [[concepts/graphify-incremental-merge]] — different input type, different entity vocabulary, different God Node profile, and different failure modes.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Full corpus vs. incremental:** 78 meeting notes processed as a complete build, not an incremental addition to an existing graph. Output: `SecondBrain/Inbox/meetings/graphify-out/graph.html`, `graph.json`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md`.\n- **God Nodes in meeting graphs:** high-connectivity nodes in a meetings corpus are recurring meeting subjects and primary attendees, not over-general concept abstractions. On 2026-06-17, `BAIR Research Initiative` and `Eric Rash` each had 9 edges — the dominant connecting threads across 78 professional conversations.\n- **Chunk output truncation recovery:** graphify chunk 2 was truncated mid-stream at the output limit. Salvage routine extracted structured objects from pre-truncation content (markdown-fenced + partial JSON), recovering 142/142 nodes and 171/197 edges (87% edge recovery). The remaining 26 edges were unrecoverable; re-running the full chunk is not always necessary or cost-effective when partial recovery achieves high node completeness.\n- **Entity deduplication failure — first-name ambiguity in orgs:** bare first-name nodes (Tyler, Kevin, Cody) were initially flagged as potential duplicates. Three `semantically_similar_to` edges were speculatively added, wrongly merging Tyler Held with Tyler Wright, Kevin Robinson with Kevin Washington, and Cody Soto with Cody Hall (6 distinct people). User correction removed the 3 false edges and renamed bare nodes to full names; final graph: 531 nodes, 489 edges, 99 communities.\n- **Always confirm disambiguation with user:** the correct default for bare first-name nodes in a sports-science organizational context is \"treat as distinct until explicitly confirmed otherwise.\" The cost of a false merge (removing a real person from the graph) exceeds the cost of a false non-merge (two nodes for the same person).\n- **Manifest/cost tracking before cleanup:** cleanup ran before outputs were saved to the manifest and cost-tracking files. Lesson: always write manifest and outputs before the cleanup step in graphify pipeline runs.\n\n## Details\n\nThe meetings corpus graphify run is epistemically different from running graphify over research papers or project documentation. Meeting notes capture relational structure — who met with whom, what topics recurred across conversations, which initiatives span multiple relationship threads — rather than primarily conceptual structure. The knowledge graph's most valuable insight is therefore not a taxonomy of concepts but the connectivity pattern among people, initiatives, and recurring topics. God Nodes in meeting graphs are legitimate high-connectivity entities — the people and programs that appear across the widest range of professional conversations — rather than vocabulary inflation artifacts. `BAIR Research Initiative` with 9 edges indicates this initiative was referenced across many distinct meetings with different people; `Eric Rash` with 9 edges reflects his role as the primary meeting attendee whose name anchors the corpus.\n\nThe entity deduplication challenge in meeting graphs is particularly acute because meeting notes abbreviate names to first names in informal transcripts or use only the first name in one-on-one meeting titles. A sports-science department at a large university will have multiple staff members sharing common given names (Tyler, Kevin, Cody, Eric, Blake) far more frequently than a small research group or startup. Graphify's semantic similarity-based entity resolution performs well for concept nodes and technical terms, but is unreliable for distinguishing people with identical first names. \"Tyler Held\" and \"Tyler Wright\" share an identical first name with different last names; \"Kevin Robinson\" and \"Kevin Washington\" are semantically similar as strings without organizational context. The correct architectural response is to flag potential first-name duplicates for explicit user review rather than auto-merging, and to default bare-name nodes to \"distinct\" rather than \"merged\" in organizational contexts.\n\nThe chunk truncation salvage technique is operationally important for large corpus graphify runs where a single chunk's output can exceed token output limits. Rather than immediately re-running the failed chunk (expensive and potentially repetitive), the salvage approach extracts the nodes and edges arrays from whatever content was produced before the truncation point — using markdown-fence detection and partial-JSON parsing to recover well-formed sections. On 2026-06-17, this approach achieved 100% node recovery and 87% edge recovery from the truncated chunk. The 13% edge loss (26 edges) is an acceptable degradation for most analytical purposes, and the decision of whether to re-run for full edge completeness can be deferred based on the specific use case. See [[concepts/graphify-incremental-merge]] for the chunk truncation salvage pattern applied in the incremental-merge context.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/graphify-incremental-merge]] — The incremental single-document merge workflow; On 2026-05-13, all 9 GSD-generated hooks required manual rewriting — replacing PowerShell constructs with plain `node` and `bash` commands — before the hooks would fire correctly.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- GSD writes hook commands using the PowerShell call operator `&` before quoted executable paths (e.g., `& \"C:/Program Files/nodejs/node.exe\" ...`), which bash does not understand.\n- Claude Code's hook execution environment is bash on all platforms, including Windows — it does not use PowerShell even when the user's interactive terminal is PowerShell.\n- The fix: replace `& \"C:/Program Files/nodejs/node.exe\"` with plain `node` (relying on `node` being on the bash `PATH`), and rewrite any other PowerShell-specific constructs to POSIX shell equivalents.\n- GSD does not detect the execution environment when generating hooks; it produces PowerShell syntax unconditionally on Windows.\n- All 9 GSD-generated hooks required this rewrite; a Claude Code restart is needed afterward for changes to `settings.json` to take effect.\n\n## Details\n\nThis failure belongs to a recognizable class of Claude Code hook gotcha: a tool observes the user's interactive shell environment (PowerShell on Windows) when generating hooks, but Claude Code's hook runner is a separate, minimal bash process that does not inherit the interactive shell's type, syntax, or environment. The mismatch is syntactic in the GSD case — bash does not parse the `&` call operator at all — rather than merely a PATH issue, but the underlying assumption failure is the same: \"if it works in my terminal, it will work as a Claude Code hook.\"\n\nThe same class of problem appeared during the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` hook setup on 2026-04-14 (see [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]), where `uv` had to be referenced by its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) because Claude Code's hook environment might not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`. Both cases are instances of the same root cause, explored in [[connections/hook-execution-environment-path-assumptions]]. The practical prevention strategy is consistent across both cases: always normalize hook commands to their most portable form — plain binary names that are on a standard bash `PATH`, and POSIX shell syntax rather than shell-specific constructs — regardless of what the interactive terminal accepts.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-cli-marketplace-setup]] - The GSD installation session this issue arose in; the hook rewrite was a required step before the environment was functional.\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] - An earlier (2026-04-14) hook setup that hit the same class of failure from a different angle (missing `PATH` entry rather than shell syntax mismatch).\n- [[connections/hook-execution-environment-path-assumptions]] - Cross-cutting connection that pairs this GSD bash-rewrite lesson with the `uv` PATH lesson as instances of the same \"hook environment ≠ interactive shell\" failure mode.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-13.md]] - GSD hook rewriting session (17:09): PowerShell `&` syntax vs. bash discovery, 9-hook rewrite, and required restart.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\inbox-triage-methodology.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Inbox Triage Methodology (Structured 6-Category Audit)\"\naliases: [inbox triage, communication triage, structured inbox audit, 6-category inbox, needs_reply follow_ups forms_owed, communication management, Outlook audit, age importance prioritization]\ntags: [productivity, workflow, email, communication, triage, morning-briefing, baylor-athletics]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-08.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-08\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Inbox Triage Methodology (Structured 6-Category Audit)\n\nA structured inbox triage is an ad-hoc deep-audit process that produces a comprehensive categorized snapshot of all pending communications in an email client. Unlike the automated morning email briefing (see [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]]), which delivers a pre-processed summary at a fixed daily time, the inbox triage is run on demand — typically when the communication queue has grown large or when a full reset of communication state is needed. On 2026-06-08, a full audit of Eric Rash's Outlook inbox at Baylor Athletics produced a structured JSON of 50 categorized items across 6 buckets, establishing a prioritized reply and follow-up plan for the session.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **6-category taxonomy:** `needs_reply` (11), `follow_ups` (3), `meetings_to_schedule` (3), `forms_owed` (3), `still_open` (6), `FYI/newsletters` (24). This taxonomy mirrors the 6-section structure of [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]], making triage output directly consumable by the automated morning briefing pipeline and the [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] must-do generator.\n- **Structured JSON audit:** the triage produces a machine-readable structured output categorizing all pending items before any replies are written, enabling systematic prioritization across the full queue rather than time-boxing around the first items encountered.\n- **Prioritization heuristic: age × importance.** Overdue compliance items (timecards, hard-deadline forms) rank first; then aged replies sorted oldest-first; then newer but high-urgency items. The 2026-06-08 audit surfaced a 9-day-overdue Playfly LLC timecard verification as the single highest-urgency item.\n- **FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume:** 24 of 50 items (48%) required no action. Segregating these into a dedicated FYI category is essential to keeping actionable items visible and preventing low-urgency volume from masking real obligations.\n- **Communication debt compounds with age:** 11–13 day stale items (Quin Sandler check-in 11 days stale, Kyle Van Pelt collaboration thread 13 days stale) represent accumulated relational risk; the age-based sort within categories surfaces these items explicitly before newer but less urgent ones.\n\n## Details\n\nThe structured inbox triage serves a different function than daily briefings or on-ramp automation. A morning briefing is a push-based system delivering a pre-processed communication summary each day; the inbox triage is a pull-based reset that generates a complete ground-truth snapshot of the full communication queue at a single point in time. The triage is most valuable when the queue has gone unmanaged for several days and the true scope of outstanding obligations is unclear. By producing a structured JSON audit before any responses are written, the triage makes the full scope visible simultaneously — enabling optimal prioritization across the entire queue rather than reactive processing of items in arrival order.\n\nThe 2026-06-08 triage revealed a characteristic distribution: FYI/newsletters (48%) were the largest single category by volume but required no action; `needs_reply` (11 items, 22%) was the most operationally important actionable category; and the three remaining actionable categories (`follow_ups`, `meetings_to_schedule`, `forms_owed`) each contained 3 items. This distribution validates the morning email briefing system's 6-section design hypothesis — that most inbox volume is low-urgency FYI, while high-urgency obligations are concentrated in a smaller set of actionable items. The Playfly LLC timecard (9 days overdue) exemplifies the `forms_owed` category's compliance-critical character: unlike email replies where a delay primarily affects relationships, an overdue timecard carries institutional consequences that escalate with each passing day. Age-based prioritization within each category makes these escalating risks visible immediately rather than requiring manual scanning for overdue items.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]] — The automated daily briefing system whose 6-section format this triage taxonomy mirrors; the triage output can directly populate the briefing's NEEDS REPLY, FOLLOW UPS, MEETINGS TO SCHEDULE, FORMS/TASKS OWED, STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS, and FYI sections without schema translation.\n- [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] — The lean-mode on-ramp pipeline that consumes inbox triage output (alongside OKR scoreboards and carry-forward items) to generate the day's must-do list; a completed triage is one of the primary inputs that makes the on-ramp's communication-triage section substantive on days following multi-day queue growth.\n- [[connections/inbox-triage-and-morning-briefing-taxonomy]] — The cross-cutting connection documenting how the same 6-category taxonomy spans this manual audit tool, the automated morning briefing, and the on-ramp distillation pipeline as a shared architectural contract.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-08.md]] — Full inbox audit session (08:04): 50 items categorized across 6 buckets (11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters), age × importance prioritization applied, Playfly LLC timecard flagged as 9-day overdue, reply and follow-up action items identified across all actionable categories.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\ingest-book-skill.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Ingest-Book Skill: Pipeline, Cost Model, and Model-Split Guidance\"\naliases: [ingest-book, book atomization, ingest-book skill, BookInbox, per-chapter checkpoint, book cost model, LLM pipeline model split, Haiku atomization warning, Sonnet atomization, book ingestion cost, _book.md, chapter checkpoint]\ntags: [claude-code, skills, knowledge-management, llm, cost-optimization, second-brain, sports-science, automation]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-12.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-12\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Ingest-Book Skill: Pipeline, Cost Model, and Model-Split Guidance\n\nThe `ingest-book` skill is a Claude Code skill that ingests books into the SecondBrain library through a three-stage pipeline: deterministic PDF extraction (zero LLM tokens), per-chapter orchestration (cheap-tier model acceptable), and quality-driven atomization (Sonnet or stronger required). On 2026-06-12, a pilot run ingested Periodization Ch1–2, measured the full cost profile, and baked model-split guidance directly into the skill with an explicit \"do NOT use Haiku\" instruction for the atomization stage. The skill lives in `~/.claude/skills/` (a working-tree path, not a git repo), so changes apply immediately without a commit.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Three-stage pipeline with mandatory model-tier separation:** (1) extraction = deterministic Python, zero model tokens — mechanical PDF parsing, chunking, and metadata extraction; (2) chapter orchestration = Haiku-tier acceptable — coordinating chapter sequence and tracking state; (3) atomization = Sonnet or stronger, no exceptions — converting raw chapter text into discrete, permanently-indexed knowledge entries.\n- **Pilot cost profile:** ~214K raw input tokens read, ~38K atomized output tokens produced for a full 12-chapter book. Realistically ~400K–800K billed input per book in a single session; prompt caching and per-chapter checkpointing reduce actual spend significantly relative to a naive single-context run.\n- **Three cost levers that preserve quality:** (a) atomize only chapters you will actively consult rather than ingesting the full book upfront; (b) checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches to flush the context window and benefit from prompt caching across batches; (c) let deterministic Python extractors handle all mechanical lifting before any LLM token is spent.\n- **Model downgrade is the wrong cost lever:** using Haiku for atomization saves tokens but produces permanently inferior entries that degrade every advisor response built on those entries. Bad atomization is not correctable without re-ingesting the chapter. Cost reduction must come from reducing input volume, not reducing output quality.\n- **Resumable mid-book via `_book.md`:** in-progress ingestion state is stored in `_book.md`; Periodization Ch3–12 remain pending and are resumable in any future session via `ingest-book` without re-processing completed chapters.\n\n## Details\n\nThe three-stage pipeline design separates mechanical work from intellectual work at the model-selection boundary. Extraction — converting PDF bytes to structured text, identifying chapter boundaries, extracting titles and section headers — is fundamentally deterministic and benefits from zero LLM involvement. Running extraction as pure Python produces consistent, auditable output without token cost and without the risk of LLM-introduced variation in structural parsing. Orchestration — coordinating which chapter to process next, tracking state, managing the ingestion queue — requires some intelligence but not deep judgment; a fast, cheap model is appropriate because mistakes at the orchestration layer are recoverable (rerun the failed step). Atomization — converting raw chapter text into discrete, memsearch-indexable knowledge entries with accurate titles, content, and cross-references — is the quality-determining step for the entire system. Each atomized entry is permanent: it either accurately captures the source material's prescriptive content or it introduces a subtle distortion that propagates to every advisor response that cites it. This permanence is why Haiku is disqualified: the quality-per-token ratio at the atomization stage is dominated by entry accuracy, not token efficiency.\n\nThe per-chapter checkpoint + `/clear` pattern is the primary cost management strategy that does not sacrifice quality. A 12-chapter book processed in a single session accumulates a growing context window as each chapter's input and output stack on top of prior chapters. By inserting a `/clear` between chapter batches — flushing the context window — each new batch benefits from a fresh, smaller context that is cheaper to process and more likely to be served from the prompt cache. The `_book.md` state file makes this pattern safe: the skill records which chapters have been atomized and which remain, so sessions interrupted mid-book can be resumed from the last completed checkpoint without re-processing earlier chapters. The ~400K–800K billed estimate for a full book reflects a checkpoint-aware run; a naive single-context run would be materially more expensive. The cross-book convergence check — activated when a second domain book lands in `BookInbox` — adds a synthesis pass that identifies convergent and divergent claims across sources, but this pass only runs after both books are atomized, not during initial ingestion.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/book-advisor-system]] — The advisor architecture that consumes the entries produced by this ingestion pipeline; atomization quality at the Sonnet+ stage directly determines advisor response quality.\n- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The semantic search infrastructure that indexes atomized entries; the 805-chunk index confirmed operational after Python migration recovery serves as the retrieval layer for all advisor queries built on ingested books.\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] — A related knowledge compilation pipeline (conversation logs → knowledge articles) that shares the \"gather mechanically, synthesize with quality\" design philosophy and the same separation between cheap gathering and quality-sensitive synthesis.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-meta-skills-bundle]] — An earlier (2026-05-20) session on skill curation and selective installation; the `ingest-book` skill follows the same principle of evaluating each tool for genuine unique value before adding it to the skills layer.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-12.md]] — Pilot cost measurement, model-split guidance baking into skill, per-chapter checkpoint strategy, resumable `_book.md` state design, \"do NOT use Haiku\" instruction documented (18:08).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\jinja2-none-safety-pattern.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Jinja2 None-Safety: `is not none` vs. `default()`\"\naliases: [Jinja2 default filter gotcha, is not none guard, None-safe Jinja2 templates]\ntags: [jinja2, templating, python, gotcha, web-dev]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-24.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-24\nupdated: 2026-04-24\n---\n\n# Jinja2 None-Safety: `is not none` vs. `default()`\n\nJinja2's `default()` filter does not reliably handle `None` values across all Jinja2 versions - it is designed primarily to substitute a fallback for *undefined* variables, not for variables that are explicitly set to `None`. The reliable alternative, adopted on 2026-04-24 for trend chart data in the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]]'s `report.html.j2` template, is an explicit `{% if value is not none %}` guard.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- `default()` is intended to provide a fallback value for *undefined* template variables, but its handling of variables that are present but set to `None` is inconsistent across Jinja2 versions.\n- The robust pattern for optional numeric/metric values is an explicit `{% if value is not none %}` check before using or rendering the value, rather than relying on `default()` to coerce `None` to a fallback.\n- This pattern was applied to trend chart data in `report.html.j2` as part of completing Task 9 of the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]].\n- The distinction matters specifically for fields that can be legitimately `None` (e.g., a metric that hasn't been recorded yet for a given period) as opposed to fields that are simply missing/undefined from the template context.\n\n## Details\n\nThis gotcha falls into a recognizable class of bugs: a library or templating engine handles a particular value (\"undefined\" vs. explicitly `None`) differently than a developer might assume, and the difference only surfaces when real data contains that edge case - here, a trend series with a gap (a period with no recorded Weight Room score, represented as `None` rather than simply absent). Relying on `default()` to \"just handle\" `None` works in some Jinja2 versions/configurations but not others, making it a fragile choice for production report templates that need to render correctly regardless of which periods have data.\n\nThe fix - an explicit `is not none` guard - is unambiguous and version-independent: it directly tests for the Python `None` value rather than relying on Jinja2's undefined-handling machinery. This is conceptually similar to another framework-quirk lesson recorded in [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-deployment]], where Neon (serverless Postgres) returns date/timestamp columns as native JS `Date` objects that don't serialize automatically across a server/client boundary - in both cases, a framework returns or handles a value in a form slightly different from the naive expectation, and the fix is an explicit, defensive check/conversion rather than relying on the framework's default behavior.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]] - The project and specific template (`report.html.j2`, trend charts) where this pattern was applied.\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-deployment]] - An earlier (2026-04-14) instance of a similar class of framework-serialization/type-handling gotcha (Neon `Date` objects needing explicit conversion).\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-04-24.md]] - Task 9 implementation session (17:06), where this pattern was adopted for trend chart data.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\keystone-os-tezino-project.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"KeystoneOS Tezino Narrative Project\"\naliases: [Tezino, Phase 1 data gaps, force plate backfill, CMJ backfill, IMTP, VALD]\ntags: [keystoneos, sports-science, vald, catapult, data-pipeline, force-plate]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-10.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-04-14.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-04-25.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-09.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-10\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# KeystoneOS Tezino Narrative Project\n\nThe Tezino narrative project is a KeystoneOS effort to build a data-driven narrative of an athlete's (Tezino's) physical readiness across a training cycle. The registry is populated via a periodic DEV sweep — an audit of all projects in the DEV directory that classifies each as confirmed-live, ambiguous (requires user decision), or inactive. On 2026-06-11, a DEV sweep was executed as Phase B of KeystoneOS Round 2 (a four-phase plan: Ingest, Sweep, Route, Schedule): 32 candidates were found, 3 were auto-promoted to confirmed-live, and 5 were deferred for user confirmation before a next-session gate.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **DEV sweep classification into three buckets:** all DEV directory projects are evaluated as **confirmed-live** (actively worked on; should be in the registry), **ambiguous** (unclear current status; requires explicit user decision), or **inactive** (not recently touched; excluded by default). Only confirmed-live and user-confirmed ambiguous projects enter the registry.\n- **2026-06-11 sweep results (32 candidates):** 3 promoted to confirmed-live — `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem`, `Travel_Map`, `morning-briefing`. 5 deferred for user veto/add — `ai-analyst`, `FootballWeightTargetTool`, `PlayerProfiles_FB`, `SportScienceResearchRepo`, `token-dashboard`.\n- **Ambiguous projects are NOT auto-promoted:** promoting uncertain projects risks incorrect context injection and stale routing in future sessions. User confirmation is a hard gate before any ambiguous project enters the registry.\n- **Registry feeds the AGENTS.md routing table (Phase C):** confirmed-live projects in the registry become entries in AGENTS.md's canonical one-hop routing table (see [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]]), making their context resolvable in a single lookup by any model.\n- **Phase B of a four-phase Round 2 plan:** the sweep is one step in a complete KeystoneOS build-out sequence: Phase A (Ingest: graphify merge of new knowledge), Phase B (Sweep: DEV inventory), Phase C (Route: AGENTS.md routing table rewrite), Phase D (Schedule: morning cadence task). Four commits shipped (`116b536`…`8ce3b5b`).\n\n## Details\n\nThe DEV sweep pattern addresses a recurring problem in multi-project AI-assisted workflows: context drift, where the AI system's view of active projects diverges from reality as new projects are created, old ones are abandoned, and DEV directories accumulate without formal closure. By treating the DEV directory as the ground truth and periodically classifying its contents, the sweep resynchronizes the registry with actual development activity. The three-bucket classification is deliberately conservative: rather than inferring project status from directory structure or file modification timestamps alone, the sweep flags ambiguous cases for explicit human decision rather than silently including or excluding them. This prevents the registry from silently accumulating cold projects that consume context tokens in future sessions without contributing useful routing information — and prevents silently excluding projects that are genuinely ongoing.\n\nThe five deferred candidates from 2026-06-11 illustrate the ambiguous-project challenge. `SportScienceResearchRepo`, `PlayerProfiles_FB`, and `token-dashboard` are all previously-documented active projects referenced in existing KB articles, but their current activity level is uncertain. `ai-analyst` and `FootballWeightTargetTool` are less documented in existing KB articles and may be inactive or superseded. Including them without user confirmation risks injecting stale project context into sessions that rely on the registry for routing; excluding them risks missing projects that are genuinely ongoing. The deferred-for-confirmation pattern puts the decision where it belongs — with the user who has ground-truth knowledge of current priorities — while ensuring the decision is not deferred indefinitely by documenting the candidates explicitly as a next-session action item.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] — The AGENTS.md routing table that the project registry feeds: confirmed-live registry entries become the one-hop routing table entries, enabling cross-model project context resolution in a single lookup.\n- [[concepts/graphify-incremental-merge]] — Phase A of the same KeystoneOS Round 2 session; the graphify incremental merge (Ingest) and the DEV sweep (Sweep) are sequential phases of the same four-part infrastructure build-out.\n- [[concepts/project-triage-retrospective]] — The 4-bucket cold-project triage for personal project management; the DEV sweep is the KeystoneOS analog — a more automated, registry-focused version of the same \"force explicit decisions about project status rather than passive accumulation\" discipline.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-11.md]] — KeystoneOS Round 2 Phase B DEV sweep session (16:53): 32 DEV candidates evaluated, 3 confirmed-live promoted (ForcePlate_DecisionSystem, Travel_Map, morning-briefing), 5 ambiguous deferred (ai-analyst, FootballWeightTargetTool, PlayerProfiles_FB, SportScienceResearchRepo, token-dashboard), ambiguous-not-auto-promoted rule established, four commits pushed.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\memsearch-tool-maintenance.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Memsearch: Setup, Python Migration Recovery, and Indexing\"\naliases: [memsearch, memsearch index, memsearch flush patch, memsearch shebang path, memsearch Python migration, 805 chunks indexed, memsearch explicit paths, memsearch reinstall, cross-project memory search, memsearch shim, memsearch ETIMEDOUT, memsearch concurrent contention, memsearch exit 1 silent, Python path capture staleness, venv broken after Python migration, morning_briefing venv rebuild]\ntags: [claude-code, memory, tooling, windows, python, infrastructure, maintenance, search]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-11.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-13.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-17.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-16\nupdated: 2026-06-17\n---\n\n# Memsearch: Setup, Python Migration Recovery, and Indexing\n\nMemsearch is a local semantic search tool that indexes Claude Code's Tier A project-memory files, enabling cross-project retrieval of durable knowledge without directly accessing each project's files. On 2026-06-11, memsearch indexing failures were diagnosed and resolved: the root cause was a Python migration that left a hardcoded stale path inside memsearch.exe, making it unable to locate its runtime. Recovery required reinstalling memsearch into the new Python environment, re-applying the flush patch, and replacing the stale shim. After recovery, 805 chunks were confirmed indexed and searchable. On 2026-06-13, a concurrent-contention ETIMEDOUT pattern was observed and characterized. On 2026-06-17, the same Python-path-capture failure class was confirmed in a second tool: the `morning-briefing` pipeline's `.venv` was broken since 2026-06-12 because it referenced `C:\\Python314` which had since been removed — the fix was rebuilding the venv against the current Python installation.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Cross-project Tier A search:** Tier A project-memory files (see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]]) are cross-project searchable via memsearch — not siloed to a single project context. Future sessions can surface facts from `project_<name>.md` and `user_career_timeline.md` files regardless of which project they are working in.\n- **Python migration breaks memsearch:** memsearch.exe embeds a path to the Python executable at install time (hardcoded shebang or binary-embedded interpreter path). When Python is migrated — old installation deleted, new one installed at a different path — memsearch fails because its embedded path is no longer valid. The failure is an install-time path capture becoming stale, not a configuration issue.\n- **Recovery sequence (three steps):**\n  1. Reinstall memsearch into the new Python environment so the new Python path is embedded in the binary\n  2. Re-apply the flush patch (a memsearch modification enabling integration with Claude Code's Stop hook)\n  3. Replace the stale shim file with one pointing to the new installation\n- **After recovery on 2026-06-11:** 805 chunks indexed and confirmed searchable.\n- **`index` command requires explicit paths:** memsearch's `index` command does not auto-discover project memory directories; the hook or invocation script must pass explicit file and directory paths. Implicit discovery is not supported — the explicit-paths requirement makes indexing scope deterministic and auditable.\n- **ETIMEDOUT concurrent contention (2026-06-13):** when multiple Claude Code sessions or background jobs invoke memsearch near-simultaneously, they contend for the same index and produce ETIMEDOUT errors. On 2026-06-13, 6 ETIMEDOUTs were logged over 24 hours, with 3 occurring within 1.2 seconds of each other at 13:40. Timeouts are non-fatal by design — they do not corrupt the index; subsequent invocations succeed once contention clears.\n- **Silent `exit 1` (2026-06-13):** a separate failure class from ETIMEDOUTs; one silent `exit 1` with no surviving diagnostic output was observed. The cause is unknown. This failure class is harder to diagnose because no error text is preserved; if recurring, it warrants adding stderr capture to the hook script.\n- **Python path-capture staleness affects standard venvs too (2026-06-17):** the same failure class that breaks memsearch.exe (Python path captured at creation time, becomes stale when the installation moves) also affects standard Python `.venv` environments. The `morning-briefing` pipeline's `.venv` was broken from 2026-06-12 because its `pyvenv.cfg` referenced `C:\\Python314`, which no longer existed after a Python version migration. The fix is identical in structure: rebuild the venv against the current Python (`python -m venv .venv && pip install -r requirements.txt`). Any Python tool with a captured environment path — whether a compiled binary or a standard venv — becomes non-functional when the referenced Python installation is removed.\n\n## Details\n\nThe Python shebang path problem in memsearch represents a distinct class of tool-configuration staleness from environment-variable and PATH issues. Unlike `setx` propagation failures (where a new value is written to the registry but not yet visible in running processes — see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]) or Task Scheduler PATH omissions (where the system spawns a process without the user's PATH — see [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]), the memsearch issue lives in the tool's own binary: a specific file path was captured at install time and embedded in the executable. When that path ceases to exist, the binary fails at startup regardless of what the current environment looks like. The diagnostic fingerprint is: `memsearch.exe` appears to exist, its location is on PATH, but running it produces errors about Python or interpreter paths. The correct remediation is reinstallation — not PATH configuration or environment variable adjustment — because the problem is inside the binary, not in the environment surrounding it.\n\nThe flush patch is a memsearch modification specific to the Claude Code integration: it wires memsearch into the Stop hook workflow so that each conversation turn's memory captures are immediately indexed as new chunks without requiring a manual re-index command. The patch must be re-applied after any reinstallation because reinstalling memsearch produces a fresh, unmodified binary. The durable practice for maintaining patched tools is: (1) document the patch in a known location so it is not forgotten, (2) reinstall cleanly, (3) re-apply the documented patch. The 805-chunk count after recovery confirms all previously-indexed Tier A files were successfully re-ingested — a full re-index (rather than an incremental one) is the safest recovery approach, as partial re-indexing after a broken state risks inconsistent or duplicate chunks.\n\nThe 2026-06-13 ETIMEDOUT contention pattern reflects an architectural constraint: memsearch maintains an exclusive lock on its index file during writes. When multiple concurrent Claude Code sessions — or the primary session plus background jobs like the memory-compiler flush — all attempt to write to the index within the same narrow window, lock contention produces ETIMEDOUTs in the losing processes. Because the failures are non-fatal by design, occasional contention under normal multi-session usage is acceptable. If the rate increases significantly, the mitigation is to stagger memsearch-dependent hooks using a random jitter or backoff strategy in the hook script rather than allowing simultaneous blind invocations.\n\nThe 2026-06-17 morning-briefing venv failure generalizes the Python path-capture staleness to a broader class. Both memsearch.exe (compiled binary with embedded interpreter path) and a standard `.venv` (directory with `pyvenv.cfg` containing `home = C:\\Python314`) become non-functional when `C:\\Python314` is removed. The difference is only in where the captured path lives: inside a compiled binary vs. in a plain-text configuration file. The detection pattern is the same — the tool appears to exist but fails to start, with error messages referencing a Python path that no longer exists — and the fix is the same: rebuild the environment against the current Python installation. On 2026-06-17, the `morning-briefing` venv had been silently broken since 2026-06-12, meaning the pipeline had not been running for 5 days. The rebuild confirmed the pipeline resumed correctly with all sections populated. Any Python-based tool installed before a Python version migration should be audited for venv/binary path staleness immediately after the migration, rather than waiting for a silent failure to surface during use.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The three-tier memory architecture that memsearch serves: Tier A project-specific files are described as \"cross-project searchable via memsearch,\" and the explicit-paths requirement in the `index` command determines which Tier A files are actually indexed and retrievable.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — The broader discipline of maintaining Claude Code's tooling environment; the memsearch reinstall is a maintenance operation in the same class as plugin cache migrations and MCP re-authentication resolutions documented there.\n- [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] — A related class of tool-configuration staleness where a value is captured at a point in time and does not update when the system changes; the mechanism differs (shebang path vs. environment snapshot) but the failure pattern is structurally identical.\n- [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]] — The morning briefing system whose Python pipeline's `.venv` was broken by the same Python path-capture staleness class documented here; the venv rebuild was part of a broader loose-ends session that also added the `GwsSection` module and committed design documentation.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-11.md]] — Memsearch failure diagnosis and recovery session (16:53): root cause identified as stale hardcoded Python path left by migration, reinstall + flush-patch re-apply + shim replacement completed, 805 chunks confirmed indexed, explicit-paths requirement for `index` command documented.\n- [[daily/2026-06-13.md]] — Concurrent contention characterization (17:26 Memory Flush): 6 ETIMEDOUTs + 1 silent exit 1 over 24h, 3 ETIMEDOUTs within 1.2s at 13:40 identified as concurrent sessions/background jobs contending for the same index; timeouts confirmed non-fatal.\n- [[daily/2026-06-17.md]] — morning-briefing `.venv` broken since 2026-06-12 (referenced `C:\\Python314`, since removed); venv rebuilt against current Python, pipeline confirmed running end-to-end; generalizes Python path-capture staleness from memsearch.exe (compiled binary) to standard `.venv` environments (pyvenv.cfg).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Model-Agnostic Repo Setup: Dual Context Files (CLAUDE.md + AGENTS.md)\"\naliases: [AGENTS.md dual file, CLAUDE.md dual file, model-agnostic repo, Codex handoff checklist, pre-commit sync hook, hooksPath, import approach docs, PLATFORMS.md, CLAUDE.md import pointer, mirror approach docs, @AGENTS.md stub, root CLAUDE.md consolidation, hook-enforced mirror, untracked files worktree caveat, AGENTS.md routing table, thin adapter model files, multi-model routing table, GEMINI.md adapter, one-hop routing table, three-model adapter]\ntags: [claude-code, tooling, git, codex, openai, workflow, configuration, multi-model]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-22.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-05-26.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-05-28.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-02.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-11.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-22\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Model-Agnostic Repo Setup: Dual Context Files (CLAUDE.md + AGENTS.md)\n\nOn 2026-05-22, the FaceComps repo was configured to work with both Claude Code and OpenAI Codex by maintaining two standalone context files — `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` — backed by a tracked pre-commit hook that blocks commits when the files diverge (the \"mirror approach\"). On 2026-05-26, a different approach was recommended: treating `AGENTS.md` as the single source of truth with `CLAUDE.md` as an `@import` pointer (the \"import approach\"), explicitly allowing the files to diverge with tool-specific content, and retiring the mirror divergence hook in favor of a planned `PLATFORMS.md` switching guide. On 2026-05-28, the import approach was applied concretely to the Baylor Load Simulator root: the root `CLAUDE.md`, which had lagged as a parallel copy of `AGENTS.md`, was collapsed to a one-line `@AGENTS.md` stub — matching the pattern already in use under the `simulator/` subdirectory. On 2026-06-02, working in the FaceComps repo confirmed a critical constraint: when a repo's pre-commit hook **enforces** byte-identity via staged blob hash comparison, the import pattern is structurally incompatible — the hook contract is non-negotiable and overrides the preference framework. On 2026-06-11, the KeystoneOS project established the mature form of the import approach for multi-model repositories: `AGENTS.md` as a canonical **one-hop routing table** with `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` as thin adapters that defer to it for all shared project context.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Mirror approach (2026-05-22):** `AGENTS.md` is a full standalone copy of `CLAUDE.md`; a tracked `.githooks/pre-commit` hook blocks commits when the two files have diverged (detected via staged blob hash comparison). Activate on each fresh clone with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`; bypass intentionally with `--no-verify`. Commits shipped to `origin/main` on 2026-05-22: `AGENTS.md` (`d9ee159`), `.gitignore` update (`46ffec9`), pre-commit hook (`2e57390`).\n- **Import approach (2026-05-26):** `AGENTS.md` is the single source of truth for shared project context; `CLAUDE.md` contains an `@import` pointer to `AGENTS.md` plus Claude Code-specific annotations (hook event names, skill syntax, MCP references). A `PLATFORMS.md` switching guide explains which file each tool reads and how to hand off between Claude Code and Codex. The pre-commit mirror hook is retired because the two files are expected to legitimately differ.\n- **Root stub consolidation (2026-05-28):** In the Baylor Load Simulator repo, `simulator/CLAUDE.md` already used the import approach (pointing to `simulator/AGENTS.md`), but the repo root `CLAUDE.md` had silently diverged into a full parallel copy of root `AGENTS.md`. This was collapsed to a single one-line `@AGENTS.md` stub. The lesson: in monorepos with subdirectories, every `CLAUDE.md` instance — root and subdirectory alike — must consistently use the chosen approach; a lagging parallel copy creates the same drift hazard as the mirror approach without the protection of the pre-commit divergence hook.\n- **Hook-enforced mirror (2026-06-02, FaceComps):** When a pre-commit hook enforces byte-identical `CLAUDE.md` = `AGENTS.md` via staged blob hash comparison, the import pattern is structurally incompatible — a one-line `@AGENTS.md` stub will always fail the hash check against a full `AGENTS.md`. In such repos, the mirror pattern is the only viable option and the hook contract takes precedence over the preference framework. The FaceComps repo reconciled both files to byte-identical mirrors (`commit 8815925`) for exactly this reason.\n- **One-hop routing table for multi-model repos (2026-06-11):** In a repository targeting multiple AI model ecosystems (e.g., both Claude Code's `CLAUDE.md` and Gemini's `GEMINI.md`), `AGENTS.md` serves as a canonical one-hop routing table — all model-specific project questions resolve by reading `AGENTS.md` plus the appropriate thin adapter file. `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` become minimal wrapper files containing only tool-specific syntax and invocation conventions; all shared project context is centralized in `AGENTS.md`. This is the import approach taken to its logical conclusion for multi-model repositories.\n- **Pre-commit hook behavior detail:** the `.githooks/pre-commit` hook compares *staged blob hashes* of `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`, not working-tree bytes. When editing either file, both must be staged simultaneously before committing, or the hook will block the commit on a false-positive divergence.\n- **Untracked-files caveat for worktree isolation:** when a repo contains important untracked source-data directories (e.g., FaceComps's `SourceFaces/SCRIPTS/`), working directly on `main` may be preferable to a worktree because those untracked files would be absent in a fresh worktree. Worktree isolation should be skipped when the work requires access to untracked files that cannot be brought into the worktree.\n- **When to use which approach:** use the mirror approach when the two files will be semantically identical (same instructions, different filenames, full compatibility required), or when a pre-commit hook enforces byte-identity; use the import approach when the files are expected to legitimately diverge with tool-specific content and no enforcement hook exists; use the one-hop routing table when the repo targets three or more model ecosystems and centralized routing clarity is the primary goal.\n- **Pre-handoff checklist for Codex:** before switching from Claude Code to OpenAI Codex on the same task, verify: branch is clean, `origin` is in sync, `AGENTS.md` is present and current, any required hook is configured, `.env.local` exists, and the Codex CLI is installed.\n\n## Details\n\nThe mirror approach (2026-05-22) reflects the starting assumption that Claude Code and Codex need identical context — same instructions, same project documentation — with only the filename differing per tool convention. Standalone copies were chosen over `@include` or symlinks because tool-specific include syntax is not standardized: a Claude Code `@import` pointer that Claude Code resolves correctly may be invisible to Codex or a future agent runtime, while a symlink requires filesystem support that may not exist in all environments. The pre-commit hook provides a continuous integration check at the commit boundary, making divergence a locally-caught error rather than silent drift. Because the hook lives in a tracked `.githooks/` directory, it is part of the repo's history and available to all contributors. The `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` activation step is a one-time setup on each new clone; both `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` should document this requirement.\n\nThe import approach (2026-05-26) acknowledges that `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` are expected to diverge as tooling matures: Claude Code-specific annotations (hook event names, skill invocation syntax, MCP tool references) are meaningless to Codex, and Codex-specific task framing (step-by-step output constraints, sandbox restrictions) may not belong in the Claude Code context file. Rather than a mirror that enforces identity, the import approach designates `AGENTS.md` as the canonical document and makes `CLAUDE.md` a pointer-plus-extensions file. This removes the need for a divergence-checking hook (the files are allowed to differ by design) and moves cross-platform guidance into an explicit `PLATFORMS.md` document.\n\nThe 2026-05-28 application of the import approach to the Baylor Load Simulator root reveals a subtle real-world drift risk: the `simulator/` subdirectory had already adopted the import pattern (its own `CLAUDE.md` was a one-line stub pointing to `simulator/AGENTS.md`), but the repo root's `CLAUDE.md` had not been updated to match and had grown into a full duplicate of root `AGENTS.md`. Because the mirror approach's pre-commit hook was not active in this repo, there was no automated check to catch the divergence — any hand-edit to one file would silently break the cross-tool handoff without warning. Collapsing the root `CLAUDE.md` to a `@AGENTS.md` stub eliminates this hidden risk and makes the repo's context-file pattern consistent at every level. The practical rule: when adopting the import approach, perform an audit of every `CLAUDE.md` in the repo (root and subdirectory) to ensure all instances use the stub form before assuming the pattern is fully applied.\n\nThe 2026-06-02 FaceComps session produced a fourth case that closes an implicit gap in the mirror/import preference framework: what happens when a pre-commit hook *enforces* byte-identity rather than merely recommending it? In FaceComps, the `.githooks/pre-commit` hook compares staged blob hashes of `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` and blocks commits when they diverge. A one-line `@AGENTS.md` import stub produces a blob hash that is categorically different from the full `AGENTS.md` blob — the hook would reject every commit on the branch. Reconciling both files to byte-identical mirrors (`commit 8815925`) was the only way to satisfy the hook contract. This case also surfaced a related worktree consideration: FaceComps has untracked source-data files in `SourceFaces/SCRIPTS/` that are essential to the active work but would be absent in a fresh worktree. Working directly on `main` (authorized by the user) was the pragmatic response; worktree isolation is appropriate when the branch can stand alone, but not when the work depends on untracked files that live only in the main working tree.\n\nThe 2026-06-11 KeystoneOS session established the most advanced form of the import approach: the one-hop routing table. In a repository serving three or more model ecosystems, the import approach's \"AGENTS.md as source of truth\" framing gains a more operational name — a routing table — because the primary design goal is not merely correctness but navigational efficiency. Any model opening the repository for the first time should be able to resolve every context question (project structure, active files, conventions, active projects) in exactly two reads: AGENTS.md (the routing table) and its own adapter file (CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md). The \"10 cold-agent routing questions\" validation performed on 2026-06-11 operationalized this standard: ten representative questions were posed from a cold-agent starting state, and each resolved correctly in two file reads. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md were reduced to thin adapters containing only the tool-specific invocation syntax (hook event names for Claude Code; Gemini-specific model configuration for Gemini) while all project context, active project list, and routing logic moved to AGENTS.md. This also means that improving project routing — adding a new project, updating a project description, adding a cross-project relationship — requires editing only AGENTS.md rather than keeping multiple adapter files in sync.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-worktree-gotchas]] — The `.claude/worktrees/` gitignore addition was motivated in part by the `ExitWorktree remove` orphan-commit behavior documented there; both gotchas surfaced in the same 2026-05-22 session.\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-fall-camp-mode]] — The 2026-05-26 simulator session where the import 2026-05-21, a design spec for an automated morning email briefing system was written and committed to `Desktop/DEV/morning-briefing/docs/2026-05-21-morning-briefing-design.md`. The system ingests email and calendar sources, distills them into a structured 6-section briefing, and delivers the result from Gmail to the user's work Outlook inbox at approximately 07:30 each morning. A durable markdown copy is saved to the SecondBrain vault regardless of delivery status. The implementation plan was started but not completed — the session hit its context-window limit mid-generation. On 2026-06-08, a full manual inbox audit validated the 6-section taxonomy against real Outlook inbox content, confirming the category distribution and the practical utility of separating FYI/newsletters from actionable sections.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Delivery config:** trigger at 07:20 so the briefing arrives ~07:30; send **from** `eric.rash11@gmail.com` **to** the user's work Outlook address (primary inbox). Silent failures that leave the inbox empty are worse than a degraded briefing.\n- **Durable markdown copy:** each day's briefing is saved to `Desktop/SecondBrain/morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` regardless of email delivery outcome — the vault copy is a non-negotiable design requirement, not an optional log.\n- **Self-review caught a spec gap:** a checklist self-review step during implementation plan generation identified that carryover items (STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS) were not being matched against today's new email threads for resolution detection — a behavioral omission in spec Section 8 that would have caused stale items to accumulate even after they were addressed in follow-up threads. The session hit the context-window limit while patching this gap, leaving the implementation plan incomplete.\n\n## Details\n\nThe design spec's graceful-degradation principle is the most architecturally significant decision in the system. Making the briefing always send *something* — even a degraded version with a banner such as \"⚠ Calendar source unavailable today\" — is a conscious choice to prefer visible, annotated failures over silent ones. A pipeline that fails silently produces no signal that something broke; a degraded briefing with an explanatory banner tells the user what the system intended and why it could not fully deliver. This framing also means the implementation must treat each source (email, calendar, carryover state) as independently degradable — no single source failure should prevent the briefing from sending.\n\nThe self-review step during implementation plan generation caught a real behavioral defect in the spec before any code was written.
