This empirical validation supports the design decision to separate FYI from actionable sections rather than interleaving them. The error manifests as a shell crash mid-command with no meaningful diagnostic output, and its intermittent nature makes it difficult to diagnose from the error message alone.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- The error message pattern is `add_item: fork failed: Resource temporarily unavailable` or a similar `add_item ... fork` heap message; the exact wording varies by MSYS version.\n- The failures are intermittent — the same command often succeeds on the next attempt — and can appear during any git operation that spawns a subprocess (diff, staging, rebase, complex commit hooks).\n- **Immediate fix:** close and reopen the Git Bash terminal window. A fresh terminal process starts with a clean memory layout, resolving heap fragmentation accumulated during a long session.\n- **Persistent fix:** run `/usr/bin/rebaseall` from a standalone MSYS shell (not from inside VS Code's integrated terminal or another application). `rebaseall` rebases the MSYS DLL stack to resolve base-address conflicts that cause heap allocation failures when a fresh terminal restart does not help.\n- **Mitigation during active work:** split heavy git operations (large diffs, multi-file staging, complex rebases) into smaller sequential steps. Smaller commands reduce the per-process memory footprint and lower the probability of triggering a fork allocation failure mid-operation.\n- On 2026-05-26, these errors influenced the decision to execute Fall Camp feature tasks inline rather than via subagent delegation, since subagent tasks involve heavier sequential git command sequences.\n\n## Details\n\nThe MSYS fork error is a class of Windows-specific failure that does not occur in native PowerShell or cmd.exe because those shells use Windows native process APIs rather than POSIX `fork()`. MSYS Git Bash emulates POSIX process creation on Windows by copying the parent process's heap layout into child processes at `fork()` time. If the parent process's heap has been fragmented by previous operations in the same session, or if the base addresses that MSYS DLLs expect to occupy are already taken by other loaded libraries, the fork-copy operation fails with a heap allocation error. This is a systemic MSYS limitation rather than a bug in any particular git command.\n\nThe `rebaseall` tool addresses the root cause of DLL base-address conflicts by reassigning MSYS DLLs to non-conflicting base addresses in memory. It must be run from a standalone MSYS shell — not VS Code's integrated terminal or a shell embedded in another application — because the rebasing process modifies DLLs that cannot be in use while being rebased. The terminal-restart fix resolves the immediate heap-fragmentation case but does not fix the DLL-conflict case; if restarts do not help after several attempts, `rebaseall` is the correct next step. In day-to-day practice, the most practical mitigation is splitting git operations into smaller steps: rather than issuing a single large staging or rebase command, break it into multiple smaller commands that individually stay within the allocation budget. This pattern also aligns with good git hygiene for other reasons (cleaner history, easier recovery) independent of the MSYS fork issue.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-worktree-gotchas]] — Another Windows-specific git environment issue (CRLF normalization and `ExitWorktree remove` branch deletion) in the same development environment; both articles document cases where Windows's git emulation layer introduces failure modes absent on macOS/Linux.\n- [[concepts/windows-git-ssh-https-rewrite]] — A prior (2026-05-13) Windows git environment fix (SSH → HTTPS URL rewrite) in the same Git for Windows / MSYS environment, addressing a different class of Windows-specific git friction.\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-fall-camp-mode]] — The project where these errors were encountered on 2026-05-26, leading to the inline-over-subagent execution choice for TDD tasks.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-26.md]] — Fork error encountered during Fall Camp feature TDD tasks (12:28); fix and mitigation approaches documented and applied.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\okr-review-facilitation-framework.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"OKR Review Meeting Facilitation Framework\"\naliases: [OKR meeting facilitation, 4-question KR frame, Target Reality Blocker Next, Eric's lean, run-of-show OKR, KR deep-dive guide, Thursday check-in rollout, leader lean practice, steering not asking]\ntags: [productivity, okr, facilitation, applied-performance, baylor-athletics, meeting-design, leadership, workflow]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-04.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-04\nupdated: 2026-06-04\n---\n\n# OKR Review Meeting Facilitation Framework\n\nOn 2026-06-04, four facilitation artifacts were built for the Applied Performance unit's first Thursday OKR check-in: an 11-slide HTML deck, a facilitation run-of-show script, a KR deep-dive discussion guide with pre-populated \"Eric's lean\" positions, and a one-page printable agenda with a live-capture notes column. The session established a repeatable 4-question frame for each KR review and a \"leader's lean\" practice that converts status reviews into steering sessions.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **4-question frame per KR: Target → Reality → Blocker → Next action.** Each KR receives ≤3 minutes in the round-robin. The frame is applied consistently across all 9 KRs to prevent any single KR from consuming disproportionate discussion time and to ensure every KR produces a concrete next action, not just a status recitation.\n- **\"Leader's lean\" positions pre-populated before the meeting:** the meeting leader walks in with a directional position on each KR's status and next-action candidate, not just open questions. This converts a status review into a steering session — the leader is stress-testing a position, not discovering one in the room.\n- **4 artifacts produced for the Applied Performance first Thursday check-in:** (1) 11-slide HTML presentation deck, (2) run-of-show facilitation script with time cues, (3) KR deep-dive discussion guide (all 9 KRs, 4-question framing + Eric's lean on each), (4) one-page printable agenda with notes column for live capture during round-robin. Artifacts placed in Staff_Meetings folder.\n- **Ownership split clarified (Applied Performance unit):** AJ owns KRs 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.3 / 2.2; Blake owns KRs 2.1 / 3.1 / 3.2 / 3.3. Ownership governs discussion accountability; Eric remains DRI on all 9.\n- **Pre-meeting verification required for two leans:** KR 1.1 (who owns the VB relationship) and KR 3.2 (Putz vs. Boyd warmth) were flagged as uncertain. Leans on uncertain facts must be verified before the meeting; surfacing a wrong lean for the first time in the room undermines the steering intent.\n\n## Details\n\nThe 4-question frame (Target → Reality → Blocker → Next action) is a compression mechanism that forces each KR discussion to produce a concrete output. Without a fixed frame, OKR reviews tend to degenerate into one of two failure modes: either the first few KRs receive exhaustive attention while later ones are rushed, or the conversation stays at the level of status reporting without ever arriving at a course-correction decision. The ≤3-minute time cap enforces discipline across a 9-KR round-robin while the consistent question sequence ensures the same type of information is surfaced for every KR — making it easy to compare KRs and identify systemic blockers (e.g., if multiple KRs share the same blocker, it becomes visible in a structured review in a way it would not in an unstructured one). The notes column on the printable agenda operationalizes live capture: attendees can write their own observations on the \"Reality\" or \"Blocker\" questions during the presentation rather than having to recall them afterward.\n\nThe \"leader's lean\" practice addresses a common failure mode in leadership review meetings: the meeting convener arrives with open questions but no position, expecting the group to converge on a decision without a starting anchor. Pre-populating directional leans — even flagging uncertain ones explicitly — converts the meeting's energy from \"what should we think about this?\" to \"here's where I'm leaning; help me stress-test or refine it.\" Leans that are verifiably correct (e.g., a KR where progress is clearly on track and the next action is obvious) sharpen the meeting's focus by allowing quick confirmation and moving on. Leans that are flagged as uncertain (KRs 1.1 and 3.2 on 2026-06-04) prompt the right pre-work: the leader verifies the uncertain lean before the meeting rather than discovering the gap in front of the group. This practice is most valuable for KRs with a clear decide-or-course-correct moment rather than KRs in a passive monitoring state.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/applied-performance-okr-system]] — The 9-KR OKR system these facilitation artifacts serve; the ownership split (AJ/Blake), Thursday cadence, and 9 Key Results are the system context for this facilitation framework.\n- [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]] — A complementary structured-interview methodology (4-question daily debrief) that applies the same fixed-question-format discipline at the individual daily level; both practices use question-set compression to prevent coverage gaps and ensure consistent outputs across instances.\n- [[concepts/project-triage-retrospective]] — The 4-bucket cold-project triage methodology applies a similar \"force explicit decisions, no passive neglect\" principle to project management that the leader's lean applies to meeting facilitation; both practices combat the drift toward ambiguity.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-04.md]] — OKR staff-meeting rollout prep session (14:02): 4 artifacts built, 4-question KR frame, Eric's lean positions on all 9 KRs, ownership split clarification, pre-meeting verification items flagged for KRs 1.1 and 3.2.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\okr-tracker-cli.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"OKR Tracker CLI (okr-tracker/okr.py)\"\naliases: [okr.py, okr-tracker, OKR CLI, PyYAML OKR tracker, OKR scoreboard markdown, YAML OKR data]\ntags: [productivity, okr, python, cli, tooling, baylor-athletics, applied-performance]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-01.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-01\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# OKR Tracker CLI (okr-tracker/okr.py)\n\nOn 2026-06-01, a lightweight Python CLI OKR tracker was built at `okr-tracker/okr.py` to support the [[concepts/applied-performance-okr-system]]. The tool reads YAML OKR data and generates a scoreboard markdown file, operating with zero external dependencies beyond PyYAML — a deliberate design choice driven by the SecondBrain vault's no-community-plugins constraint and IT policy restrictions on scheduled automation.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **YAML data + generated scoreboard markdown:** OKR state (objectives, key results, confidence scores, ownership) lives in a YAML file; the CLI generates a readable markdown scoreboard on demand.\n- **Dependency-light by design:** PyYAML-only on Python 3.14 (PyYAML 6.0.3 already available in Eric's environment) — no Dataview, no database, no web framework.\n- **Plugin-free:** deliberately avoids Obsidian Dataview or any community plugin dependency, consistent with the vault's plain-markdown design (see [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]]).\n- **Seed confidence numbers:** the initial YAML data was seeded with estimated confidence values; Eric noted these may need adjustment if estimates feel off after review.\n- **No scheduler:** the CLI is run on demand; no cron job or automated scheduler was configured due to IT policy constraints — the same constraint that kept the vault's `backup.sh` manual.\n\n## Details\n\nThe design philosophy of the OKR tracker is minimum viable tooling: a YAML file provides human-readable, version-controllable OKR state; a Python script reads it and outputs a formatted markdown scoreboard. This approach avoids the dependency chain of Obsidian community plugins — specifically Dataview, which is the natural plugin-based solution for dynamic OKR dashboards in Obsidian — and is consistent with the SecondBrain vault's intentional plain-markdown-only constraint. Because the generated scoreboard is a standard markdown file, it can be placed directly inside the vault and read without any special rendering or plugin support.\n\nThe YAML-plus-script pattern is also portable: the tracker data and generator script live in `okr-tracker/` as a standalone directory, independent of the vault's internal structure. This separation means updates to the tracker (adding new fields, changing scoreboard layout, adding trend data) do not require touching vault notes directly. The trade-off is that scoreboard updates are not automatic — the CLI must be run explicitly to refresh the generated file — but for a Thursday-cadence check-in workflow, on-demand generation is sufficient. The IT policy constraint prohibiting cron schedulers reinforces this design choice by making on-demand execution the only viable path. See [[connections/vault-constraints-shape-tooling-design]] for how this constraint propagated from vault infrastructure into both this tracker and the vault's backup script.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/applied-performance-okr-system]] — The OKR framework this CLI serves; the 9 KRs, ownership cascade, and Thursday cadence provide the data model the tracker reads and scores.\n- [[concepts/secondbrain-vault-infrastructure]] — The vault's no-community-plugins constraint directly motivated the plugin-free, PyYAML-only design of this tracker.\n- [[connections/vault-constraints-shape-tooling-design]] — Explores how the SecondBrain vault's architectural constraints (no plugins, plain markdown, no scheduler) propagated into the design choices of both this CLI and the backup script.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-01.md]] — OKR tracker design and build session (17:20): YAML data model, scoreboard markdown generation, PyYAML-only dependency, seed confidence numbers noted, no-scheduler decision driven by IT policy.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\perch-api-integration-reference.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Perch API Integration Reference (Auth, Endpoints, 1RM)\"\naliases: [Perch API, perch_ingest.py, /v3/sets, Bearer auth Perch, pct_1rm, Perch org 959]\ntags: [perch, api, sports-science, weight-room, baylor-athletics, data-pipeline]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-25.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-25\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Perch API Integration Reference (Auth, Endpoints, 1RM)\n\nOn 2026-04-25, the Perch API integration powering Baylor football's weight-room data ingest (`src/perch_ingest.py`) was debugged and rewritten after the original implementation's assumptions about authentication and endpoints proved wrong. The corrected integration completed a full ingest of 436 athletes and 12,300 set records into `data/perch.duckdb`, fulfilling the data-activation step left open at the end of [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]].\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Authentication: the `Bearer` header scheme works with Perch's API token even though the token looks truncated (63 hex characters); the `JWT` scheme - which looked like the \"correct\" choice given the token's format - does not work.\n- `GET /stats` returns empty for lift data; `POST /v3/sets`, filtered by `exercise_id`, is the correct endpoint. It paginates via a `next_token`, returns 500 records per page, and is sorted newest-first, so a sync can stop early once it reaches records before the season start date.\n- `fetch_users()` was rewritten to call `POST /v2/users` with the org's `group_id` (itself fetched dynamically via `GET /v2/user`); the response's user list is keyed `\"data\"`, not `\"users\"` as originally assumed. Baylor University's Perch org ID is `959`.\n- Exercise IDs were confirmed for the four lifts the Weight Room domain tracks: Back Squat = 1, Bench Press = 2, Power Clean = 19, Hang Power Clean = 48.\n- 1RM (one-rep max) is computed as `weight / pct_1rm`, where `pct_1rm` is a 0-1 decimal (e.g., 175 lbs / 0.854 ≈ 205 lbs); only roughly half of `/v3/sets` records have `pct_1rm` populated, so the ingest filters to those records for 1RM calculations.\n\n## Details\n\nThis session was effectively the \"probe\" step anticipated by [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]]'s remaining action item - \"first running `--probe` to verify the ingest script's API field-name constants\" before a full backfill. The probe revealed that nearly every initial assumption about the API was wrong in a specific, fixable way: the auth scheme (`JWT` vs `Bearer`), the primary data endpoint (`/stats` vs `/v3/sets`), the user-list endpoint and response shape (`/v2/users` with a `\"data\"` key, using a dynamically-fetched `group_id` rather than a hardcoded one), and the response pagination model (`next_token`-based, 500/page, newest-first). None of these were discoverable from naive assumptions about a typical REST API - each had to be confirmed empirically against the live API.\n\nOnce these corrections were made, the full ingest ran successfully: 436 athletes and 12,300 set records were written to `data/perch.duckdb` (not committed to git, per `.gitignore`, consistent with how other local databases are handled in this codebase). `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTEXT.md` were updated with the verified API details - auth scheme, endpoint paths, pagination model, exercise IDs, org ID, and the 1RM formula - and pushed to `main` as commit `5cdb51e`, so future sessions (or a fresh `--probe` run) won't need to rediscover these facts. With the data populated, the Weight Room domain's report-generation logic (built in [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]]) will activate automatically on the next report run, without further code changes. A final data-shape requirement also surfaced: `data.py` expects full exercise names in the database (e.g., `\"Back Squat\"`), not shorthand codes, so the ingest writes full names to match.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]] - The feature whose final data-activation step this API integration work completes.\n- [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] - A similarly-motivated local API reference for a different Baylor sports-tech vendor (Catapult), compiled via empirical discovery after documentation proved insufficient.\n- [[connections/api-credential-assumptions-can-be-backwards]] - Explores the parallel between this session's auth-scheme surprise (Bearer working, JWT not) and a later Catapult token failure.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-04-25.md]] - Perch API debugging/rewrite session (16:06): auth, endpoint, pagination, and 1RM-formula discoveries; full ingest run and documentation update.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\perch-weight-room-domain-feature.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Perch/Weight Room Domain Feature\"\naliases: [Perch, Weight Room domain, perch.duckdb, perch_ingest.py, report.html.j2, trend-wr chart]\ntags: [software-development, subagent-driven-development, jinja2, reporting, weight-room, baylor-athletics, perch]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-24.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-04-25.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-24\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Perch/Weight Room Domain Feature\n\nOn 2026-04-24, the final task (Task 9: HTML template) of a 9-task \"Perch/Weight Room domain\" feature was completed using [[concepts/subagent-driven-development]], closing out a full implementation that included updated `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTEXT.md` documentation and a final round of commits to Git. The intent is to let future sessions answer \"what does this file export and how do I call it?\" directly from the project docs, without opening and re-reading the source file — reducing context-window cost and speeding up session start-up when returning to an established codebase.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- A **file map section** inside `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` lists, for each key source file: the file path, its primary exports (component name, function signatures, type definitions), and usage notes (props, required arguments, return values, side effects).\n- The pattern targets files that are called frequently across sessions but rarely change structurally — candidate files are the \"integration points\" of a codebase: API clients, calculation libraries, sync orchestration functions.\n- On 2026-05-28, three Baylor Load Simulator files were documented this way: `SimulatorClient.tsx` (the React client component's prop interface), `loadCalc.ts` (the load calculation function signature and parameters), and `syncPractice.ts` (the sync orchestration entry point and its options shape).\n- This pattern is additive to the `@AGENTS.md` import stub approach (see [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]]): the stub ensures Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md`, and the file-map section inside `AGENTS.md` provides the symbol-level detail that makes re-reading source files unnecessary in routine sessions.\n- The file-map section belongs under a clearly labeled heading (e.g., `## Simulator file map`) and should be updated whenever a documented API surface changes — treating it as live documentation rather than a one-time snapshot.\n\n## Details\n\nThe context-window cost of re-reading source files in each session is non-trivial for an established codebase: a single read of `SimulatorClient.tsx` to locate a component's prop interface may consume hundreds of tokens and require the session to read several hundred lines of JSX before reaching the relevant export. A file-map entry for the same component — two to five lines listing the prop names, types, and defaults — answers the question in under 50 tokens. Across a session that touches three or four integration points, the accumulated savings can shift a modest portion of the context budget toward productive work rather than orientation.\n\nThe pattern works best for files with stable, narrow, well-defined API surfaces: data-model classes, utility functions, API client adapters, and calculation libraries are good candidates; broad page components with many internal sub-components, or files under active refactoring, are poor candidates (the map would go stale quickly). A practical heuristic: if a file has been read by the assistant in two or more consecutive sessions primarily to look up a function signature or a component's expected inputs, it belongs in the file map. The file-map section should list only the exported API surface — not implementation details, not internal helper functions — so that it remains a concise lookup index rather than an inline copy of the source. When a documented file is substantially refactored, updating the file-map entry is the same category of maintenance task as updating a `CLAUDE.md` known-gotchas section: a few minutes of documentation work that pays dividends across many future sessions.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] — The broader context-file strategy this file-map pattern lives inside: the `@AGENTS.md` import stub ensures Claude Code reads the file where the file map lives; the 2026-05-28 session applied both patterns in the same documentation pass.\n- [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-fall-camp-mode]] — The Baylor Load Simulator project whose `AGENTS.md` received the file-map section; the Fall Camp mode's `loadCalc` / `syncPractice` parameterization work (2026-05-26) is exactly the kind of session that benefits from pre-documented API surfaces on re-entry.\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] — The memory compiler's `session-start.py` hook injects the knowledge-base index at session start for a similar reason: pre-loading a compact, structured summary so the session does not need to re-read raw artifacts to orient itself.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-28.md]] — File-map addition session (14:27): \"Simulator file map\" section documenting SimulatorClient.tsx, loadCalc.ts, and syncPractice.ts API surfaces added to the Baylor Load Simulator's AGENTS.md.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\project-triage-retrospective.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology\"\naliases: [cold-project triage, 4-bucket triage, project retrospective, cold-projects-triage.html, resume/decide/done/archive, Risk_Stratification_Engine, project sprawl]\ntags: [productivity, project-management, workflow, retrospective, triage, prioritization]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-21.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-21\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology\n\nOn 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.\n- **Cold-project 4-bucket triage:** cold projects (not touched during the retrospective window) are sorted into: **Resume** (active work, blocked on a specific next action), **Decide** (uncertain whether to continue; needs a deliberate go/no-go decision), **Done** (formally closeable), **Archive/Kill** (permanently deprioritized or abandoned). The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.\n- **Triage output artifact:** `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html` — a self-contained HTML file summarizing all bucketed projects with statuses and next actions, usable offline without re-running the triage.\n- **Hottest cold project:** `Risk_Stratification_Engine` was flagged as the highest-priority cold project to resume next.\n- **Project sprawl as a recurring pattern:** the user explicitly noted difficulty maintaining orientation across many concurrent initiatives; periodic retrospectives and triage dashboards were identified as the structural remedy.\n\n## Details\n\nThe retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the \"what exists and where it stands\" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).\n\nThe 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous \"maybe later\" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the \"what was triaged\" question from the \"what should I do next\" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.\n\nThe retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were \"almost done\" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/zotero-research-library-pp-cli]] — v0.1 was declared functionally complete during this retrospective after a successful `sync --full` run cleared the broken cached version left by the prior 304 bug.\n- [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] — A complementary daily-orientation mechanism (2026-06-10 morning briefing pipeline) that provides a forward-looking daily view; the retrospective provides the backward-looking weekly view of the same \"maintain orientation\" goal.\n- [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]] — Also designed on 2026-05-21, addressing the same \"maintain orientation across many competing demands\" problem at a daily cadence rather than a weekly retrospective cadence.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-21.md]] — Retrospective and triage session (17:57): 7-day recap, 7 open loops, 4-bucket cold-project triage, cold-projects-triage.html artifact, Risk_Stratification_Engine flagged as hottest cold project.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\secondbrain-vault-infrastructure.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"SecondBrain Vault Infrastructure\"\naliases: [SecondBrain vault location, SecondBrain GitHub backup, vault not OneDrive-synced, erash11/SecondBrain, backup.sh vault, SecondBrain plain markdown, vault no plugins]\ntags: [obsidian, second-brain, infrastructure, backup, git, windows, configuration]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-01.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-01\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# SecondBrain Vault Infrastructure\n\nThe SecondBrain Obsidian vault is located at `C:\\Users\\eric_rash\\Desktop\\SecondBrain\\` and is notably **not** OneDrive-synced — OneDrive on this machine points to a separate Baylor institutional path. Three design systems were reviewed — Swiss Modern, Bold Signal, and Electric Studio — and Swiss Modern was selected based on its compatibility with a traffic-light status color system, appropriate data-forward aesthetic, and correct visual hierarchy for flag and status badges. The master template was validated across all 8 slides at both 1440×900 and 375×667 viewports, with a `box-sizing: border-box` overflow bug found and fixed during review.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Swiss Modern selected** (white background, light grid, black/red accent palette): the monochromatic base leaves the full chromatic range available for green/yellow/red status badges, which is the essential requirement for sports coaching presentations where traffic-light color conventions carry clinical or operational meaning.\n- **Bold Signal disqualified** because the preset's focal highlight landed on the yellow (Monitor/caution) card rather than the red (Flag/danger) card, fighting the intended visual hierarchy for flag-first communication. When a presentation's information hierarchy is severity-ordered, the design system's focal element must align with the highest-severity indicator.\n- **Electric Studio disqualified** because its cobalt/black/white palette claimed the \"intense signal\" visual slot that traffic-light red requires. Using cobalt for decorative active-state elements creates ambiguity: coaches and athletic trainers trained on green/yellow/red status conventions cannot cleanly read a red badge against a cobalt decorative context.\n- **Traffic-light compatibility is the primary palette constraint** for sports coaching presentations: when the core visual language is status-coded color, the background palette must not use those hues for non-status structural or decorative elements. This is a first-class design requirement to evaluate before all other aesthetic criteria.\n- **`box-sizing: border-box` gotcha**: panels with explicit percentage widths that omit `box-sizing: border-box` cause element overflow outside their container. In Electric Studio's right panel, status badges clipped off-screen; fix applied to all three preset files by adding `box-sizing: border-box` to all percentage-width panel declarations.\n- **`file://` URL mangling in browser tool**: the browser tool's URL parser converts `file://path` to `https://file:///path`, producing a broken navigation target. Use a local HTTP server (e.g., `python -m http.server`) instead of `file://` paths when serving and validating HTML slides through browser automation.\n\n## Details\n\nThe Swiss Modern design system achieves a \"calm and precise\" aesthetic through a sparse grid structure, constrained typography, and a single red accent against an otherwise white/light-grey ground plane. This restraint makes the preset unusually suitable for sports science communication: the slide frame recedes, allowing data visualizations and status indicators to carry maximum visual weight without competing with decorative background elements. The core principle — that the presentation frame must not compete with the information it presents — is satisfied structurally by Swiss Modern's minimal palette, rather than depending on discipline in individual slide design.\n\nThe three-preset evaluation process for sports presentations has a reusable checklist derived from this session: (1) identify the dominant communicative color the presentation will use (traffic-light status codes, heatmap range, team colors), (2) confirm the chosen preset does not claim that color range for any structural or decorative purpose, (3) verify visual hierarchy by checking which element draws the eye first on a representative status-heavy slide — if the answer is not the highest-severity status indicator, the preset fights the content. The `box-sizing` and `file://` URL findings are implementation gotchas that apply to any HTML slide construction workflow, independent of the design preset chosen. The `box-sizing: border-box` issue is particularly common when copying panel CSS between style blocks originally written for full-page layout contexts; the same percentage-width panel that fills correctly in a full-page layout will overflow its container inside a fixed-height slide element if the box model is not explicitly set to `border-box`. The three style preview files were stored at `.ecc-design/slide-previews/` for reuse, and the master template was committed after full viewport validation.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/athlete-monitoring-rtp-presentation]] — A conference presentation on athlete monitoring/RTP workflows designed the same day (Session 20:28), targeting a mixed sports science audience rather than institutional coaching staff. On 2026-04-21, round 7 used 10 parallel subagents to add papers with IDs 334-383 to the database. A follow-up session on 2026-04-22 resolved a set of `year: 0`/blank-data quality issues left over from earlier rounds, including two that round 7 itself had flagged.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Each import round assigns a contiguous block of IDs (round 7: 334-383, 50 papers) across 10 parallel subagents, with each agent handling a 5-paper batch.\n- Before writing agent prompts for a new round, the format/schema is confirmed against a recently-completed batch file to keep entries consistent across rounds.\n- Agents complete in non-sequential order; completions are tracked individually (round 7: agents 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 finished first, with agents 4, 6, and 10 still outstanding) before a separate \"merge agent\" consolidates all 10 batch files into `papers.json` and pushes the result.\n- The `papers.json` schema includes a `\"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE\"` marker for entries whose source PDF cannot be located on disk, used for ID 358 (a KIAA0319 genetics paper) until it was resolved on 2026-04-22.\n- On 2026-04-22, a repair session fixed 6 entries with `year: 0`/blank data carried over from earlier rounds: IDs 286 and 287 (true duplicates), 292 and 294 (unreadable filenames), 336 (a misassigned URL, recataloged from an ankle-sprain paper to Xia et al. 2024 on gut microbiota), and 358 (the KIAA0319 paper, originally blocked by non-breaking spaces in its filename) - resolving both of the data-quality issues round 7 had flagged (336 and 358).\n- A background repair agent's proposed fixes (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`) contained hallucinated author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358; these were corrected via PyPDF2 text extraction directly from the source PDFs before committing, and round 8 was set to begin at ID 384 (~319 papers remaining across rounds 8-12).\n\n## Details\n\nThe batch-import campaign works through a large backlog of football-related research PDFs in fixed-size rounds, each adding 50 papers via 10 parallel 5-paper agent batches. This parallelization lets a round's worth of extraction work happen concurrently, but it also means completion tracking has to happen at the individual-agent level - in round 7, seven of the ten agents (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9) finished before the remaining three (4, 6, 10), and the round could not be merged until all ten reported done. Once all batch files are complete, a dedicated merge agent consolidates them into the shared `papers.json` and pushes the update, advancing the repo's paper count (333 -> 383 after round 7).\n\nRound 7 also surfaced several data-quality edge cases that the pipeline has conventions for handling rather than blocking on. ID 358 could not be matched to any PDF on disk and was marked `\"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE\"` per schema rather than skipped entirely. ID 336's source PDF had a curly apostrophe in its filename (URL-encoded as `%E2%80%99` in its `driveUrl`), which prevented the file from being read - this was logged as an open issue to investigate and fix rather than resolved inline. ID 343's PDF was misnamed \"NFL Play Smart\" but actually contained an unrelated hamstring-injury paper (Vermeulen et al.), requiring the agent to catalog it under its true content rather than its filename. ID 340 (Dupont et al., on lumbar disk herniation) used a Wolters Kluwer \"in-press\" DOI format whose final form was uncertain, so it was flagged for staff verification rather than guessed at. Together these conventions - explicit \"unreadable\" markers, content-based (not filename-based) cataloging, and flagging-for-review rather than guessing - keep the dataset complete and auditable even when individual source files are problematic.\n\nThe 2026-04-22 session closed out exactly the two issues round 7 had flagged - ID 358 (unreadable filename) and ID 336 (curly-apostrophe filename/misassigned URL) - alongside four additional `year: 0`/blank entries (286, 287, 292, 294) discovered separately. The session began by discovering that a previous session's background repair agent, which had produced a candidate fix file (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`), had not actually finished its work - so the fix was resumed from scratch rather than assumed complete. Worse, where the agent HAD produced output, its proposed citations for IDs 286, 287, and 358 had hallucinated author lists despite identifying the correct paper topics; for ID 336, the agent had also proposed the wrong replacement paper entirely (an ankle-sprain study) before the correct one (Xia et al. 2024, on gut microbiota) was identified. All three hallucinated citations were caught and corrected by extracting the actual text of the source PDFs with PyPDF2 (run via Bash) and re-citing from that verified text. The session also confirmed that non-breaking spaces and curly apostrophes embedded in PDF filenames - the root cause of IDs 358 and 336's original \"unreadable\" status - break Claude Code's `Read` tool, and that the practical workaround is PyPDF2 text extraction via Bash combined with exact byte-level filename inspection rather than retyping filenames by hand.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/graphify-vault-separation]] - \"daily/2026-04-24.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-24\nupdated: 2026-04-24\n---\n\n# Subagent-Driven Development (Two-Stage Review)\n\nSubagent-Driven Development is a Claude Code skill/methodology for implementing tasks from a written plan via subagents, followed by two independent review passes - a spec-compliance review and a separate code-quality review - before a task is considered done. It was used on 2026-04-24 to complete the final task of the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]].\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Tasks are drawn from a written plan document (e.g., `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-04-24-perch-weight-room-domain.md`), with each task implemented by a subagent.\n- After implementation, a spec-compliance reviewer checks the result against the plan's stated requirements using a checklist; Task 9 passed this stage 12/12.\n- A second, separately-focused code-quality reviewer then reviews the same implementation for correctness and quality issues independent of the spec checklist.\n- On Task 9, the code-quality reviewer caught a real bug - two chart-cleanup arrays in `report.html.j2` missing a `\"trend-wr\"` entry - that had passed both the implementer's self-review and the spec-compliance review.\n- After the implementer fixed the flagged bug, the code-quality reviewer re-reviewed and passed it, completing the task.\n\n## Details\n\nThe methodology separates \"did this match the plan?\" from \"is this code actually correct and well-written?\" into two distinct review passes, each performed independently. This separation matters because a fully spec-compliant implementation can still contain bugs that the spec's acceptance checklist simply doesn't enumerate - in this case, the plan's requirements for Task 9 didn't explicitly call out every chart-cleanup array that needed a `\"trend-wr\"` entry, so the spec-compliance reviewer had nothing to flag even though it checked all 12 of its listed items. The code-quality reviewer, working from a different lens (general code correctness rather than a fixed checklist), caught the omission.\n\nThis two-stage structure is a development-process instance of a broader pattern also seen in data-pipeline work: a single review/verification pass, however thorough by its own criteria, can miss errors that a differently-focused second pass would catch. See [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]] for how this Task 9 experience parallels an earlier citation-verification fix in [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]]. Practically, the methodology produced a clean outcome for the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]]: with Task 9's bug fixed and re-reviewed, the full 9-task feature reached 26/26 passing tests across 11 commits.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]] - The project whose final task (Task 9) was completed using this methodology.\n- [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]] - Generalizes this two-stage review pattern alongside an earlier, differently-shaped verification lesson.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-04-24.md]] - Task 9 implementation and two-stage review session (17:06).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\surgery-nlp-extraction.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Surgery NLP Extraction from Clinical Notes (Two-Section Pattern)\"\naliases: [surgery NLP extraction, Section A structured surgery, Section B note surgery mentions, undocumented surgery discovery, operative notes regex, Note_Expanded surgery mining, Surgical Procedure registry, 105 surgery rows, two-section clinical extraction]\ntags: [baylor-athletics, sports-medicine, nlp, data-pipeline, python, clinical-data, text-mining]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-14.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-14\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Surgery NLP Extraction from Clinical Notes (Two-Section Pattern)\n\nThe surgery NLP extraction is a two-section pipeline for identifying surgical events from a clinical dataset that stores information in both structured records and free-text notes. The pattern was developed on 2026-06-14 as Task #4 of the Ath_Medicine project (see [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]]), extracting 105 total surgical events across 45 structured events and 60 free-text mentions. The two-section approach is motivated by the observation that structured clinical registries systematically undercount actual procedures because not all surgical events get formally coded into structured fields at the time of care.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Two-section design, not one pass:** Section A mines the structured `Surgical Procedure` and `Arthroscopic Surgery` record types; Section B mines the `Note_Expanded` free-text field. Both sections are required because the two data sources are not redundant — Section B yields events invisible to Section A.\n- **Section A (45 events):** extracts from formally coded `Surgical Procedure` / `Arthroscopic Surgery` records using regex on operative notes. Fields extractable: procedure type, surgeon name. These are events the clinical system officially documented in structured form.\n- **Section B (60 events, 44 athletes):** scans `Note_Expanded` free-text across the full dataset for surgery-related language. Output: 60 additional surgery mentions not present in the structured registry, spanning 44 distinct athletes. Several of these represent likely real surgeries that were never formally registered.\n- **Undocumented surgery discovery:** Section B surfaced probable undocumented ACL repairs and orthopedic procedures for multiple athletes not captured in the structured records. This gap is clinically and administratively significant — it documents both a documentation-system failure and provides an audit starting point for reconciling the official registry against actual clinical care.\n- **`.append()` bug fix:** the extraction script used Python list `.append()` calls followed by `.append(\"\")` to add blank lines between output sections. Bug: for the 6 calls already followed by a blank-line `.append(\"\")`, a redundant `, \"\"` second argument had been passed to the first call; for the B.2 subsection (no following blank-line append), the fix was splitting into two `.append()` calls. Always audit Python list append patterns when generating structured multi-section markdown output.\n- **Total: 105 rows, correct columns, no stray pipe characters** in the markdown table output — verified clean after bug fix.\n\n## Details\n\nThe two-section approach addresses the fundamental data architecture problem of clinical information systems: structured records capture what clinicians formally code, while free-text notes capture what clinicians actually documented. These two populations overlap but are not identical. In the Ath_Medicine dataset, the `Surgical Procedure` and `Arthroscopic Surgery` record types in the structured system represent events where a coder or clinician took the explicit step of creating a formal surgical record. The `Note_Expanded` field, by contrast, contains free-form clinician-authored text that may reference surgical history, operative findings, or post-operative status without triggering formal record creation. The gap between the two populations — 60 events in Section B not captured by Section A — represents the underdocumented surgical history of 44 athletes.\n\nThe operational significance of Section B's findings extends beyond the immediate data analysis task. When a surgery is documented only in free text and not in the structured registry, it is invisible to any downstream reporting that relies on coded records (e.g., injury registries, insurance claims, surgical complication tracking). For the Ath_Medicine project's Senior Staff annual report, using only structured records would undercount total surgical volume and miss patterns in specific athlete populations. The Section B findings are therefore not merely a data-quality artifact — they are the starting point for a targeted audit to determine which undocumented events represent actual registry gaps versus notes about prior surgeries or non-Baylor procedures. The `.append()` bug illustrates a common Python string-building pitfall in multi-section report generation: when appending both content and blank-line separators, the ordering and redundancy of append calls must be traced explicitly to avoid doubled separators or missing blank lines. The fix pattern — two sequential `.append()` calls when a content line must be followed by a blank line — is more readable and less error-prone than passing multiple arguments to a single call.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]] — The parent project this extraction pipeline serves; Task #4 context, sensitivity rules (athlete names anonymized in outbound docs), and the broader backlog sprint methodology.\n- [[concepts/clinical-note-nlp-clustering]] — The companion Task #5 NLP pipeline that clusters the same `Note_Expanded` field using TF-IDF + LSA + KMeans, operating on the same free-text data source but for discovery rather than event extraction.\n- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — Section B's discovery of undocumented surgeries is an instance of the \"step down to a more primitive, lower-level check\" principle: reading the free-text notes directly rather than trusting the structured registry to represent the complete clinical picture.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-14.md]] — Task #4 design and execution session (17:48–17:56): two-section approach designed, Section A (45 structured events) and Section B (60 free-text mentions, 44 athletes) extracted, `.append()` bug diagnosed and fixed, 105-row output verified clean, undocumented surgeries documented.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\tezino-camp-prep-spc-monitoring.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring\"\naliases: [Tezino_CampPrep, SPC injury monitoring, XmR athlete monitoring, two-tier stress model, foot-specific mechanical stress, camp prep dashboard, ADR-0001 Tezino validation, Tezino injury pattern, 5th MT fracture monitoring, consecutive July injuries]\ntags: [keystoneos, sports-science, spc, load-management, injury-prevention, data-pipeline, reporting, baylor-athletics, football]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-09.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-09\nupdated: 2026-06-09\n---\n\n# Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring\n\nOn 2026-06-09, a design grill session produced the full architecture for `Tezino_CampPrep` — an SPC (Statistical Process Control)-based injury prevention monitoring project for a Baylor defensive lineman (~290 lbs) who suffered consecutive mid-July injuries in 2024 and 2025 under the same mechanism and in the same calendar window. The session locked a two-tier stress model, an XmR-based monitoring frame with three embedded methodological traps to avoid, a retrospective-validation-plus-live-tool decision, and a Friday HTML dashboard design for staff review.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Injury pattern driving the project:** Tezino suffered a 5th metatarsal (MT) fracture on 2024-07-10 via an acceleration mechanism during a S&C session, then an eerily parallel hip strain in July 2025 under the same mechanism, exactly one year later. Both injuries landed in the June–July summer ramp window, establishing it as the highest-risk calendar zone. The project's core hypothesis is that the pre-injury training process was detectable before each injury, and can be monitored prospectively in 2026.\n- **Two-tier stress model:** Systemic tier (tonnage, total reps, ≥80% 1RM reps, player load, distance) + foot-specific mechanical tier (acceleration count/density, HSR with a threshold appropriate for a ~290-lb DT, COD/impacts, lower-body axial lifts only). Explainability is a first-class requirement — every metric needs a plain-language \"why this counts toward the foot\" justification so coaching and medical staff can interpret the dashboard without an analyst present.\n- **SPC frame and three methodological traps to avoid:** XmR individuals charts on a small metric panel, with control limits from a **healthy 2026 baseline window only**. Pre-injury 2024/2025 data zones are overlaid as shaded warning bands (not control limits), so \"tracking with 2024\" reads as an alarm rather than reassurance. Three traps: (1) setting limits from injured summers defines \"in control\" as the process that broke the athlete; (2) training load is intentionally non-stationary during a ramp, so chart ramp rates (delta), not raw loads; (3) too many ±3σ charts burn credibility through false alarms — the panel must be small and defensible.\n- **Retrospective validation + live tool, regardless of validation outcome:** both are built. ADR-0001 mandates that the retrospective validation result be reported honestly on the dashboard itself — whether the method would have flagged the 2024 and 2025 injuries in advance, or would not have. The live monitor is a single regenerable HTML dashboard, refreshed with one command, run on Fridays, staff-presentable from day one. No automation until the manual loop proves itself over 2–3 weeks.\n- **Data sources resolved:** Perch set-level data is accessible via a script reusing existing `PlayerProfiles` API credentials; the cache holds derived 1RMs from 2023-03 through 2026-04, and the raw `/v3/sets` endpoint provides set-level records — described as \"just a script,\" not a data gap. Catapult provides player load, distance, acceleration, and HSR. PFF was demoted to context layer only (snap counts framing season load entering each offseason) — it contributes nothing to the summer ramp or XmR charts.\n\n## Details\n\nThe project's core design challenge is the absence of a written return-to-performance progression plan for Tezino. In a standard SPC use case, control limits are derived from the prescribed training plan, and a chart flags deviation from that plan. Without an accessible plan, the substitute is process-change detection: limits derived from a healthy 2026 baseline window define \"the process we know does not break him,\" and any departure from that process triggers investigation — independent of whether there is a formal target to deviate from. The 2024 and 2025 pre-injury data zones are retained as overlay bands rather than discarded, because they serve a forensic function: they show what \"the process that led to injury\" looked like, making a trajectory-toward-injury visible and alarming before threshold crossing. The critical architectural decision is that these historical injured-state bands must not be used as control limits — doing so would implicitly define \"acceptable variance\" to include the state the athlete was in immediately before each fracture and strain.\n\nThe two-tier model separates monitoring into systemic load (overall organismic stress per session) and foot-specific mechanical load (stressors most directly relevant to metatarsal fracture and hip strain via acceleration mechanism). This separation is both methodologically and communicatively significant. Systemic metrics give a recovery-capacity picture; foot-specific metrics isolate \"the stress of the specific mechanism that broke him.\" Presenting them in separate tiers allows staff to distinguish \"is he globally overloaded?\" from \"is he specifically over-stressed in the mechanism we're managing?\" — different diagnostic questions requiring different interventions. The lower-body axial lift constraint for the foot-specific tier reflects the mechanical load transmission path for a 5th MT fracture: barbell compound lifts (squat, clean) load the foot axially, while upper-body or seated work does not. The ~290-lb DT classification for HSR thresholds recognizes that a high-speed running definition designed for skill positions is inappropriate for a lineman of this size — the threshold must be calibrated to the athlete's movement profile.\n\nThe grill session paused at metric panel selection, leaving a defined next-session entry point documented in `docs/grill-session-state.md`: Catapult acceleration band definitions, the appropriate HSR threshold for a 290-lb DT, which Perch lifts qualify as lower-body axial, the exact 80% 1RM cut definition, baseline window choice (what constitutes \"healthy 2026 data\"), and camp report dates. Project artifacts live in `Tezino_CampPrep/`: `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001` (validation-honesty commitment), `docs/INJURY-TIMELINE.md`, `docs/grill-session-state.md`, and extracted data in `data/`.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/keystone-os-tezino-project]] — The narrative project holding Tezino's force-plate and VALD CMJ history; the mRSI decline (0.577 → 0.407 through summer 2025) and IMTP slide documented there are the readiness indicators that contextualize the injury pattern this monitoring system is designed to prevent from recurring in 2026.\n- [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]] — The Perch API client from `PlayerProfiles` whose credentials and `/v3/sets` endpoint are reused for set-level weight room data, avoiding a new integration — described as \"just a script\" once the credential reuse is established.\n- [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] — The Catapult Connect v6 API reference documenting the GPS metrics (player load, distance, acceleration, HSR) that feed the foot-specific mechanical tier of the two-tier stress model.\n- [[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]] — A parallel Baylor sports-science monitoring pipeline (ACWR for Women's Tennis) that also builds both a retrospective analysis and a prospective ramp model; the \"build retrospective validation and live tool simultaneously, report result honestly\" design principle parallels the counterfactual-plus-actual dual-model approach used there.\n- [[concepts/baylor-fall-camp-macro-load-model]] — A complementary macro load management framework at the team level; the Tezino SPC monitoring is the individual-athlete counterpart operating below the team periodization structure during the same summer ramp window.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-09.md]] — Design grill session (18:03): two-tier stress model, SPC frame, three methodological traps, ADR-0001 validation-honesty decision, live dashboard design (Friday HTML, one-command refresh), data-source resolution (Perch PlayerProfiles, Catapult), PFF demotion to context-only, grill-state document created with next-session entry point.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\the-monitor-newsletter.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"The Monitor Newsletter (Issue 01 Production)\"\naliases: [The Monitor, Issue 01, Blake Wright Q&A, ForceDecks explainer, Research Corner, brainstorm preview server, Template A, Template B]\ntags: [newsletter, content-production, baylor-athletics, documentation, web-dev]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-22.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-22\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# The Monitor Newsletter (Issue 01 Production)\n\n\"The Monitor\" is a newsletter project - almost certainly tied to Baylor Athletics given its sports-science content and overlap with other Baylor deliverables - whose first issue, Issue 01, was in production on 2026-04-22. Outstanding next steps were left for the following session: open `issues/issue_01/issue_01.html` directly in Chrome to confirm Blake's photo renders correctly, then export the issue to PDF via Chrome's Print dialog (Save as PDF, with background graphics enabled).\n\nThe photo-rendering issue is a useful general lesson about diagnosing \"broken\" output: when Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview, the natural assumption would be a bad file path or HTML error, but the actual cause was that the brainstorm preview server simply doesn't serve image assets at all. The fix wasn't to change the HTML or path (both were already correct) but to change the verification method - opening the file directly in Chrome via `file://` instead of trusting the preview server's rendering. This \"the tool you're using to check isn't the same as the thing that matters\" pattern echoes a similar lesson recorded the same day for [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], where a background agent's confident-looking output also turned out to need a more primitive, direct verification step; see [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]]. An initial diagnosis pointing to the Python statusline script was empirically disproved by benchmarking both a Python and a Node.js implementation (~60ms vs ~65ms — both below perceptual threshold). The true root cause was VS Code's default WebGL GPU renderer, which causes tearing during high-frequency token repaints. The fix is `\"terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration\": \"canvas\"` in VS Code's user `settings.json`.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Root cause:** VS Code's integrated terminal uses WebGL rendering by default; WebGL causes visible tearing/flickering during high-frequency terminal output such as Claude Code's token streaming.\n- **Fix:** set `\"terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration\": \"canvas\"` in `%APPDATA%/Code/User/settings.json`. The canvas renderer uses software compositing that repaints the terminal holistically per frame, eliminating WebGL tearing at a minor performance cost.\n- **Escalation path:** if `\"canvas\"` does not resolve the flicker (driver/GPU-specific), escalate to `\"off\"` (DOM rendering — fully flicker-proof but does not use hardware acceleration).\n- **The disproved hypothesis:** the Python statusline script in `~/.claude/settings.json` was initially suspected because it spawns a Python process on each statusline refresh. Benchmarked cold-start was ~60ms for Python and ~65ms for Node.js — both below perceptual threshold — and statusline does not refresh per-token, only per-turn.\n- **Identify the terminal first:** VS Code integrated terminal, Windows Terminal, and conhost have completely different rendering stacks, configuration locations, and applicable fixes — confirm the active terminal before diagnosing.\n\n## Details\n\nThe investigation followed a methodical sequence that demonstrates the importance of measuring before committing to a code change. The Python statusline theory was plausible on its face — Python processes carry startup overhead on Windows, and the statusline runs a Python subprocess on each refresh. Rather than accepting this diagnosis and shipping a Node.js rewrite, the session benchmarked both implementations under matching conditions. Both clocked ~60–65ms cold-start, well under the ~100ms perceptual threshold, and critically, statusline refreshes are tied to conversation-turn events rather than individual token arrivals — making the statusline entirely uninvolved in the per-token streaming path. The Node.js port was reverted immediately after the benchmark. The investigation then correctly pivoted to the rendering environment itself.\n\nThe real cause became clear once the terminal context was confirmed as VS Code's integrated terminal (not Windows Terminal, as initially assumed). VS Code's terminal defaults to WebGL rendering, which provides good performance for static content and smooth scrolling but is known to tear during rapid, high-frequency cell updates — precisely what Claude Code token streaming produces. The `\"canvas\"` renderer replaces per-cell WebGL updates with whole-frame software compositing, which eliminates the tearing artifact. If even canvas cannot keep pace with a given system's GPU or driver, the `\"off\"` setting (pure DOM rendering) is the last resort: it bypasses all hardware acceleration and is immune to GPU-related artifacts, at the cost of slower performance in very large terminal buffers. This fix is applicable to any tool producing high-frequency streaming output in VS Code's integrated terminal on Windows, not exclusively Claude Code.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — Broader pattern of diagnosing and resolving Claude Code environment configuration issues; this VS Code GPU setting is another configuration layer in the same Windows tooling stack.\n- [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] — Another Windows Claude Code environment investigation (2026-05-13) where a confident first hypothesis proved wrong and the real fix emerged only after verifying the actual execution environment; both sessions illustrate that Windows-specific Claude Code issues rarely have obvious first-guess solutions.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-20.md]] — Flicker diagnosis, Python/Node.js benchmark, revert decision, terminal-type identification, and GPU acceleration fix applied (17:03).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\weekly-review-synthesis-workflow.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Weekly Review Synthesis Workflow\"\naliases: [weekly review, end-of-week synthesis, weekly-review vault note, dominant signal, week close-out, memory housekeeping, project triage refresh, adoption enforcement signal, Tier B near cap routing]\ntags: [productivity, workflow, reflection, memory, second-brain, obsidian, weekly-cadence, project-management]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-05.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-05\nupdated: 2026-06-05\n---\n\n# Weekly Review Synthesis Workflow\n\nOn 2026-06-05, an end-of-week close-out session produced a weekly review synthesis note, performed memory housekeeping, and flagged a stale project triage dashboard.
