Three design systems were reviewed — Swiss Modern, Bold Signal, and Electric Studio — and Swiss Modern was selected based on its compatibility with a traffic-light status color system, appropriate data-forward aesthetic, and correct visual hierarchy for flag and status badges. The master template was validated across all 8 slides at both 1440×900 and 375×667 viewports, with a `box-sizing: border-box` overflow bug found and fixed during review.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Swiss Modern selected** (white background, light grid, black/red accent palette): the monochromatic base leaves the full chromatic range available for green/yellow/red status badges, which is the essential requirement for sports coaching presentations where traffic-light color conventions carry clinical or operational meaning.\n- **Bold Signal disqualified** because the preset's focal highlight landed on the yellow (Monitor/caution) card rather than the red (Flag/danger) card, fighting the intended visual hierarchy for flag-first communication. When a presentation's information hierarchy is severity-ordered, the design system's focal element must align with the highest-severity indicator.\n- **Electric Studio disqualified** because its cobalt/black/white palette claimed the \"intense signal\" visual slot that traffic-light red requires. Using cobalt for decorative active-state elements creates ambiguity: coaches and athletic trainers trained on green/yellow/red status conventions cannot cleanly read a red badge against a cobalt decorative context.\n- **Traffic-light compatibility is the primary palette constraint** for sports coaching presentations: when the core visual language is status-coded color, the background palette must not use those hues for non-status structural or decorative elements. This is a first-class design requirement to evaluate before all other aesthetic criteria.\n- **`box-sizing: border-box` gotcha**: panels with explicit percentage widths that omit `box-sizing: border-box` cause element overflow outside their container. In Electric Studio's right panel, status badges clipped off-screen; fix applied to all three preset files by adding `box-sizing: border-box` to all percentage-width panel declarations.\n- **`file://` URL mangling in browser tool**: the browser tool's URL parser converts `file://path` to `https://file:///path`, producing a broken navigation target. Use a local HTTP server (e.g., `python -m http.server`) instead of `file://` paths when serving and validating HTML slides through browser automation.\n\n## Details\n\nThe Swiss Modern design system achieves a \"calm and precise\" aesthetic through a sparse grid structure, constrained typography, and a single red accent against an otherwise white/light-grey ground plane. This restraint makes the preset unusually suitable for sports science communication: the slide frame recedes, allowing data visualizations and status indicators to carry maximum visual weight without competing with decorative background elements. The core principle — that the presentation frame must not compete with the information it presents — is satisfied structurally by Swiss Modern's minimal palette, rather than depending on discipline in individual slide design.\n\nThe three-preset evaluation process for sports presentations has a reusable checklist derived from this session: (1) identify the dominant communicative color the presentation will use (traffic-light status codes, heatmap range, team colors), (2) confirm the chosen preset does not claim that color range for any structural or decorative purpose, (3) verify visual hierarchy by checking which element draws the eye first on a representative status-heavy slide — if the answer is not the highest-severity status indicator, the preset fights the content. The `box-sizing` and `file://` URL findings are implementation gotchas that apply to any HTML slide construction workflow, independent of the design preset chosen. The `box-sizing: border-box` issue is particularly common when copying panel CSS between style blocks originally written for full-page layout contexts; the same percentage-width panel that fills correctly in a full-page layout will overflow its container inside a fixed-height slide element if the box model is not explicitly set to `border-box`. The three style preview files were stored at `.ecc-design/slide-previews/` for reuse, and the master template was committed after full viewport validation.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/athlete-monitoring-rtp-presentation]] — A conference presentation on athlete monitoring/RTP workflows designed the same day (Session 20:28), targeting a mixed sports science audience rather than institutional coaching staff. On 2026-04-21, round 7 used 10 parallel subagents to add papers with IDs 334-383 to the database. A follow-up session on 2026-04-22 resolved a set of `year: 0`/blank-data quality issues left over from earlier rounds, including two that round 7 itself had flagged.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Each import round assigns a contiguous block of IDs (round 7: 334-383, 50 papers) across 10 parallel subagents, with each agent handling a 5-paper batch.\n- Before writing agent prompts for a new round, the format/schema is confirmed against a recently-completed batch file to keep entries consistent across rounds.\n- Agents complete in non-sequential order; completions are tracked individually (round 7: agents 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 finished first, with agents 4, 6, and 10 still outstanding) before a separate \"merge agent\" consolidates all 10 batch files into `papers.json` and pushes the result.\n- The `papers.json` schema includes a `\"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE\"` marker for entries whose source PDF cannot be located on disk, used for ID 358 (a KIAA0319 genetics paper) until it was resolved on 2026-04-22.\n- On 2026-04-22, a repair session fixed 6 entries with `year: 0`/blank data carried over from earlier rounds: IDs 286 and 287 (true duplicates), 292 and 294 (unreadable filenames), 336 (a misassigned URL, recataloged from an ankle-sprain paper to Xia et al. 2024 on gut microbiota), and 358 (the KIAA0319 paper, originally blocked by non-breaking spaces in its filename) - resolving both of the data-quality issues round 7 had flagged (336 and 358).\n- A background repair agent's proposed fixes (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`) contained hallucinated author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358; these were corrected via PyPDF2 text extraction directly from the source PDFs before committing, and round 8 was set to begin at ID 384 (~319 papers remaining across rounds 8-12).\n\n## Details\n\nThe batch-import campaign works through a large backlog of football-related research PDFs in fixed-size rounds, each adding 50 papers via 10 parallel 5-paper agent batches. This parallelization lets a round's worth of extraction work happen concurrently, but it also means completion tracking has to happen at the individual-agent level - in round 7, seven of the ten agents (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9) finished before the remaining three (4, 6, 10), and the round could not be merged until all ten reported done. Once all batch files are complete, a dedicated merge agent consolidates them into the shared `papers.json` and pushes the update, advancing the repo's paper count (333 -> 383 after round 7).\n\nRound 7 also surfaced several data-quality edge cases that the pipeline has conventions for handling rather than blocking on. ID 358 could not be matched to any PDF on disk and was marked `\"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE\"` per schema rather than skipped entirely. ID 336's source PDF had a curly apostrophe in its filename (URL-encoded as `%E2%80%99` in its `driveUrl`), which prevented the file from being read - this was logged as an open issue to investigate and fix rather than resolved inline. ID 343's PDF was misnamed \"NFL Play Smart\" but actually contained an unrelated hamstring-injury paper (Vermeulen et al.), requiring the agent to catalog it under its true content rather than its filename. ID 340 (Dupont et al., on lumbar disk herniation) used a Wolters Kluwer \"in-press\" DOI format whose final form was uncertain, so it was flagged for staff verification rather than guessed at. Together these conventions - explicit \"unreadable\" markers, content-based (not filename-based) cataloging, and flagging-for-review rather than guessing - keep the dataset complete and auditable even when individual source files are problematic.\n\nThe 2026-04-22 session closed out exactly the two issues round 7 had flagged - ID 358 (unreadable filename) and ID 336 (curly-apostrophe filename/misassigned URL) - alongside four additional `year: 0`/blank entries (286, 287, 292, 294) discovered separately. The session began by discovering that a previous session's background repair agent, which had produced a candidate fix file (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`), had not actually finished its work - so the fix was resumed from scratch rather than assumed complete. Worse, where the agent HAD produced output, its proposed citations for IDs 286, 287, and 358 had hallucinated author lists despite identifying the correct paper topics; for ID 336, the agent had also proposed the wrong replacement paper entirely (an ankle-sprain study) before the correct one (Xia et al. 2024, on gut microbiota) was identified. All three hallucinated citations were caught and corrected by extracting the actual text of the source PDFs with PyPDF2 (run via Bash) and re-citing from that verified text. The session also confirmed that non-breaking spaces and curly apostrophes embedded in PDF filenames - the root cause of IDs 358 and 336's original \"unreadable\" status - break Claude Code's `Read` tool, and that the practical workaround is PyPDF2 text extraction via Bash combined with exact byte-level filename inspection rather than retyping filenames by hand.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/graphify-vault-separation]] - \"daily/2026-04-24.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-24\nupdated: 2026-04-24\n---\n\n# Subagent-Driven Development (Two-Stage Review)\n\nSubagent-Driven Development is a Claude Code skill/methodology for implementing tasks from a written plan via subagents, followed by two independent review passes - a spec-compliance review and a separate code-quality review - before a task is considered done. It was used on 2026-04-24 to complete the final task of the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]].\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Tasks are drawn from a written plan document (e.g., `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-04-24-perch-weight-room-domain.md`), with each task implemented by a subagent.\n- After implementation, a spec-compliance reviewer checks the result against the plan's stated requirements using a checklist; Task 9 passed this stage 12/12.\n- A second, separately-focused code-quality reviewer then reviews the same implementation for correctness and quality issues independent of the spec checklist.\n- On Task 9, the code-quality reviewer caught a real bug - two chart-cleanup arrays in `report.html.j2` missing a `\"trend-wr\"` entry - that had passed both the implementer's self-review and the spec-compliance review.\n- After the implementer fixed the flagged bug, the code-quality reviewer re-reviewed and passed it, completing the task.\n\n## Details\n\nThe methodology separates \"did this match the plan?\" from \"is this code actually correct and well-written?\" into two distinct review passes, each performed independently. This separation matters because a fully spec-compliant implementation can still contain bugs that the spec's acceptance checklist simply doesn't enumerate - in this case, the plan's requirements for Task 9 didn't explicitly call out every chart-cleanup array that needed a `\"trend-wr\"` entry, so the spec-compliance reviewer had nothing to flag even though it checked all 12 of its listed items. The code-quality reviewer, working from a different lens (general code correctness rather than a fixed checklist), caught the omission.\n\nThis two-stage structure is a development-process instance of a broader pattern also seen in data-pipeline work: a single review/verification pass, however thorough by its own criteria, can miss errors that a differently-focused second pass would catch. See [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]] for how this Task 9 experience parallels an earlier citation-verification fix in [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]]. Practically, the methodology produced a clean outcome for the [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]]: with Task 9's bug fixed and re-reviewed, the full 9-task feature reached 26/26 passing tests across 11 commits.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/perch-weight-room-domain-feature]] - The project whose final task (Task 9) was completed using this methodology.\n- [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]] - Generalizes this two-stage review pattern alongside an earlier, differently-shaped verification lesson.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-04-24.md]] - Task 9 implementation and two-stage review session (17:06).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\surgery-nlp-extraction.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Surgery NLP Extraction from Clinical Notes (Two-Section Pattern)\"\naliases: [surgery NLP extraction, Section A structured surgery, Section B note surgery mentions, undocumented surgery discovery, operative notes regex, Note_Expanded surgery mining, Surgical Procedure registry, 105 surgery rows, two-section clinical extraction]\ntags: [baylor-athletics, sports-medicine, nlp, data-pipeline, python, clinical-data, text-mining]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-14.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-14\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Surgery NLP Extraction from Clinical Notes (Two-Section Pattern)\n\nThe surgery NLP extraction is a two-section pipeline for identifying surgical events from a clinical dataset that stores information in both structured records and free-text notes. The pattern was developed on 2026-06-14 as Task #4 of the Ath_Medicine project (see [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]]), extracting 105 total surgical events across 45 structured events and 60 free-text mentions. The two-section approach is motivated by the observation that structured clinical registries systematically undercount actual procedures because not all surgical events get formally coded into structured fields at the time of care.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Two-section design, not one pass:** Section A mines the structured `Surgical Procedure` and `Arthroscopic Surgery` record types; Section B mines the `Note_Expanded` free-text field. Both sections are required because the two data sources are not redundant — Section B yields events invisible to Section A.\n- **Section A (45 events):** extracts from formally coded `Surgical Procedure` / `Arthroscopic Surgery` records using regex on operative notes. Fields extractable: procedure type, surgeon name. These are events the clinical system officially documented in structured form.\n- **Section B (60 events, 44 athletes):** scans `Note_Expanded` free-text across the full dataset for surgery-related language. Output: 60 additional surgery mentions not present in the structured registry, spanning 44 distinct athletes. Several of these represent likely real surgeries that were never formally registered.\n- **Undocumented surgery discovery:** Section B surfaced probable undocumented ACL repairs and orthopedic procedures for multiple athletes not captured in the structured records. This gap is clinically and administratively significant — it documents both a documentation-system failure and provides an audit starting point for reconciling the official registry against actual clinical care.\n- **`.append()` bug fix:** the extraction script used Python list `.append()` calls followed by `.append(\"\")` to add blank lines between output sections. Bug: for the 6 calls already followed by a blank-line `.append(\"\")`, a redundant `, \"\"` second argument had been passed to the first call; for the B.2 subsection (no following blank-line append), the fix was splitting into two `.append()` calls. Always audit Python list append patterns when generating structured multi-section markdown output.\n- **Total: 105 rows, correct columns, no stray pipe characters** in the markdown table output — verified clean after bug fix.\n\n## Details\n\nThe two-section approach addresses the fundamental data architecture problem of clinical information systems: structured records capture what clinicians formally code, while free-text notes capture what clinicians actually documented. These two populations overlap but are not identical. In the Ath_Medicine dataset, the `Surgical Procedure` and `Arthroscopic Surgery` record types in the structured system represent events where a coder or clinician took the explicit step of creating a formal surgical record. The `Note_Expanded` field, by contrast, contains free-form clinician-authored text that may reference surgical history, operative findings, or post-operative status without triggering formal record creation. The gap between the two populations — 60 events in Section B not captured by Section A — represents the underdocumented surgical history of 44 athletes.\n\nThe operational significance of Section B's findings extends beyond the immediate data analysis task. When a surgery is documented only in free text and not in the structured registry, it is invisible to any downstream reporting that relies on coded records (e.g., injury registries, insurance claims, surgical complication tracking). For the Ath_Medicine project's Senior Staff annual report, using only structured records would undercount total surgical volume and miss patterns in specific athlete populations. The Section B findings are therefore not merely a data-quality artifact — they are the starting point for a targeted audit to determine which undocumented events represent actual registry gaps versus notes about prior surgeries or non-Baylor procedures. The `.append()` bug illustrates a common Python string-building pitfall in multi-section report generation: when appending both content and blank-line separators, the ordering and redundancy of append calls must be traced explicitly to avoid doubled separators or missing blank lines. The fix pattern — two sequential `.append()` calls when a content line must be followed by a blank line — is more readable and less error-prone than passing multiple arguments to a single call.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]] — The parent project this extraction pipeline serves; Task #4 context, sensitivity rules (athlete names anonymized in outbound docs), and the broader backlog sprint methodology.\n- [[concepts/clinical-note-nlp-clustering]] — The companion Task #5 NLP pipeline that clusters the same `Note_Expanded` field using TF-IDF + LSA + KMeans, operating on the same free-text data source but for discovery rather than event extraction.\n- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — Section B's discovery of undocumented surgeries is an instance of the \"step down to a more primitive, lower-level check\" principle: reading the free-text notes directly rather than trusting the structured registry to represent the complete clinical picture.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-14.md]] — Task #4 design and execution session (17:48–17:56): two-section approach designed, Section A (45 structured events) and Section B (60 free-text mentions, 44 athletes) extracted, `.append()` bug diagnosed and fixed, 105-row output verified clean, undocumented surgeries documented.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\tezino-camp-prep-spc-monitoring.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring\"\naliases: [Tezino_CampPrep, SPC injury monitoring, XmR athlete monitoring, two-tier stress model, foot-specific mechanical stress, camp prep dashboard, ADR-0001 Tezino validation, Tezino injury pattern, 5th MT fracture monitoring, consecutive July injuries]\ntags: [keystoneos, sports-science, spc, load-management, injury-prevention, data-pipeline, reporting, baylor-athletics, football]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-09.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-09\nupdated: 2026-06-09\n---\n\n# Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring\n\nOn 2026-06-09, a design grill session produced the full architecture for `Tezino_CampPrep` — an SPC (Statistical Process Control)-based injury prevention monitoring project for a Baylor defensive lineman (~290 lbs) who suffered consecutive mid-July injuries in 2024 and 2025 under the same mechanism and in the same calendar window. The session locked a two-tier stress model, an XmR-based monitoring frame with three embedded methodological traps to avoid, a retrospective-validation-plus-live-tool decision, and a Friday HTML dashboard design for staff review.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Injury pattern driving the project:** Tezino suffered a 5th metatarsal (MT) fracture on 2024-07-10 via an acceleration mechanism during a S&C session, then an eerily parallel hip strain in July 2025 under the same mechanism, exactly one year later. Both injuries landed in the June–July summer ramp window, establishing it as the highest-risk calendar zone. The project's core hypothesis is that the pre-injury training process was detectable before each injury, and can be monitored prospectively in 2026.\n- **Two-tier stress model:** Systemic tier (tonnage, total reps, ≥80% 1RM reps, player load, distance) + foot-specific mechanical tier (acceleration count/density, HSR with a threshold appropriate for a ~290-lb DT, COD/impacts, lower-body axial lifts only). Explainability is a first-class requirement — every metric needs a plain-language \"why this counts toward the foot\" justification so coaching and medical staff can interpret the dashboard without an analyst present.\n- **SPC frame and three methodological traps to avoid:** XmR individuals charts on a small metric panel, with control limits from a **healthy 2026 baseline window only**. Pre-injury 2024/2025 data zones are overlaid as shaded warning bands (not control limits), so \"tracking with 2024\" reads as an alarm rather than reassurance. Three traps: (1) setting limits from injured summers defines \"in control\" as the process that broke the athlete; (2) training load is intentionally non-stationary during a ramp, so chart ramp rates (delta), not raw loads; (3) too many ±3σ charts burn credibility through false alarms — the panel must be small and defensible.\n- **Retrospective validation + live tool, regardless of validation outcome:** both are built. ADR-0001 mandates that the retrospective validation result be reported honestly on the dashboard itself — whether the method would have flagged the 2024 and 2025 injuries in advance, or would not have. The live monitor is a single regenerable HTML dashboard, refreshed with one command, run on Fridays, staff-presentable from day one. No automation until the manual loop proves itself over 2–3 weeks.\n- **Data sources resolved:** Perch set-level data is accessible via a script reusing existing `PlayerProfiles` API credentials; the cache holds derived 1RMs from 2023-03 through 2026-04, and the raw `/v3/sets` endpoint provides set-level records — described as \"just a script,\" not a data gap. Catapult provides player load, distance, acceleration, and HSR. PFF was demoted to context layer only (snap counts framing season load entering each offseason) — it contributes nothing to the summer ramp or XmR charts.\n\n## Details\n\nThe project's core design challenge is the absence of a written return-to-performance progression plan for Tezino. In a standard SPC use case, control limits are derived from the prescribed training plan, and a chart flags deviation from that plan. Without an accessible plan, the substitute is process-change detection: limits derived from a healthy 2026 baseline window define \"the process we know does not break him,\" and any departure from that process triggers investigation — independent of whether there is a formal target to deviate from. The 2024 and 2025 pre-injury data zones are retained as overlay bands rather than discarded, because they serve a forensic function: they show what \"the process that led to injury\" looked like, making a trajectory-toward-injury visible and alarming before threshold crossing. The critical architectural decision is that these historical injured-state bands must not be used as control limits — doing so would implicitly define \"acceptable variance\" to include the state the athlete was in immediately before each fracture and strain.\n\nThe two-tier model separates monitoring into systemic load (overall organismic stress per session) and foot-specific mechanical load (stressors most directly relevant to metatarsal fracture and hip strain via acceleration mechanism). This separation is both methodologically and communicatively significant. Systemic metrics give a recovery-capacity picture; foot-specific metrics isolate \"the stress of the specific mechanism that broke him.\" Presenting them in separate tiers allows staff to distinguish \"is he globally overloaded?\" from \"is he specifically over-stressed in the mechanism we're managing?\" — different diagnostic questions requiring different interventions. The lower-body axial lift constraint for the foot-specific tier reflects the mechanical load transmission path for a 5th MT fracture: barbell compound lifts (squat, clean) load the foot axially, while upper-body or seated work does not. The ~290-lb DT classification for HSR thresholds recognizes that a high-speed running definition designed for skill positions is inappropriate for a lineman of this size — the threshold must be calibrated to the athlete's movement profile.\n\nThe grill session paused at metric panel selection, leaving a defined next-session entry point documented in `docs/grill-session-state.md`: Catapult acceleration band definitions, the appropriate HSR threshold for a 290-lb DT, which Perch lifts qualify as lower-body axial, the exact 80% 1RM cut definition, baseline window choice (what constitutes \"healthy 2026 data\"), and camp report dates. Project artifacts live in `Tezino_CampPrep/`: `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001` (validation-honesty commitment), `docs/INJURY-TIMELINE.md`, `docs/grill-session-state.md`, and extracted data in `data/`.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/keystone-os-tezino-project]] — The narrative project holding Tezino's force-plate and VALD CMJ history; the mRSI decline (0.577 → 0.407 through summer 2025) and IMTP slide documented there are the readiness indicators that contextualize the injury pattern this monitoring system is designed to prevent from recurring in 2026.\n- [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]] — The Perch API client from `PlayerProfiles` whose credentials and `/v3/sets` endpoint are reused for set-level weight room data, avoiding a new integration — described as \"just a script\" once the credential reuse is established.\n- [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] — The Catapult Connect v6 API reference documenting the GPS metrics (player load, distance, acceleration, HSR) that feed the foot-specific mechanical tier of the two-tier stress model.\n- [[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]] — A parallel Baylor sports-science monitoring pipeline (ACWR for Women's Tennis) that also builds both a retrospective analysis and a prospective ramp model; An initial diagnosis pointing to the Python statusline script was empirically disproved by benchmarking both a Python and a Node.js implementation (~60ms vs ~65ms — both below perceptual threshold). The true root cause was VS Code's default WebGL GPU renderer, which causes tearing during high-frequency token repaints. The fix is `\"terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration\": \"canvas\"` in VS Code's user `settings.json`.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Root cause:** VS Code's integrated terminal uses WebGL rendering by default; WebGL causes visible tearing/flickering during high-frequency terminal output such as Claude Code's token streaming.\n- **Fix:** set `\"terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration\": \"canvas\"` in `%APPDATA%/Code/User/settings.json`. The canvas renderer uses software compositing that repaints the terminal holistically per frame, eliminating WebGL tearing at a minor performance cost.\n- **Escalation path:** if `\"canvas\"` does not resolve the flicker (driver/GPU-specific), escalate to `\"off\"` (DOM rendering — fully flicker-proof but does not use hardware acceleration).\n- **The disproved hypothesis:** the Python statusline script in `~/.claude/settings.json` was initially suspected because it spawns a Python process on each statusline refresh. Benchmarked cold-start was ~60ms for Python and ~65ms for Node.js — both below perceptual threshold — and statusline does not refresh per-token, only per-turn.\n- **Identify the terminal first:** VS Code integrated terminal, Windows Terminal, and conhost have completely different rendering stacks, configuration locations, and applicable fixes — confirm the active terminal before diagnosing.\n\n## Details\n\nThe investigation followed a methodical sequence that demonstrates the importance of measuring before committing to a code change. The Python statusline theory was plausible on its face — Python processes carry startup overhead on Windows, and the statusline runs a Python subprocess on each refresh. Rather than accepting this diagnosis and shipping a Node.js rewrite, the session benchmarked both implementations under matching conditions. Both clocked ~60–65ms cold-start, well under the ~100ms perceptual threshold, and critically, statusline refreshes are tied to conversation-turn events rather than individual token arrivals — making the statusline entirely uninvolved in the per-token streaming path. The Node.js port was reverted immediately after the benchmark. The investigation then correctly pivoted to the rendering environment itself.\n\nThe real cause became clear once the terminal context was confirmed as VS Code's integrated terminal (not Windows Terminal, as initially assumed). VS Code's terminal defaults to WebGL rendering, which provides good performance for static content and smooth scrolling but is known to tear during rapid, high-frequency cell updates — precisely what Claude Code token streaming produces. The `\"canvas\"` renderer replaces per-cell WebGL updates with whole-frame software compositing, which eliminates the tearing artifact. If even canvas cannot keep pace with a given system's GPU or driver, the `\"off\"` setting (pure DOM rendering) is the last resort: it bypasses all hardware acceleration and is immune to GPU-related artifacts, at the cost of slower performance in very large terminal buffers. This fix is applicable to any tool producing high-frequency streaming output in VS Code's integrated terminal on Windows, not exclusively Claude Code.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — Broader pattern of diagnosing and resolving Claude Code environment configuration issues; this VS Code GPU setting is another configuration layer in the same Windows tooling stack.\n- [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] — Another Windows Claude Code environment investigation (2026-05-13) where a confident first hypothesis proved wrong and the real fix emerged only after verifying the actual execution environment; both sessions illustrate that Windows-specific Claude Code issues rarely have obvious first-guess solutions.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-20.md]] — Flicker diagnosis, Python/Node.js benchmark, revert decision, terminal-type identification, and GPU acceleration fix applied (17:03).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\weekly-review-synthesis-workflow.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Weekly Review Synthesis Workflow\"\naliases: [weekly review, end-of-week synthesis, weekly-review vault note, dominant signal, week close-out, memory housekeeping, project triage refresh, adoption enforcement signal, Tier B near cap routing]\ntags: [productivity, workflow, reflection, memory, second-brain, obsidian, weekly-cadence, project-management]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-05.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-05\nupdated: 2026-06-05\n---\n\n# Weekly Review Synthesis Workflow\n\nOn 2026-06-05, an end-of-week close-out session produced a weekly review synthesis note, performed memory housekeeping, and flagged a stale project triage dashboard. Two sequential errors surfaced and were resolved: a missing host key, then a publickey auth failure. The permanent fix was a global git URL rewrite that transparently redirects all `git@github.com:` SSH URLs to `https://github.com/`, requiring no SSH key pair for public repositories.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Plugin marketplaces that clone via `git@github.com:` SSH URLs will always fail on Windows machines without a configured SSH key pair — this is a systemic issue affecting all such clones, not a per-repo problem.\n- Two errors appear sequentially: first \"No ED25519 host key known for github.com\" (strict host checking rejects the unknown server), then after the host key is added, \"Permission denied (publickey)\" (no SSH private key to authenticate with).\n- Permanent fix for public repos: `git config --global url.\"https://github.com/\".insteadOf \"git@github.com:\"` — converts all SSH GitHub URLs to HTTPS transparently for every git operation on the machine.\n- To add GitHub's host keys to `~/.ssh/known_hosts` when native `ssh-keyscan` is not on `PATH`: use Git for Windows's bundled `ssh-keyscan` at `C:/Program Files/Git/usr/bin/ssh-keyscan`. Add all three key types: ECDSA, RSA, and Ed25519.\n- The HTTPS URL rewrite is sufficient for public repositories; private repositories requiring SSH authentication still need a proper SSH key pair configured.\n\n## Details\n\nThe two-error sequence is worth understanding because it can appear to be two separate problems requiring two separate fixes. It is not — both errors share the same root cause (no SSH credentials to authenticate with GitHub). Adding the host key to `~/.ssh/known_hosts` eliminates the first error but does not touch the authentication issue; the \"Permission denied (publickey)\" error was always going to appear once the host key error was resolved. Understanding this prevents the temptation to keep patching host key issues when the real fix is to change the transport protocol entirely.\n\nThe `url.insteadOf` git config option intercepts URL parsing at the git level before any network call, so it applies transparently to all git operations (clone, fetch, pull, push, submodule init) that target the rewritten pattern. Scoping with `--global` makes it machine-wide, appropriate when the goal is universal compatibility rather than per-repo behavior. The rewrite affects only the protocol (SSH to HTTPS), not the repository path or access permissions, making it safe for all public repositories and any private repositories using token-based HTTPS authentication. Any tool or installer that generates SSH-style GitHub URLs — including plugin marketplace CLIs, dependency managers, and IDE integrations — will benefit from this rewrite on a Windows machine without SSH keys.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-cli-marketplace-setup]] - The marketplace plugin installation session this SSH clone failure blocked; the URL rewrite was a prerequisite before `cli-printing-press` could install.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] - A later (2026-06-10) environment maintenance pass on the same Claude Code installation, resolving different configuration drift issues (plugin cache, MCP re-auth) via the same `/doctor` diagnostic workflow.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-13.md]] - Plugin clone failure diagnosis and fix session (17:19): sequential error discovery, host key population via Git for Windows ssh-keyscan, and global HTTPS URL rewrite configuration.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\windows-setx-env-propagation.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Windows `setx` Environment Variable Propagation Delay\"\naliases: [setx stale environment, Windows env var propagation, VS Code stale environment, setx registry, HKCU environment snapshot, GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN setx]\ntags: [windows, environment-variables, vscode, claude-code, configuration, gotcha]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-03.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-03\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Windows `setx` Environment Variable Propagation Delay\n\nOn 2026-06-03, while setting `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` via `setx` to resolve a Claude Code `/doctor` warning, a new terminal tab opened inside VS Code still showed the old environment — despite `setx` having completed successfully. The root cause is a fundamental Windows process-model behavior: `setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately, but processes already running (and their children) retain a frozen copy of the environment from when they were launched.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **`setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately** — the value appears in `HKCU\\Environment` (for user-scoped vars) the moment the command returns. Any process launched fresh from Explorer, `Win + R`, or a standalone new terminal window will see the updated value.\n- **Already-running processes are unaffected** — a running VS Code instance, its terminal tabs, its embedded Claude Code process, and any other child processes all inherited their environment snapshot at VS Code's launch time and cannot see values added via `setx` afterward.\n- **New terminal tabs inside VS Code inherit VS Code's launch-time snapshot** — opening a new tab does not re-read the Windows registry. The child shell inherits the parent (VS Code) process's frozen environment, not the current registry state.\n- **Fix: fully quit and reopen the parent application** — closing VS Code completely (File > Exit, confirming the process exits in Task Manager) and relaunching it causes it to spawn with the updated environment, which all child processes then inherit.\n- **Per-session workaround without restart:** use `$env:VARNAME = \"value\"` in PowerShell or `export VARNAME=value` in bash within the current terminal. This sets the value for that shell process only (not persisted to registry) but takes effect immediately in that session.\n- **Reuse existing PATs when scope matches** — on 2026-06-03, `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` already existed with sufficient GitHub scopes. Running `setx GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN <same-value>` reused that token rather than generating a redundant new PAT.\n\n## Details\n\nThe `setx` command is the standard Windows mechanism for persisting environment variables across sessions — unlike `set` in CMD (current session only) or `$env:VARNAME = \"value\"` in PowerShell (current process only), `setx` writes to the Windows registry and makes the change available to all future processes. The critical constraint, however, is that qualifier: \"future processes.\" The Windows process model gives each process an independent copy of the environment inherited from its parent at creation time. Modifying the registry does not broadcast changes to already-running processes — they continue indefinitely with their original snapshot.\n\nVS Code is a particularly common trap for this failure mode because it is typically a long-running application. A developer who runs `setx` in a terminal, opens a new VS Code terminal tab expecting to see the new value, and finds the old state naturally assumes the `setx` failed. The command succeeded — the new terminal tab's shell simply inherited VS Code's launch-time environment. The diagnostic check: open a terminal that is **not** a child of VS Code (e.g., a standalone PowerShell window launched from the Start menu or `Win + R → powershell`) and verify `$env:VARNAME` there. If the value appears, `setx` worked correctly and the issue is purely propagation to the existing VS Code process tree. The authoritative fix is to close VS Code fully and reopen it. The same failure class applies to any long-running parent application — browser DevTools, Electron apps, terminal multiplexers — wherever a sub-process's environment was determined at the parent's launch rather than by the current system state.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — The `/doctor` diagnostic session where this gotcha surfaced; the `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` requirement for the GitHub MCP plugin triggered the `setx` invocation that exposed it.\n- [[connections/hook-execution-environment-path-assumptions]] — A structurally related failure class: Claude Code hook processes launch with a minimal bash environment that does not inherit the interactive shell's PATH customizations, for the same underlying reason — process environment is fixed at spawn time, not dynamically inherited from the current system state.\n- [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] — Places this `setx` issue alongside the hook-PATH issue as instances of the same Windows process-model behavior.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-03.md]] — GitHub PAT `setx` session (~15:00): `setx` behavior explained, VS Code stale-env diagnosis, full-restart prescription, and `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` reuse pattern. Lesson saved to `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (Environment Notes section).\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\windows-task-scheduler-path-config.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Windows Task Scheduler: Full Executable Path Requirement\"\naliases: [Task Scheduler path, pwsh.exe Task Scheduler, Task Scheduler PowerShell full path, Task Scheduler silent failure, scheduled task PATH, morning cadence task path, C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe, Task Scheduler minimal environment]\ntags: [windows, task-scheduler, powershell, automation, configuration, gotcha, infrastructure, scheduling]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-11.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-16\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Windows Task Scheduler: Full Executable Path Requirement\n\nWindows Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal environment that does not include the standard user PATH. Consequently, executables must be specified by their full absolute path in Task Scheduler actions — using a bare executable name (e.g., `pwsh.exe`) fails silently, with the scheduled task appearing to run but producing no actual output or effect. On 2026-06-11, this was encountered while registering KeystoneOS's morning cadence task: `pwsh.exe` failed silently until replaced with `C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe`.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **Task Scheduler uses a minimal spawn environment without user PATH:** unlike an interactive terminal, Task Scheduler's process environment does not include directories added to PATH by user profile scripts, installer tools, or shell configuration. Only the system PATH (machine-level registry entries) is available.\n- **Bare executable names fail silently:** `pwsh.exe`, `python.exe`, `node.exe`, `uv.exe` — any tool installed by a user-mode installer — will produce a \"program not found\" condition that Task Scheduler logs as a task failure without surfacing a clear error in the UI.\n- **Fix: use full absolute paths.** Examples: `C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe` (PowerShell 7), `C:\\Windows\\System32\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0\\powershell.exe` (Windows PowerShell 5.1). Obtain the correct path interactively via `(Get-Command pwsh.exe).Source`.\n- **Diagnose via Last Run Result in Task Scheduler properties:** error codes like 0x1 (general failure) or 0xFFFD0000 (program not found) are visible in the task's Last Run Result field. A \"0x0\" success code with no observable output is the signature of the silent-failure mode where the scheduled action completed immediately without doing anything.\n- **Applies to all Windows automation systems that spawn with minimal environments:** Task Scheduler, Windows Service installers, COM servers, and scheduled CI runners share this constraint — any tool not in the machine-level system PATH must be called by absolute path.\n\n## Details\n\nWindows Task Scheduler runs under the SYSTEM account or a specified user account, but either way it launches processes with an environment derived from machine-level registry entries (`HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Session Manager\\Environment`), not the richer user PATH that includes directories added by package managers (Chocolatey, Winget, Scoop), language runtimes (Python, Node, Go), or developer tool installers (uv, cargo). PowerShell 7's installation, for example, typically adds its directory to the user PATH or a machine PATH during setup, but this entry may be a user-level registry value (`HKCU\\Environment`) that Task Scheduler's minimal spawn environment does not include. The practical consequence: any tool installed by a user-mode installer or whose PATH entry is a user-level registry entry rather than a machine-level one must be called by absolute path in Task Scheduler actions.\n\nThe silent failure mode is particularly confusing because the task reports successful execution in Task Scheduler's interface while producing no actual work. The distinguishing symptom is a task whose history log shows the action starting and immediately terminating with a non-zero exit code. The reliable diagnostic is to construct a minimal test action that writes a timestamp to a known file path — if the file is not updated after the task fires, the executable is not being found. Once the correct full path is confirmed via `(Get-Command pwsh.exe).Source` in an interactive terminal, that full path is substituted in the Task Scheduler action. This gotcha is an instance of the broader Windows pattern documented in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]]: processes spawned by the system (hooks, schedulers, services) inherit a frozen, minimal environment at creation time that does not reflect the user's interactive shell configuration.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] — The cross-cutting Windows pattern that explains this gotcha: Task Scheduler spawns processes with a fixed minimal environment determined at job execution time, not the user's current interactive shell configuration. The Task Scheduler case is a fourth instance alongside setx propagation, hook PATH issues, and GSD bash-syntax mismatch.\n- [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] — A complementary Windows environment gotcha: `setx` writes to the registry immediately but already-running processes don't see the change. Task Scheduler's problem is the inverse: even after a new environment variable is written, Task Scheduler's minimal spawn environment may not include the user PATH where the variable would matter.\n- [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] — Another tool-invocation environment mismatch where an assumed execution environment (interactive PowerShell) doesn't match the actual one (minimal bash); Task Scheduler's minimal PATH is the scheduling-system analog of Claude Code's minimal hook environment.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-06-11.md]] — Morning cadence task registration session (16:53): `pwsh.exe` silent failure diagnosed, fix with full path `C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe` applied, lesson saved to project memory.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\zotero-api-integration-reference.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Zotero API Integration Reference (Quirks and Gotchas)\"\naliases: [Zotero API quirks, Zotero-Write-Token, MultiWriteResponse, If-Modified-Since-Version, since=N, Zotero 412 retry, Zotero format=keys]\ntags: [zotero, api, research-tools, data-pipeline, gotcha, reference]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-18.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-18\nupdated: 2026-05-18\n---\n\n# Zotero API Integration Reference (Quirks and Gotchas)\n\nEight non-obvious Zotero API behaviors were identified and baked into the `zotero-research-library-pp-cli` HTTP client during Wave 4 of the tool's development on 2026-05-18. These quirks collectively make Zotero's API behave meaningfully differently from a naive REST-JSON assumption, particularly around sync versioning, write idempotency, partial-failure responses, and binary format passthrough.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- **`If-Modified-Since-Version` vs `since=N`:** the header is a conditional GET instruction (\"return nothing if unchanged\") and must NOT be auto-injected on batch fetches within an active sync run. Use the `since=N` query param exclusively for incremental sync; the header belongs only on requests where a 304 response is an acceptable no-op.\n- **Write idempotency:** all write requests require a `Zotero-Write-Token` header (a client-generated idempotency token); repeat submissions of the same token are safely ignored by the server.\n- **Partial-success writes:** the API returns a `MultiWriteResponse` when a batch write partially succeeds — some items created/updated, others rejected — requiring per-item inspection rather than treating the response as all-or-nothing.\n- **Optimistic locking on writes:** a 412 Precondition Failed response indicates another client has written since the last read; the fix is to re-fetch the current `Last-Modified-Version` and retry the write with the updated version.\n- **Format-specific response handling:** `format=keys`, BibTeX, and RIS responses must be passed through as raw bytes, not decoded as JSON; the HTTP client must detect these formats and skip JSON deserialization.\n- **File-upload short-circuit:** the upload authorization endpoint may return `exists: 1`, meaning the file is already on the server and the byte-upload step should be skipped entirely.\n- **403 vs 401:** 403 = Forbidden (access control issue, the credential is valid but lacks permission), 401 = Unauthenticated (bad or missing API key); these require different error-handling branches.\n\n## Details\n\nThe `If-Modified-Since-Version` / `since=N` distinction is the most operationally dangerous quirk because a misapplication produces a silently successful-looking failure: the sync completes without error, but zero items are written. The header tells the Zotero server \"return 304 and no body if nothing has changed since this version.\" In a sync run that starts by fetching the library's current version number (via `format=versions`), the locally stored version immediately updates to the current server version. If that version is then automatically sent as `If-Modified-Since-Version` on the subsequent batch-fetch calls in the same run, the server legitimately interprets this as \"nothing has changed since the version I just told you about\" and responds 304 — even though the client has never actually fetched the items. The `since=N` query parameter, by contrast, is an additive filter (\"return only items modified after version N\") and is safe to use within a sync run because it does not cause 304 short-circuiting. The practical rule: auto-injection of `If-Modified-Since-Version` in an HTTP client layer is always a mistake; the header must be set deliberately, only on requests where a 304 is an acceptable outcome.\n\nThe write-path quirks (write token, `MultiWriteResponse`, 412 retry) collectively reflect Zotero's multi-client, collaborative-library design. Unlike a simple single-user API where each write either succeeds or fails atomically, Zotero is designed for libraries that may be edited concurrently by multiple Zotero clients. The idempotency token prevents duplicate item creation if a write request is retried due to a network error. The partial-success response model means a single API call can have mixed results across the items in a batch. And the 412/optimistic-locking pattern ensures no client's write can silently clobber another's: the current library version must be known and asserted on every write, and any mismatch requires a read-then-retry cycle. This is significantly more complex than Catapult's or Perch's write models — see [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] and [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]] for comparison.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/zotero-research-library-pp-cli]] - The CLI tool whose HTTP client implements all eight of these quirks; the `If-Modified-Since-Version` bug was discovered during Wave 5 real-library testing.\n- [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] - A parallel local API reference for a different research/sports-tech tool, compiled for similar reasons — to capture non-obvious API behaviors (token types, endpoint sequencing, data-format quirks) before they cause failures in integration code.\n- [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]] - Another empirically-discovered API reference in this ecosystem, covering auth-scheme surprises and endpoint/pagination assumptions that proved wrong in the initial implementation.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-18.md]] - Wave 4 HTTP client implementation session (13:37): eight quirks baked in from advisor knowledge; sync bug tracing and the `If-Modified-Since-Version` root-cause diagnosis.\n\n```\n\n### concepts\\zotero-research-library-pp-cli.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Zotero Research Library CLI (`zotero-research-library-pp-cli`)\"\naliases: [zotero-research-library-pp-cli, Zotero CLI, printing-press Zotero tool, zotero sync CLI, pp-zotero-research-library, Zotero v0.1]\ntags: [zotero, cli, printing-press, sqlite, research-tools, data-pipeline]\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-05-18.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-05-19.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-05-21.md\"\ncreated: 2026-05-18\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Zotero Research Library CLI (`zotero-research-library-pp-cli`)\n\nA Zotero Research Library CLI tool, built as part of the printing-press project, was developed in waves on 2026-05-18. Waves 1–5 were completed in a single session, producing 32 source files, ~3,000 LOC, and 21 passing unit tests. The tool was validated against a real Zotero library (2,064 items, version 4500), during which a critical self-inflicted sync bug was discovered and fixed. On 2026-05-19, the working binary (`auth`, `doctor`, `sync`) was installed as the `/pp-zotero-research-library` v0.1 Claude Code slash command. On 2026-05-21, v0.1 was formally declared **functionally complete** after `sync --full` successfully ingested all 2,064 items in ~75 seconds, clearing the broken cached state left by the prior 304 bug.\n\n## Key Points\n\n- Architecture is wave-based: Wave 1 (CLI skeleton), Wave 2 (auth), Wave 3 (doctor), Wave 4 (SQLite+FTS5+WAL store + HTTP client with Zotero API quirks), Wave 5 (sync command); Waves 6–8 (search/read commands, write commands, metadata/SKILL.md) deferred.\n- The `doctor` subcommand validates connectivity and exits with code 5 on failure; a bug was caught and fixed where JSON-output mode was incorrectly exiting 0 on failure (text mode had always exited 5 correctly).\n- The SQLite store uses FTS5 for full-text search and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode for concurrent read access.\n- **Critical sync bug discovered during testing:** the HTTP client auto-injected `If-Modified-Since-Version` as a header on all requests. During a sync run, the first `format=versions` call updated the stored library version to 4500, then subsequent batch-fetch calls sent that same version as a header — the server returned 304 Not Modified and zero items were upserted despite 2,064 items existing. Fix: remove auto-injection of this header; use only the `since=N` query param for incremental sync.\n- **Recovery from broken cache:** after the 304 bug stored `last_version = 4500` before any items were actually fetched, the correct recovery is `sync --full` — which ignores the cached version and re-pulls the entire library. This step was deferred.\n- **v0.1 scope and slash command (2026-05-19):** the three working commands (`auth`, `doctor`, `sync`) were installed as `/pp-zotero-research-library` v0.1. The full printing-press flow to add remaining features requires a dedicated interactive session (~30–60 min, ~5 checkpoints) where the user is present.\n\n## Details\n\nThe wave-based development model allowed each wave's completion to be validated independently before the next wave was started, with the `doctor --json` output against a real library serving as the first live integration check at the end of Wave 3. The SQLite store's choice of FTS5 and WAL reflects the tool's design as a local-first research assistant: FTS5 enables fast full-text search across all synced items without a search backend, while WAL allows concurrent reads from other processes (e.g., a separate query process) without blocking the sync writer.\n\nThe sync bug found during Wave 5 testing is the most operationally significant finding from the development session. The HTTP client had been designed defensively to auto-inject `If-Modified-Since-Version` on all requests, intending to avoid redundant re-fetches of unchanged data. In practice, within a single sync run, this was self-defeating: once the first API call updated the locally stored library version, all subsequent calls in the same run saw that version as a header and received 304s, making the sync appear to complete successfully while writing nothing. The root cause is a sequencing assumption mismatch — the header is appropriate for \"nothing has changed since my last complete sync,\" but not for \"I am mid-way through fetching data from a sync whose version I have just learned.\" This distinction is captured in detail in [[concepts/zotero-api-integration-reference]]. The practical recovery path — `sync --full` — ignores the cached version entirely and was confirmed to work correctly on 2026-05-21 (2,064 items, ~75 seconds), formally closing the v0.1 milestone.\n\nOn 2026-05-19, rather than running the full `/printing-press zotero` flow (which produces a comprehensive CLI covering all planned commands but requires live user attendance at ~5 checkpoints over 30–60 minutes), the existing Waves 1–5 binary was installed directly and a SKILL.md was hand-authored to honestly document the v0.1 scope. The SKILL.md explicitly states which commands are implemented and refuses all others with a clear \"not yet implemented\" message, avoiding silent failures for users who invoke the full command surface before it is built. The deferred full-scope work — search, add, items, collections, tags, BBT bridge, and bib export — is planned for a future interactive `/printing-press zotero` session where the user can attend each checkpoint live. See [[concepts/printing-press-cli-slash-commands]] for the broader context of that workflow constraint.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/zotero-api-integration-reference]] — The eight Zotero API quirks baked into this tool's HTTP client, including the `If-Modified-Since-Version` / `since=N` distinction that caused the sync bug.\n- [[concepts/claude-code-cli-marketplace-setup]] — The printing-press project ecosystem this CLI is being built as part of; GSD and `cli-printing-press` plugins provide the skill/command scaffolding.\n- [[concepts/printing-press-cli-slash-commands]] — The 2026-05-19 session that registered the v0.1 binary as `/pp-zotero-research-library` and documented the printing-press workflow's interactive checkpoint requirement.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [[daily/2026-05-18.md]] — Wave 1–5 development session (13:37): architecture, test results, real-library connectivity check, sync bug discovery and fix.\n- [[daily/2026-05-19.md]] — v0.1 scoping decision, SKILL.md authoring, and slash command registration (16:53).\n- [[daily/2026-05-21.md]] — `sync --full` confirming 2,064 items in ~75 seconds, BBT backfill constraint documented, v0.1 declared functionally complete (17:57).\n\n```\n\n### connections\\api-credential-assumptions-can-be-backwards.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Connection: API Credential Assumptions Can Be Backwards\"\nconnects:\n  - \"concepts/perch-api-integration-reference\"\n  - \"concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference\"\n  - \"concepts/keystone-os-tezino-project\"\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-04-25.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-10.md\"\ncreated: 2026-04-25\nupdated: 2026-06-15\n---\n\n# Connection: API Credential Assumptions Can Be Backwards\n\n## The Connection\n\nOn 2026-04-25, debugging Perch's API integration revealed that a token which *looked* wrong (truncated to 63 hex characters, suggesting it might need the `JWT` auth scheme) was actually fine - it just needed the `Bearer` scheme instead. About six weeks later, on 2026-06-10, the [[concepts/keystone-os-tezino-project]] hit the mirror-image problem with Catapult: an OpenField token that *looked* fine (not flagged as expired, matching the expected format) was actually dead, rejected everywhere as \"Unauthenticated.\"\n\n## Key Insight\n\nBoth incidents are instances of the same underlying lesson: surface-level signals about API credentials - token length/format, naming conventions like \"JWT,\" or the absence of an explicit \"expired\" error - are unreliable indicators of whether a credential will actually work. In the Perch case, the credential's *appearance* (truncated-looking, suggesting JWT) pointed away from the scheme that actually worked (Bearer). In the Catapult case, the credential's *appearance* (valid format, no expiry flag) pointed toward \"this should work\" when it didn't. [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]], compiled the same day as the Tezino failure, captures the root cause for the Catapult side: integration tokens are shown once and are non-refreshable, unlike 60-minute OAuth tokens, so a token can look identical to a working one while being silently revoked. [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]] doesn't have an equivalent root-cause document for Perch's auth quirk, but the practical lesson is the same: when an API integration fails (or appears to require a particular scheme/format), verify the credential and auth scheme directly against the live API rather than reasoning from the credential's appearance or name.\n\n## Evidence\n\n- 2026-04-25 (16:06): \"Token appeared truncated (63 hex chars) but was valid - About a month later, on 2026-05-13, installing GSD (`get-shit-done-cc`) hit the same class of failure from a different direction: GSD generated hooks using PowerShell `&` call-operator syntax, but Claude Code executes hooks through bash regardless of platform — requiring all 9 hooks to be rewritten — see [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]].\n\n## Key Insight\n\nClaude Code's hook runner is a minimal bash process, not the user's interactive shell. It does not inherit the user's `PATH` customizations, shell functions, aliases, or shell choice (PowerShell on Windows, zsh on macOS, etc.). Any tool or installer that generates hook commands by observing or targeting the interactive shell's environment will produce hooks that may work interactively but fail silently or noisily when Claude Code fires them.\n\nThe two incidents differ in their surface presentation — one is a missing binary (PATH), the other is incompatible shell syntax (PowerShell `&` in bash) — but both stem from the same assumption failure: \"if it works in my terminal, it will work as a Claude Code hook.\" The preventive rule is consistent across both cases: normalize hook commands to their most portable form. Prefer absolute paths for binaries not guaranteed to be on a minimal bash `PATH`, and use POSIX shell syntax rather than shell-specific constructs. When in doubt, test the exact hook command under `bash -c \"...\"` in a fresh terminal (not the interactive one) to simulate the hook runner's environment.\n\n## Evidence\n\n- 2026-04-14: \"Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.\" — [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]\n- 2026-05-13 (17:09): \"GSD writes hooks with PowerShell `&` syntax (`& \"C:/Program Files/nodejs/node.exe\"`), but Claude Code executes hooks through bash — all 9 hooks needed to be rewritten to use plain `node` and `bash` commands.\" — [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] - The 2026-05-13 PowerShell `&` syntax incompatibility: shell-syntax mismatch between GSD's generated hooks and Claude Code's bash executor.\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] - The 2026-04-14 `uv` PATH failure: binary not on `PATH` in Claude Code's minimal hook environment.\n\n```\n\n### connections\\inbox-triage-and-morning-briefing-taxonomy.md\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: \"Connection: Inbox Triage and Morning Briefing Share a 6-Category Communication Taxonomy\"\nconnects:\n  - \"concepts/inbox-triage-methodology\"\n  - \"concepts/morning-email-briefing-design\"\n  - \"concepts/daily-onramp-automation\"\nsources:\n  - \"daily/2026-06-08.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-05-21.md\"\n  - \"daily/2026-06-10.md\"\ncreated: 2026-06-08\nupdated: 2026-06-16\n---\n\n# Connection: Inbox Triage and Morning Briefing Share a 6-Category Communication Taxonomy\n\n## The Connection\n\nOn 2026-05-21, the morning email briefing system was designed with a 6-section format: NEEDS REPLY, FOLLOW UPS, MEETINGS TO SCHEDULE, FORMS/TASKS OWED, STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS, FYI (see [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]]). Two days later, on 2026-04-24, [[concepts/subagent-driven-development]] applied a structurally similar idea to a software task: a spec-compliance reviewer passed an implementation 12/12, but a second, independently-focused code-quality reviewer caught a real bug (missing `\"trend-wr\"` entries in `report.html.j2`) that the spec-compliance review and the implementer's self-review had both missed. On 2026-05-21, the same principle surfaced in a planning context: a self-review checklist pass during implementation plan generation for [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]] caught a real spec gap (carryover items not being matched against today's email threads for resolution detection, per spec Section 8) before any code was written.\n\n## Key Insight\n\nIn all three cases, a single review or verification pass — however thorough by its own criteria — was insufficient, and the fix was to add a *differently-focused* second pass rather than to repeat the first one more carefully. Re-running the same check would likely have produced the same blind spot, because each blind spot was inherent to what that check was designed to look for: citation plausibility (not authorial accuracy), spec-checklist compliance (not general code correctness), or format completeness (not behavioral completeness across state transitions). The generalizable practice is to layer review and verification stages so that each stage targets a different class of failure: one checks \"does this match what was asked for,\" while another checks \"is this actually correct/true/complete,\" using a different method or vantage point for each. The three examples span scale — a data repair fix (2026-04-22), a feature code review (2026-04-24), and a design-spec review (2026-05-21) — demonstrating that the principle applies at every level of software and system design, not just in automated code review workflows.\n\n## Evidence\n\n- 2026-04-22 (10:57): A background repair agent's `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` contained hallucinated author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358 despite correctly identifying the papers' topics; The grounding decision cannot be delegated to the retrieval score; it requires evaluating whether the entry's *content* actually supports the response being considered.\n\nThis is a specific instance of the broader \"verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer\" principle documented in [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]]: the retrieval score is an intermediate layer — a proxy for content relevance — that fails in the same way a preview server fails to represent actual browser rendering, or a repair agent's confident-looking citation fails to represent accurate authorship. The score optimizes for embedding-space proximity, not for answer quality; these come apart precisely when the domain vocabulary is rich enough that topically adjacent but prescriptively empty content scores highly. The implication for any system using memsearch for knowledge retrieval: score thresholds are appropriate pre-filters (retrieve candidates above a minimum similarity), but a content-inspection step after retrieval is architecturally necessary before committing to a grounded response.\n\n## Evidence\n\n- 2026-06-12 (18:08): \"Off-library protein question correctly disclosed grounding gap despite 0.98 memsearch scores\" — the acceptance test explicitly validated that score-based acceptance would have produced a false positive for an off-library query.\n- The miss-log was designed specifically for this case: off-library disclosures are recorded even when memsearch returned high-scoring results, preserving an audit trail of cases where the score-based gate would have failed if used as the sole decision criterion.\n- Structural implication documented in `CREATING-ADVISORS.md`: \"Judge advisor grounding by entry *content*, not retrieval score\" — this lesson was elevated to a hard-won lesson in the canonical advisor guide, not merely treated as a pilot-specific observation.\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/book-advisor-system]] — The advisor architecture whose acceptance testing surfaced this retrieval-score failure mode; On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` hook setup required calling `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) because Claude Code's hook runner launches with a minimal bash environment that does not include the user's interactive-shell PATH customizations (see [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]). On 2026-05-13, GSD generated hooks using PowerShell syntax because the tool observed the user's interactive shell at install time — but Claude Code's hook executor is a bash process that does not reflect the interactive shell's type or configuration (see [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]). On 2026-06-11, Windows Task Scheduler's morning cadence task failed silently when `pwsh.exe` was used as the executable — because Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal system environment that does not include user PATH entries, requiring the full absolute path `C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe` (see [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]).\n\n## Key Insight\n\nAll four incidents express the same underlying behavior of the Windows (and general POSIX) process model: **a process's environment is determined at spawn time and does not update when the system's configuration subsequently changes.** The failure manifests differently in each case — a `setx` value missing in VS Code's terminal, a binary absent from a hook's PATH, a hook command written for the wrong shell, an executable not found by a scheduled task — but the root cause is identical. The developer changes the system state (writes a registry key, installs a tool to PATH, configures an interactive shell, installs a runtime) and expects a running or freshly-spawned process to reflect that change. It doesn't, because each process type (long-running GUI app, hook runner, Task Scheduler action) has its own frozen environment snapshot, and these snapshots can differ from each other and from the \"current\" system state simultaneously.\n\nThe non-obvious implication for Claude Code tooling and Windows automation: every layer of the toolchain has its own frozen environment at spawn time. The `setx` issue means a running VS Code doesn't see new registry values; the hook-PATH issue means the hook runner doesn't see the interactive shell's PATH; the Task Scheduler issue means the scheduler doesn't see the user PATH at all, only the machine-level system PATH. All four require the same diagnostic question — \"when was this process spawned, and what did the system look like then?\" — rather than \"what does the system look like now?\" The preventive rule across all cases: never rely on the ambient environment of a spawned process; always use absolute paths, explicit environment setup, or fully-qualified invocations.\n\n## Evidence\n\n- 2026-06-03 (~15:00): \"`setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately, but only newly-launched processes read it. New terminal tabs inside an already-running VS Code still inherit the stale env from when VS Code launched. Must fully quit and reopen VS Code for children to see the updated variable.\" — [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]\n- 2026-04-14: \"Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.\" — [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]\n- 2026-05-13 (17:09): \"GSD writes hook commands using the PowerShell call operator `&`... but Claude Code's hook execution environment is bash on all platforms, including Windows.\" — [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]\n- 2026-06-11 (16:53): \"Task Scheduler on Windows requires full executable paths — `pwsh.exe` alone fails silently; must use `C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe` or equivalent\" because Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal system PATH that does not include user-installed tool directories. — [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]\n\n## Related Concepts\n\n- [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] — The `setx` registry-propagation gotcha: VS Code children inherit a launch-time snapshot.\n- [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] — The `uv` absolute-path requirement: hook runners launch with a minimal PATH that omits user-configured directories.\n- [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] — The GSD PowerShell-syntax mismatch: hook runners use bash regardless of the user's interactive shell on Windows.\n- [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]] — The Task Scheduler minimal-PATH gotcha: scheduled tasks spawn with machine-level system PATH only, requiring full absolute executable paths.\n- [[connections/hook-execution-environment-path-assumptions]] — The earlier connection article covering the uv PATH and GSD syntax issues as a pair; this article extends that pattern to the `setx` stale-env case and the Task Scheduler minimal-PATH case as additional instances of the same failure class.\n\n```\n\n## Daily Log to Compile\n\n**File:** 2026-06-18.md\n\n# Daily Log: 2026-06-18\n\n## Sessions\n\n## Memory Maintenance\n\n### Session (01:12)\n\n**Option A — Expand the script in place (~12 min, 11 slides)**\nLonger transitions, a short opening story, extended \"live demo\" narration for slides 7–8, Q&A-style moments baked into the script.\n\n**Option B — Add 4–6 slides (~18–20 min)**\nThe current deck is tight and purposeful — 11 slides for ~5–7 min of story.
